Dumuzid's Dream|||Mesopotamian.a: Dumuzid tells his sister the dream in his own voice. In it he sees rushes and reeds, tall trees, water poured over his coals, and his shepherd's stick gone. The dream ends with overturned churns and cups, the statement that Dumuzid was dead, and a haunted sheepfold.

q.t: "A dream, my sister! A dream! In my dream, rushes were rising up for me, rushes kept growing for me; a single reed was shaking its head at me; twin reeds -- one was being separated from me.

Epic of Gilgamesh|||Mesopotamian.a: In this Old Babylonian tablet Gilgamesh reports a dream to his mother, who is described as knowing all things. He sees his own likeness in the streets of Erech, with an axe brandished and people gathered around. His mother interprets it, and the text says "Gish understood the dream."

q.t: Dream, which he reported to his mother: "[My mother,] I have seen another [Dream.] My likeness I have seen in the streets [Of Erech] of the plazas.

Atharvaveda (hymns on manas and the hear.a: In these charms, sleep is induced in a household by incantation, and the speaker asks to stay awake until dawn. Several charms address discord and anger by asking that kinsmen share one mind, one heart and one purpose, using terms such as "harmony of mind" and "harmony of heart." Jealousy is described as heart-burning and a fluttering spirit, and the charm asks that the jealous man's spirit be dead.

q.t: O sleep, put thou to sleep all people with the magic that induces sleep! Put the others to sleep until the sun rises; may I be awake until the dawn appears, like Indra, unharmed, uninjured!
The fire that is within your souls, the scheme that hath entered your minds, do I frustrate with my oblation, with my ghee: delight in me shall ye take, O kinsmen!
Same be your intention, same your hearts! Same be your mind, so that it may be perfectly in common to you!

Avesta — Gāthās, Yasna, Vendīdād, Yašts,.a: The Vendidad Sade passage in the Anquetil-Duperron edition describes what happens to the soul after death. The Dew obsesses the corpse for three nights, and at dawn the Dew Vazirefch tries to bind the soul of the Darvands. The souls of the Just cross the Tchinevad bridge and are welcomed by Bahman into the Gorotmân.

q.t: The souls of the Just will go upon this high and terrifying mountain. They will pass the Tchinevad bridge which inspires dread, accompanied by the celestial Izeds angels/divine beings.

Homer, Iliad & Odyssey|||Greek.a: In the Odyssey pages shown, Penelope's thoughts are compared to a lion's among a crowd of beasts before sweet sleep seizes her and her joints are loosened. Minerva fashions a phantom in the likeness of Iphthime, which enters the chamber and speaks to her as she sleeps at the gates of dreams. Penelope speaks of pains that irritate her in mind and soul, and she tells Telemachus his mind is no longer firm.

q.t: As many thoughts as a lion has among a crowd of wild beasts, Fearing, when they lead him into a crafty circle: So various were the thoughts of her, whom a sweet sleep seized.
Telemachus, your mind is no longer firm, nor your thought. When you were still a boy, you thought of more prudent things in your mind.

Aitareya Upaniṣad / Āraṇyaka|||Indian.a: Adhyaya 6 asks which one is the self, listing seeing, hearing, smelling, articulating speech and distinguishing sweet and sour. It names Brahman, Indra and Prajapati as consciousness, and says that all living beings are led by consciousness and established in it. A separate formula sets the breaths, eye, mind and ear each in the heart, and the heart in the self.

q.t: That which is the heart and the mind, this is consciousness, perception, discernment, knowledge, wisdom, sight, firmness, thought, reflection, impulse, memory, intention, desire, and will. All these are merely names of consciousness.
In my mind is the moon established; in the mind is the heart; in the heart is the self; that is the truth of the gods.

Taittirīya Upaniṣad (with Sureśvara's Vā.a: The commentary names the Manomaya-kosa, the mind-made sheath, as the collection of the senses, with the Manas as chief among eleven. It describes the Self as the Witness of all thoughts and perceptions, and assigns the thought "I know" to the ego, a function of the antah-karana. Brahman is said to be perceived through the vritti of the buddhi, as though hidden in a cave.

q.t: Of these eleven senses, the Manas mind is the chief, and therefore the Manomaya-kosa mind-made sheath is named after it. The mind is the chief because all other senses depend on it to function.

It is the ego—the buddhi intellect or understanding —that thinks "I know" or "I do not know." This ego is merely a function of the mind [original: antah-karana-vritti] and is the seat of pratyabhijna the faculty of recognition or identity.
The intellect is spoken of as a cave because those who have turned their minds inward see Brahman hidden deep within the intellect, even though he is surrounded by kama desire and avidya ignorance.

Hebrew Bible (Tanakh)|||Hebrew & Jewish.a: In Genesis and Daniel, dreams come to kings and to Joseph and are brought to interpreters, who are asked to tell the dream and its meaning. The troubled spirit of Pharaoh and of Nebuchadnezzar is described together with the loss of sleep. Joseph credits God with the answer to a dream, and his own dreams are told to his brothers and his father, who respond to them.

q.t: In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar dreamed dreams; and his spirit was troubled, and his sleep went from him.

Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I have dreamed a dream, and there is no one who can interpret it; but I have heard it said of you that you can understand a dream to interpret it." Joseph answered Pharaoh, saying, "It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace."
And Joseph dreamed a dream, and he told it his brethren: and they hated him yet the more.

Heraclitus, fragments (on psychē and the.a: In the passages, Heraclitus holds that eyes and ears are bad witnesses for men with barbarous souls. A fragment says that what we see awake is death and what we see sleeping is sleep. The commentator says reason is innate in the mind, that all things happen according to the logos, and that one should follow what is common. The commentator adds that the philosopher thought divine reason enters the breast through breathing.

q.t: θάνατός ἐστιν ὁκόσα ἐγερθέντες ὁρέομεν, ὁκόσα δὲ εὕδοντες, ὕπνος " (Strom. III. c. 3. p. 186. Sylb. p. 520. Pott.). "Death is what we see awake, but what we see sleeping is sleep."
Listening not to me but to the logos, it is wise to agree that all things are one.

Kaṭha Upaniṣad|||Indian.a: The Kaṭha pictures a person with understanding whose mind is held firm and whose senses are controlled like the well-trained horses of a chariot-driver. It ranks the senses, their objects, mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), the Great Self, the Unmanifest and the Person in rising order. The Soul is hidden in all things and is seen by subtle seers with a subtle intellect, and an intelligent man restrains speech and mind within the Understanding-Self.

q.t: Higher than the senses are the objects of sense. Higher than the objects of sense is the mind (manas the faculty of thought and coordination of the senses ); And higher than the mind is the intellect (buddhi the higher faculty of discernment and decision-making ).

Empedocles, fragments (perception by lik.a: In Leonard's translation, fragment 105 places thought in the blood around the heart. Fragment 107 says that men think, rejoice or grieve through the commingled elements, and fragment 106 says reason grows with the body's state. Fragment 103 states that all things think their thought by will of Chance.

q.t: In the blood-streams, back-leaping unto it, The heart is nourished, where prevails the power That men call thought; for lo the blood that stirs About the heart is man’s controlling thought.

Presocratic fragments (Diels): Parmenide.a: The doxographers report Anaxagoras as making nous the acting cause that arrived among mingled things and ordered them, with matter as what is acted upon. Democritus is reported to take the soul of the world to be nous within a spherical fire. Leucippus and Democritus are also reported to derive sensation from images approaching from in front.

q.t: For when all things were together, nous intellect/mind arrived and ordered them. All things were together; then nous intellect/mind arrived and ordered them.
Democritus supposes that the soul of the world is nous intellect/mind within a spherical fire.
Leucippus and Democritus [define] sensation [as being caused] by images approaching from the front.

Aṅguttara Nikāya|||Buddhist.a: The Aṅguttara sets out seven perceptions, among them impurity, death, impermanence and non-self in suffering, each described as developed through a mind accustomed to it. It lists nine sequential abodes, from the first jhāna through the bases of infinite space and consciousness to the cessation of perception and feeling. Sāriputta describes an attainment in which a monk has perception without perceiving earth in earth or this world in this world.

q.t: For a monk, monks, who dwells much with a mind practiced in the perception of non-self in the painful, the mind becomes devoid of "I-making" and "mine-making" and conceit regarding this body with consciousness and all external signs; it transcends bias, is peaceful, and well-liberated.

Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, reflects thus: "Form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, mental formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent." Thus he dwells observing impermanence in these five upādānakkhandhesu clinging-aggregates.

Here, friend, a monk has such perception: ‘This is peaceful, this is excellent, namely the calming of all activities, the relinquishing of all attachments, the destruction of craving, detachment, cessation, Nibbāna Extinction of defilements.’

Dīgha Nikāya|||Buddhist.a: The Dīgha describes eight stages of deliverance, in which the monk passes through the idea of infinite space and the infinity of reason to a state where sensations and ideas have ceased. The Mahā-Satipaṭṭhāna asks a monk to be aware whether his thought is lustful, free from lust, composed, distracted, liberated or bound. The Mahānidāna lists the ways declarations are made about the soul as having form or being formless, minute or boundless.

q.t: By passing quite beyond the state of "neither ideas nor the absence of ideas" he reaches (mentally) and remains in the state of mind in which both sensations and ideas have ceased to be—this is the eighth stage of deliverance.

So does he, regarding thought, continue to consider thought, internally or externally, or internally and externally together. He keeps on considering how thought is something that arises, or again he keeps on considering how a thought is something that passes away, or again he considers its arising and passing away together.

Either the soul is declared to have form and to be minute, in the words: "My soul has form and is minute." Or the soul is declared to have form and to be boundless, in the words: "My soul has form and is boundless."

Hippocratic corpus: On the Sacred Diseas.a: The author of On the Sacred Disease says the eyes, ears, tongue, hands and feet serve what the brain recognizes, and that breath reaches the brain first and gives it understanding. He links a rush of blood to the brain with fearful dreams and with the flushed face and reddened eyes of fear. Regimen IV says that while the body is awake the soul divides her attention among its faculties, and it distinguishes divine dreams, which diviners interpret, from dreams that signal bodily states.

q.t: According to these things, I believe that the brain has the greatest power in man. For this is the interpreter for us of the things that come from the air, if it happens to be healthy. The air provides wisdom to it.

But when the body is at rest, the soul, being set in motion and awake, administers her own household and of herself performs all the acts of the body. For the body when asleep has no perception; but the soul when awake has cognizance of all things—sees what is visible, hears what is audible, walks, touches, feels pain, ponders.
Now such dreams as are divine, and foretell to cities or to private persons things evil or things good, have interpreters in those who possess the art of dealing with such things.

Majjhima Nikāya|||Buddhist.a: In MN 43 the Activity of Body is in-breathing and out-breathing, the Activity of Speech is cognition and reflection, and the Activity of Mind is perception and sensation. On attaining the Ceasing from Perception and Sensation, the Activity of Speech disappears first, then Body, then Mind. The belief in selfhood arises when Body, Sensation, Perception, the Mentations or Consciousness are taken as self, as owned by self, or as containing self. The instructed disciple takes none of these positions. Another passage says mind and perception are manifold, so wholesome conduct arises from mind free of greed, hatred and delusion, and unwholesome thoughts arise from perceptions of sensual desire, ill will and cruelty.

q.t: In-breathing and out-breathing, friend Visākha, are the Activity of Body; cognition and reflection are the Activity of Speech; and perception and sensation are the Activity of Mind.

Such a person does not regard Body, Sensation, Perception, the Mentations, or Consciousness as 'self'; nor does he view 'self' as possessing these things; nor does he see them as being in the 'self,' nor the 'self' as being in them.

It should be said that they arise from perception. What perception? For perception is also manifold, various, and diverse: the perception of sensual desire, the perception of ill will, and the perception of cruelty.

Saṃyutta Nikāya|||Buddhist.a: These suttas list five faculties: physical pleasure, physical pain, mental happiness, mental distress and equanimity. Each is defined by the contact from which it is born, bodily or mental, and the five are grouped as pleasant, painful and neither. A faculty arises dependent on contact and ceases when that contact ceases; the one who feels it knows "I am pleased" or "I am in pain." In the Māra passage, mind, mental objects and the mind-contact consciousness base belong to Māra, while one without them leaves Māra no place.

q.t: Dependent on pleasant contact, a faculty of physical pleasure arises. Being pleased, he knows, "I am pleased." With the cessation of that very pleasant contact, the faculty of physical pleasure that arose, dependent on that pleasant contact, ceases and is stilled; he understands this.
What is the faculty of mental happiness? Whatever mental pleasure, mental ease, pleasure or ease born of mental contact—this is called the faculty of mental happiness.

The mind is yours, Wicked One; mental objects are yours; the mind-contact consciousness base is yours. But wherever there is no mind, no mental objects, no mind-contact consciousness base, there is no place for you, Wicked One.

Plato, Phaedo|||Greek.a: In Plato's Phaedo, Socrates says the truest part of things is approached by dianoia itself, pure and alone, without sight or any other aisthesis, because the body disturbs the psyche in acquiring truth and phronesis. The soul is described as fastened to the body and seeing through it as through prison bars. Philosophy urges the soul to collect itself within itself, since the soul sees the invisible and the senses deceive. The soul takes to Hades only its education and upbringing, and a daimon leads it to judgment.

q.t: Is the truest part of them contemplated through the body, or is it thus: whoever of us prepares himself most and most accurately to think through each thing about which he inquires, he would come nearest to knowing each one?
And philosophy sees that the most dreadful thing about the imprisonment is the fact that it is caused by the lusts of the flesh, so that the prisoner is the chief assistant in his own imprisonment.
For the soul brings nothing else with it to Hades the underworld except its education and upbringing, which are said to benefit or harm the departed immediately at the beginning of the journey there.

Plato, Republic (Book IX on dreams and t.a: Plato's Socrates distinguishes a reasoning part and an appetitive part of the soul, and asks whether the spirited part (thumos) is a third. The Leontius story shows anger siding with reason against desire. In Book IX, a person who calms the appetitive and spirited parts before sleep and rouses the reasoning part is least likely to have lawless dreams. Book VI ranks states of mind, placing dianoia between opinion and nous.

q.t: It is not without reason, I said, that we shall claim these to be two, and different from each other; calling the part of the soul with which it reasons the logistikon reasoning part, and the part with which it loves, hungers, thirsts, and is excited by other desires, the irrational and epithumetikon appetitive part, the companion of certain satisfactions and pleasures.

We have been led to speak of this at some length, but what we wish to know is this: that there is indeed a certain terrible, savage, and lawless kind of desire in everyone, even in those who seem to be moderate, but this becomes evident in sleep.

And it seems to me that you call the habit of mind of geometricians and others like them dianoia discursive thought, and not nous pure intellect, since dianoia is something between doxa opinion and nous.

Plato, Phaedrus (tripartite soul, divine.a: Plato's Socrates defines the soul as what moves itself, and so as ungenerated and immortal. He describes its form in a figure, a pair of winged horses and a charioteer. Knowledge is a recollection of what the soul saw in its journey with God, and the philosopher's mind keeps its wings through memory.

q.t: For a human being must understand a general conception formed by collecting into a unity by means of reason the many perceptions of the senses; and this is a recollection of those things which our soul once beheld, when it journeyed with God and, lifting its vision above the things which we now say exist, rose up into real being.

But since that which is moved by itself has been seen to be immortal, one who says that this self-motion is the essence and the very idea of the soul, will not be disgraced. For every body which derives motion from without is soulless, but that which has its motion within itself has a soul, since that is the nature of the soul;

The ancients, then, testify that in proportion as prophecy ( mantikē prophetic divination ) is superior to augury, both in name and in fact, in the same proportion madness, which comes from God, is superior to sanity, which is of human origin.

Xenophon, Memorabilia (Socrates' daimoni.a: In the Memorabilia, Socrates tells Aristodemus that he does not see his own soul, which is the master of his body, just as he does not see the masters of the world's orderly masses. He says the god implanted in man a most excellent psyche, which perceived that the gods exist and can remember what it has heard, seen or learned. In a later conversation, incontinence (akrasia) is said to exclude wisdom (sophia), draw men toward pleasant things, and stun their perception of good and bad.

q.t: "In the same way," Socrates replied, "you do not see your own soul, which is the master of your body. So, following that logic, it is open to you to say that you do nothing by judgment, but everything by chance."

Furthermore, it was not enough for the god to care for the body; but what is most important, he implanted in man a most excellent soul psyche. For what other animal's soul has perceived that the gods, who have arranged the greatest and most beautiful things, actually exist?

And as for wisdom sophia intellectual excellence, the greatest good, does it not seem to you that incontinence akrasia lack of self-control excludes it and drives men to the opposite? Or does it not seem to you that it prevents them from attending to useful things and understanding them, by drawing them away toward pleasant things, and often stuns their perception of the good and the bad

Plato, Theaetetus (perception, memory as.a: Socrates argues that the senses are instruments through which a single soul perceives. Perception cannot grasp being, so it cannot be knowledge. Memory is modelled as imprints stamped in the soul, and false opinion arises when the mind fits an imprint to the wrong present perception.

q.t: For it would be strange, my boy, if many aisthēseis perceptions/senses were seated within us, as if in wooden horses [an allusion to the Trojan horse, containing many hidden soldiers], and not that they all converge into one single idea form/concept, whether one calls it psychē soul or whatever one must call it, by which we perceive through these as instruments all that is perceptible.

Now when perception is present to one of the imprints but not to the other, and the mind applies the imprint of the absent perception to the perception which is present, the mind is deceived in every such instance.
and when it is stamped, we remember and know it as long as the image of it remains within; but whatever is erased or cannot be stamped, we have forgotten and do not know.

Plato, Timaeus (world-soul, sense-percep.a: In the Timaeus passages, the mortal kind of soul holds terrible and necessary affections: pleasure, pain, confidence, fear, wrath, hope, irrational sensation and love. The gods placed it in the breast, apart from the divine part in the head, with the neck as an isthmus between them. A midriff partitions the chest into two residences, and the commentator links the spirited and appetitive parts to this. Elsewhere the soul of the world is made first in birth and power, commanding the body as a lady and mistress.

q.t: And for this reason, fearing to defile the divine, except where it was absolutely necessary, they situated the mortal part apart from the other in a different residence of the body, having built an isthmus and boundary between the head and the breast, placing the neck in between, so that it might be separate.
God, therefore, created the soul first in birth and in power, giving it command over the body as to a lady and mistress, in the manner that follows.

Plato (attrib.), Alcibiades I (self-know.a: Proclus places the daemonic between gods and men, and the soul between intellect and body. He holds that one guardian daimon governs a person from birth until the journey to the judges, citing Socrates in the Phaedo. Souls enjoy intellect when they turn toward it and receive its light.

q.t: as far as he is a soul, Socrates preserves the analogy of nous intellect toward him; but as far as he is a soul using a body, Socrates preserves the analogy of the good daimon guardian spirit. And the same one is a daimon as regards a man, and an intellect as regards a soul.
And souls are attached to the intellect alone; but as souls using bodies, we are in need of the daemon.
But the intellectual order is another thing than the soul; and they have not obtained the same essence, nor the same power, nor the same action.

Aristotle, De anima|||Greek.a: Aristotle orders the powers of soul in sequence, with the nutritive presupposed by the sensitive and touch presupposed by the other senses. Animals differ in which senses, local movement and reason they have, and mortal creatures with reason have all the other psychic faculties. He also reviews earlier definitions of the soul, including the soul as principle of motion.

q.t: The sensitive soul, for example, presupposes the nutritive, but in the case of plants the nutritive exists apart from the sensitive. Again, the sense of touch is presupposed by all the other senses, but touch exists apart from them and does not presuppose them.
Anaxagoras does not, however, quite agree with Democritus. For Democritus absolutely identifies soul with reason, and considers truth to be that which appears to the senses.

Aristotle, Parva naturalia (De sensu, De.a: Aristotle places dreaming in the perceptive part of the soul, and within it the imaginative part, and calls the dream a phantasm. He explains that the movement set up in the sense organs by an object continues after the object has gone, as heat spreads through what is near it. Memory is tied to time, so only animals that perceive time have it, and it belongs to the same part as imagination.

q.t: It is clear that dreaming belongs to the perceptive part. And of this, to the imaginative part; what a dream is, and how it happens, we would best see from the things happening about sleep.
It is therefore clear to which part of the soul memory belongs, that it is the same part as imagination. And the things memorable are those which, in themselves, are not without imagination.

Mencius (Mengzi), xin theory|||Chinese.a: Mencius says the senses of hearing and seeing do not think and are obscured by external things, while to the mind belongs the office of thinking. The will leads the passion-nature (qi), which pervades the body, so Mencius advises maintaining a firm will. He also says men seek lost fowls and dogs but do not seek a lost mind, and that the great end of learning is to seek it.

q.t: The senses of hearing and seeing do not think, and are obscured by external things. When one thing comes into contact with another, as a matter of course it leads it away. To the mind belongs the office of thinking. By thinking, it gets the right view of things; by neglecting to think, it fails to do this.
The will is the leader of the passion-nature. The passion-nature pervades and animates the body. The will is first and chief, and the passion-nature is subordinate to it.
When men's fowls and dogs are lost, they know to seek for them again, but they lose their mind, and do not know to seek for it.

Zhuangzi (incl. ch.2 butterfly dream, ch.a: In the first passage, an officer explains the duke's illness through the breath: when it ascends without descending he is prone to anger, when it descends without ascending he loses his memory of things, and when it stays about the heart he falls ill. Commentary treats the sprites as products of a disordered mind. The second passage says reasoning cannot reach what lies beyond knowledge, and that knowing where to stop is the highest attainment. It names the Tower of Intelligence, the mind or soul as a spiritual center, whose Guardian acts unconsciously.

k.g: a Taoist term for the mind
the Spirit Terrace, referring to the mind or intelligence

q.t: When it ascends and does not descend, the patient becomes accessible to gusts of anger. When it descends and does not ascend, he loses his memory of things. When it neither ascends nor descends, but remains about the heart in the centre of the body, it makes him ill.
Those who aim by reasoning to reach it reason where reasoning has no place. To know to stop where they cannot arrive by means of knowledge is the highest attainment.

Theophrastus, De sensibus|||Greek.a: Theophrastus reports that opinions on sensation divide into two: explanation by the like (Parmenides, Empedocles, Plato) and by the contrary (Anaxagoras, Heraclitus). He says Parmenides held that perceiving and thinking are the same, with thought varying by the mixture of hot and cold. He adds that memory and forgetfulness arise from that mixture. He says Democritus and Plato define perceptible objects most fully.

q.t: Regarding sensation, the majority of opinions, and the general ones, are two: some explain it by the like, others by the contrary. Parmenides, Empedocles, and Plato [explain it] by the like, while those around Anaxagoras and Heraclitus [explain it] by the contrary.

Democritus and Plato have grasped [these matters] to the greatest extent, for they define [each thing] individually, except that the one [Plato] does not deprive perceptible objects of their nature, while Democritus makes all things affections of sensation.

Ācārāṅga Sūtra (Jaina Sūtras, SBE 22/45).a: The Ācārāṅga opens with Sudharman reporting Mahāvīra's discourse that many do not remember their direction of birth, nor whether the soul is reborn or what it was and will become. Knowing this comes by one's own realization, by a Tīrthakara's instruction, or by hearing from others. A note says karma obscures the intellect. The text also describes some beings as losing their sense when touched by wind.

q.t: Similarly, some do not know whether their soul is reborn again and again or not; nor what they were formerly, nor what they will become after having died and left this world. (3)
Some, certainly, touched by wind, shrivel up; those which shrivel up there, lose their sense there; those which lose their sense there, die there. (4)

Dhammapada (with aṭṭhakathā)|||Buddhist.a: The commentary opens by explaining the verse "Mind-preceded are the phenomena". It takes "mind" (mano) to be consciousness together with its mental factors (cetasika). It defines the self as the five aggregates and describes guarding the self through restraint of the senses, mindfulness and clear comprehension. It also lists contemplations of impermanence, suffering and non-self applied to form, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness.

q.t: In this, "mind" [original: "mano"] is consciousness. That consciousness, along with mental factors [original: "cetasika"], are called "mind-preceded." Among these phenomena, the mind is the best; therefore, it is called "mind-best."

Thus one maintains the self. What is the self here? "Self" is a name for the five aggregates pañcakkhandhā the five constituents of personality. One views those five aggregates as impermanent, as suffering, as not-self.
He contemplates form as non-self, feeling as non-self, perception as non-self, mental formations as non-self, and consciousness as non-self. This is called the contemplation of non-self.

Praśna Upaniṣad|||Indian.a: In the Fourth Praśna, Pippalada says that in sleep the hearing, seeing, smelling, tasting, touching, speaking, grasping, enjoying, excreting and moving of a person all become one in the mind (manas). The five life-functions are likened to sacrificial fires that stay awake in the body. The text pairs the mind, intellect, ego (ahamkara) and consciousness (citta) each with its own object, and places the conscious self (vijnanatman) in the Atman.

q.t: To him, Pippalada then said: "O Gargya, just as the rays of the setting sun all become one in that brilliant orb and go forth again and again when it rises, even so, truly, everything here becomes one in the mind [original: manas], the highest god.

Truly, this person—the one who sees, touches, hears, smells, tastes, thinks (mantri [original: mantṛ] ), understands (boddhri [original: boddhṛ] ), and acts, this conscious self (vijnanatman [original: vijñānātman] )—finds his ultimate home in the supreme, indestructible Soul (Atman [original: Ātman] ).

Yijing / Xici zhuan (Great Commentary)||.a: Chapter XI of the Great Commentary credits the ancient sages with a mind made clear by the virtues of the stalks, the diagrams and the lines. By their spirit-like ability they knew coming events, and their wisdom held the experience of the past. Purifying the heart with reverent caution is said to increase the spirituality and intelligence of their virtue.

q.t: The sages, having cleansed their minds by their possession of these three virtues, retired and stored them away in the secrecy of their own consciousness.
The sages went about the employment of them (moreover) by purifying their hearts and with reverent caution, thereby giving (more) spirituality and intelligence to their virtue.

Dhammasaṅgaṇī|||Buddhist.a: The text defines consciousness through a run of synonyms: mind, intellect, heart, the clear, the mind-base, the mind-faculty, the aggregate of consciousness and the mind-consciousness-element. It names the same mental state again under each heading of base, faculty, element and aggregate. Feeling, perception and volition are listed beside consciousness, and applied thought, sustained thought and one-pointedness of mind are each defined as a separate item.

q.t: That which, at that time, is mind, intellect, heart, the clear, the mental, the mind-base, the mind-faculty, consciousness, the aggregate of consciousness, and the corresponding mind-consciousness-element—this, at that time, is the one mind-base.

That which at that time is the stability of mind, steadfastness, firmness, non-distraction, non-scattering, the state of not being scattered, tranquility, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, right concentration—this is the one-pointedness of mind that exists at that time.

That which at that time is thought, mind, the mental, the heart, purity, the mind-base, the mind-faculty, consciousness, the aggregate of consciousness, the corresponding mind-consciousness element—this is consciousness at that time.

Kathāvatthu|||Buddhist.a: The debates are conducted as questions and answers about how the senses and the mind-faculty cognize their objects. One strand asks whether a faculty can cognize past or future objects, and the answer given for the eye and the mind-faculty is that only the present object is seen or cognized. Another strand asks how long a thought lasts, whether one thought-moment serves several senses, and which aggregate (feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness) includes each item.

q.t: "a monkey, roaming in a forest in the mountains, grabs a branch, lets it go, and grabs another, lets it go and grabs another; just so, monks, what is called 'thought,' 'mind,' or 'consciousness,' arises as one thing and ceases as another during the night and the day."

If there is a discourse where it is said “eye-consciousness arises dependent on the eye and visible forms,” it certainly should not be said that “ear-consciousness arises dependent on the eye and visible forms.”
Present mind-faculty exists, mental objects exist, mind-consciousness exists, physical basis exists, and mental-attention exists; does one cognize a present mental object with a present mind-faculty?

Paṭṭhāna|||Buddhist.a: The Paṭṭhāna passages describe how objects of the six sense bases condition consciousness elements and their associated states by way of the object condition. The dominance condition names desire, energy, mind, and investigation as states that may take priority over associated mental states. The text also lists knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and knowledge of passing away and rebirth as conditioned by aggregates.

k.g: consciousness that follows the main thought process and takes the same object
āvajjana; the initial turning of the mind toward an object

q.t: Whatever state is taken as an object, and because of that state certain mental states arise—namely mind and mental factors—those initial states are related to the resulting states by way of the object condition.
With the knowledge of others' minds, one knows the mind of a person who possesses a state that is not a root but is root-bearing.

Pseudo-Aristotle, Problemata (XXX.1 on m.a: These problems say the senses and intellect operate when the soul is at rest, since a soul in motion cannot perceive or think. The author explains the thoughtlessness of children, the intoxicated, and the insane this way. Dreams occur because the intellect is at a standstill. Sleep is placed in the soul's greatest motion. Another problem calls the mind a natural tool, fully present in old age.

q.t: For while the soul is in motion and being carried about, it is impossible to perceive or to think. This is why children, those who are intoxicated, and those who are insane are thoughtless.

Is it because God has given us two instruments within ourselves with which we use external tools: the hand for the body and the mind for the soul? For the mind is one of the things that exists within us naturally like a tool.

For those in a natural state, when the intellect stands fixed on one thing and does not shift in many directions, the other parts around that region also come to a stand, and the resting of these parts is sleep.

Xunzi (incl. Jiebi, 'Dispelling Obsessio.a: Xunzi says the mind dreams in sleep, daydreams at rest, and reflects when active, so it is always in motion. Its "unperturbedness" is the ability to keep dreams from disturbing knowledge. He compares the mind to a tub of muddy water that clears when undisturbed, and says doubt and clouded thought distort judgment, as when a stone in the dark looks like a tiger.

k.g: original: *t'ien* (Tian), often translated as Heaven or the natural order
original: *Tao*. The fundamental principle of the universe and the correct path of human conduct

q.t: When the mind sleeps, it dreams; when it is at rest, it indulges in daydreams; when it is active, it reflects. Therefore, the mind is always in motion.

The mind functions in exactly this way. Therefore, if it is guided by right principles and nourished by purity, nothing can unbalance it. In such a state, the mind is capable of distinguishing right from wrong and deciding what should be rejected or viewed with suspicion.
Whenever we observe things while the mind is filled with doubt and uncertainty, those things are not understood clearly. When my thoughts are unclear, I cannot decide whether a thing is true or not.

1 Enoch (Ethiopic Book of Enoch)|||Hebre.a: In the passage from this book of Enoch, a series of questions asks who can behold heaven, see a soul or a spirit and tell of it, or think the thoughts of the Holy One. The same passage asks who can know the measures of earth, heaven and the stars. It also tells the righteous to hold its words in the thoughts of their hearts.

q.t: And how should there be one who could behold the heaven and who is there who could understand the things of heaven and see a soul or a spirit and tell thereof, or ascend and see all their ends and conceive them or do like them?

Bhagavad Gītā|||Indian.a: The Gītā names the body the kshetra (field) and the one who knows it the kshetrajna (knower of the field). Its list of the field includes the ego, the intellect, the ten senses, desire, hatred, pleasure, pain, consciousness and firmness. In chapter 2, the senses can snatch away the mind, and brooding on objects leads through desire, anger and confusion of memory to loss of mind.

k.g: the senses, with the mind as the sixth

q.t: This body, O Kaunteya, is called the kshetra field. Those who know this, they call the one who knows it the kshetrajna knower of the field.

from propensity arises desire, from desire arises anger; from anger exists rashness, from rashness the confusion of memory; from the confusion of memory, the loss of mind, by which he is finally destroyed.

The five elements, self-consciousness, intellect, and furthermore the invisible, and the eleven bodily instruments, and the five perceptions of the senses; 6. desire, aversion, pain, pleasure, multiplex condition, thought, pertinacity: these are expressed in brief by the TERRENE subject to mutations.

Huangdi Neijing (on shen and dreams)|||C.a: The Neijing assigns the emotions to disorders of qi that injure particular stores. Anger and sorrow injure the ethereal soul (hun) and liver, joy injures the spirit (shen) and heart, fear injures the will (zhi) and kidneys, and anxiety injures the corporeal soul (po) and lungs. Injury to the will brings frequent forgetting of what was said. The commentary says the spirit has nowhere to return when sorrow gathers qi.

q.t: Anxiety causes the Qi to become disordered, injuring the corporeal soul [original: "魄", po]; when the corporeal soul is injured, the lungs are damaged.
Sorrow causes the heart to have nothing to rely upon, the spirit nowhere to return, and deliberation nowhere to settle; therefore, the Qi is disordered.

When violent anger does not cease, it injures the Will zhì (志). When the Will is injured, one frequently forgets what was said before, the waist and spine cannot bend forward, lean backward, bend, or extend, the body hair withers, the facial complexion looks withered and premature, and death occurs in late summer.

Pseudo-Plato, Axiochus (consolation on d.a: In this dialogue the speaker says we are a soul, an immortal creature enclosed in an earthly dungeon, and that the body left behind is no longer a man. The soul is described as diseased by bodily ills and as longing for the heaven it came from. The speaker also holds that every man's mind is immortal and feels no grief after leaving this life.

q.t: For we are a soul, that is to say, an immortal creature, being shut up and enclosed in an earthly dungeon.
Only this I know and assuredly hold fast, that every man's mind is immortal and, passing out of this life, feeleth no grief nor sorrow.

Wisdom of Solomon|||Hebrew & Jewish.a: The author speaks of an active soul and a vital spirit that God breathed into man. Solomon, the speaker, says a good soul fell to his lot and that he came into an undefiled body. Wisdom has a spirit quick of understanding, and the speaker credits her with his knowledge of the thoughts of men.

q.t: Because he was ignorant of him that moulded him, And of him that inspired into him an active soul, And breathed into him a vital spirit.
Now I was a child good by nature and a good soul fell to my lot; 20 Nay rather, being good, I came into a body undefiled.
For there is in her a spirit quick of understanding, holy, Alone in kind, manifold, Subtil, freely moving,

Lucretius, De rerum natura III–IV (natur.a: Lucretius holds that the soul and mind are mixed through veins, flesh, sinews and bones, and that the body confines them so that they make sense-giving motions. When the body breaks up, the senses of mind and soul dissolve with it. He also describes voluntary movement: idols of walking strike the mind, the will arises, and the mind then strikes the soul spread through the limbs, which moves the body.

q.t: Therefore, again and again I say, when the enveloping body has been all broken up and the vital airs have been forced out, you must admit that the senses of the mind and the soul are dissolved, since the cause of destruction is one and inseparable for both body and soul.

I say that idols of walking first present themselves to our mind and strike on the mind, as we said before: then the will arises; for no one begins to do anything, until his mind has predetermined what it wills.

Cicero, Somnium Scipionis (Republic VI)|.a: Scipio narrates that the dream comes in a deep sleep, after a long evening of talk about Africanus. Cicero's text says the soul, while enclosed in the body, can look outward and withdraw itself from the body, and so return more quickly to its home. Souls given over to pleasures and desires wander about the earth for many ages after leaving the body.

q.t: But the souls of those who have surrendered themselves to pleasures, and have delivered themselves to them as if they were slaves, and have succumbed to the rush of desires and to sensual indulgences, and have trampled upon the laws of gods and men—when they have departed from the body, they wander about the earth itself, and do not return to this place until they have been punished for many ages.
Then, when we departed to sleep, a deeper slumber than usual overcame me, both because I was exhausted from the journey and because I had stayed awake until late at night.

Prajñāpāramitā (Aṣṭasāhasrikā; Heart and.a: The Buddha, relying on the Perfection of Wisdom, is said to know tainted, untainted and passionate minds exactly as they are. Of the tainted minds the text says they are non-existent, and the passion of the mind is not its true nature. In chapter thirteen, form, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness are called immeasurable, incalculable and unequaled, equal to space.

q.t: Subhuti, that which is the passion of the mind is not the true nature [original: yathabhutata; literally "as-it-is-ness"] of the mind. That which is the true nature of the mind is not the passion of the mind.
Consciousness is also inconceivable and incomparable; in this way, all dharmas phenomena or elements of existence are inconceivable and incomparable.

Cicero, Tusculan Disputations I (the sou.a: Cicero says some cannot grasp the soul apart from the body, yet the soul in the body is harder to understand than the soul released into the free sky. He reads the Delphic precept to know oneself as an instruction to know one's soul, with the body as a vessel. He gives the soul's powers as memory, mind, thought, and foresight, and calls them divine and so eternal.

q.t: Neither are we our bodies, nor do I, speaking to you, speak to your body. When, therefore, he says "know thyself," he says this: know your soul. For the body is as it were a vessel, or some receptacle of the soul.
To be vigorous, to be wise, to invent, to remember. Therefore the soul, which as I say is divine, or as Euripides dares to say, is a god.

Cicero, De divinatione (and De fato)|||R.a: Quintus argues that the soul, called away from the body by sleep, remembers the past, perceives the present and foresees the future. He reports Plato's view that the mind-and-reason part of the soul sees truly in sleep when diet is moderate. Marcus answers that dream images arise from the soul's own motion and from remnants of waking thoughts, and he asks why a god would send dreams to sleepers and not to the waking.

q.t: When, therefore, the soul is called away by sleep from the company and contagion of the body, then it remembers the past, perceives the present, and foresees the future; for the body of the sleeper lies like that of a dead man, while the soul is vigorous and alive.

There is another reason derived from nature, which teaches how great is the power of the mind when separated from the senses of the body, which happens most especially to those who are sleeping or are moved in spirit.

When the soul is supported by the bodily members and by the five senses its powers of perception, thought, and apprehension are more trustworthy. But when these physical aids are removed and the body is inert in sleep, the soul then moves of itself.

Philo of Alexandria — De Opificio Mundi|.a: Philo ranks souls by kind, from the dullest in fish to the most precise in humans, with land animals and birds between. The human mind (nous) is called the soul of the soul, like the eye of the eye. Every human mind is related to the Divine Reason (Logos) as an impression, fragment or radiance of it. Elsewhere the senses carry outer impressions to the mind, which receives them like wax, and pleasure through the senses brings the governing mind under her power.

q.t: After all these, as was said, He made man, to whom He gave the gift of an exceptional mind nous [the higher intellect or reasoning faculty] —a kind of "soul of the soul," like the pupil in an eye.
Every human being, in terms of their mind, is related to the Divine Reason (Logos). The mind is an impression, a fragment, or a radiance of that blessed nature.
The senses report and display to the mind the things that appear on the outside, bringing them within. They stamp the impressions of each object upon it and produce a corresponding effect.

Philo of Alexandria — De Somniis|||Hebre.a: Philo calls the outward sense a "second sun." When it rises it wakes the senses of sight, hearing, taste, touch and smell, and puts to sleep the intellectual qualities of prudence, justice, knowledge and wisdom. He describes the human soul as having a foundation in outward sense and a head that is the most pure mind. He also writes that the divine region is full of incorporeal intelligences, which are immortal souls, and that the mind is in a manner the head of the soul.

k.g: ruling faculty/governing part of the soul

q.t: In reality, this light is no different from darkness. Once it rises, it arouses the senses of sight, hearing, taste, touch, and smell, as if from sleep, while it sends to sleep the intellectual qualities of prudence, justice, knowledge, and wisdom, which were previously awake.

But if we carefully investigate the soul which exists in men—the foundation of which is something corporeal, and as it were earth-like—we shall find that foundation to be the outward sense, and the head to be something heavenly, as it were the most pure mind.
It is well that we should know that the divine place and the sacred region are full of incorporeal intelligences; and these intelligences are immortal souls.

2 Enoch (Slavonic Apocalypse of Enoch)||.a: This passage states that the Lord sees all things, that when a person takes thought in the heart the Lord counsels the intellects, and that every thought is always before the Lord. Enoch also tells his children to keep their souls from all injustice that the Lord hates.

k.g: maintains the life of/sustains the soul

q.t: For the Lord sees all things; when man takes thought in his heart, then he counsels the intellects, and every thought is always before the Lord, who made firm the earth and put all creatures on it.

Seneca, Epistulae morales and De tranqui.a: In De tranquillitate animi Seneca describes the wise man as living as if lent to himself, ready to return body and life to nature when asked. He speaks of disturbances as waves of the mind and advises setting a limit to ambition and desire. He says this advice is for the imperfect and unwell, and that the wise man needs no such caution.

k.g: On the Tranquility of the Mind

q.t: Nature, which first entrusted them to us, will call for them; and to her we will say: "Receive my soul better than you gave it: I do not backslide, nor do I flee; you have prepared from a willing one what you gave to an unfeeling one: take it away."

Yet nothing will rescue them from these waves of the mind as effectively as setting a limit to their growth: and not giving fortune the authority to end it, but urging themselves to stop, far short of the extremes. Thus, some desires may sharpen the mind, but they are limited; they will not produce anything immense and uncertain.

Wang Chong, Lunheng (on spirit and ghost.a: Wang Chong writes that dreams are caused by the vital spirit, which he treats as identical to the vital spirit of the dead. He argues that a dream-killing leaves no wound, so the spirit of the dead cannot injure anyone either. He calls the soul the vital fluid (qi), moving like clouds and fog and unable to travel quickly. He describes dreams as visions that the mind shapes when good or bad luck is impending.

q.t: Dreams are caused by the vital spirit, and this spirit is identical to the vital spirit of the dead. If the vital spirit in dreams cannot injure people, the spirit of the dead cannot do so either.
The soul is the vital fluid [In ancient Chinese philosophy, qi or vital energy.]; the movement of the vital fluid is like that of clouds and fog and cannot be very quick.
Furthermore, dreams are visions. When good or bad luck is impending, the mind shapes these visions.
What, then, is this? It is true knowledge [original: "ἐπιστήμη"] regarding what is beneficial. And it is a safe, secure, and unchangeable gift.

Milindapañha|||Buddhist.a: King Milinda asks whether a soul exists, defining it as the living principle within that sees through the eye, hears through the ear, and discerns things through the mind, like a person looking out of palace windows. Nāgasena defines a dream as a suggestion coming across the path of the mind, and lists six kinds of dreamer. He says dreams occur only while the mind is active, and the mind is inactive in deep sleep and in trance.

q.t: ‘The living principle within² which sees forms through the eye, hears sounds through the ear, experiences tastes through the tongue, smells odors through the nose, feels touch through the body, and discerns things (conditions, “dhammâ”) through the mind—just as we, sitting here in the palace, can look out of any window we wish to look out of, be it the east, west, north, or south window.’
It is a suggestion 1, O king, coming across the path of the mind, which is what is called a dream.
The mind of a man who is awake, O king, is excited, open, clear, and untrammeled, and no prognostication occurs to one whose mind is so.

Pseudo-Plutarch / Aetius, De placitis ph.a: Under the Stoics, the text describes the ruling part (hegemonikon) of a newborn's soul as a sheet of paper ready for writing, on which each perception records its representation. Memories of a thing, once many are alike, make experience (empeiria). Concepts arise naturally or through instruction, and reason is completed from preconceptions in the first seven-year period. The Stoic soul is a sensitive exhalation, generated and perishable. Every soul has a ruling part that is life, sensation and impulse.

q.t: The Stoics say: When a human is born, they possess the ruling part [the hegemonikon] of their soul like a sheet of paper ready for writing. Into this, each individual perception records its own representation.

A concept [original: "ἐννόημα" notion/concept] is a phantom of the mind of a rational animal; for when a phantom [original: "φάντασμα" mental image/appearance] strikes a rational soul, then it is called a concept, having received its name from the intellect.
Some say that the soul of the whole is eternal, but the others mix into that one at the end. And every soul has some ruling part in it, which is life and sensation and impulse.
Plants do not even have the use of phantasiai impressions or appearances; for this reason, you do not speak of "the good" in their case. Therefore, the good requires the use of impressions.
For what purpose, then, has the faculty of reason [original: "logos"] been granted to us by nature? For the proper use of impressions [original: "phantasiai"].

It follows, therefore, that impurity of a soul consists of bad judgements, and purification consists in creating within it the proper kind of judgements; and a pure soul is the one which has the proper kind of judgements, for this is the only soul which is secure against confusion and pollution in its own functions.

Gautama, Nyāya-sūtra with Vātsyāyana and.a: The commentary holds that cognition is a quality of the Soul. It reasons that cognition exists within the Soul as pleasure does, and that it is self-apprehended like pleasure and pain, unlike color and similar qualities of physical matter. It gives the thoughts "I am happy" and "I am unhappy" as cases where the knower perceives himself. On dreams, it says dream-cognition has an object previously perceived in waking life, and the waking person recognises it as "this is what I saw in my dream."

q.t: Because cognition exists within the Soul, it must be regarded as a quality. Furthermore, it is a quality of the Soul and not of earth or other physical substances, because it is self-apprehended (meaning it is apprehended by mental perception).
We see the same principle with the knowing Soul and the Mind. When we have thoughts such as “I am happy” or “I am unhappy,” we find that the knower (the Soul) is perceiving himself.

Thus in reality the Dream-cognition is always one that has its object previously perceived in the waking state; and when the sleeping man who has seen a dream wakes up, he recognises the dream-cognitions as his own, the idea in his mind being ‘this is what I saw in my dream.’

Mahāvibhāṣā (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāst.a: The text treats ignorance as a covering of the mind. Because of it, one does not wish for or bear the four holy truths, and the text calls this "not-knowing." It lists the five hindrances and coverings, including desire, sloth, restlessness and torpor, and states how many hindrances are present in the state of consciousness when each one manifests. It also says ignorance arises together with restlessness across the three realms and the six consciousnesses, and with all defiled minds.

q.t: That is, because ignorance covers the mind, one does not wish or bear the four holy truths; thus, it is called not-knowing, not merely "not clear."
When the hindrance of desire is manifesting, there are three hindrances in the state of consciousness, namely desire, sloth, and restlessness.
That is, ignorance arises together with restlessness, spanning the three realms, five categories, and six consciousnesses, whether unwholesome or neutral, universally arising with all defiled minds.

Nāgārjuna, Mūlamadhyamakakārikā (with Pr.a: Nāgārjuna's text, quoting the Ratnacūḍa-paripṛcchā, argues that the mind cannot perceive the mind, as a sword blade cannot cut its own edge. In chapter 27 it says the self is not the appropriated aggregates and is not perceived apart from them, so a self without aggregates is like a sky-flower. In chapter 17 the commentary defines the mind (cetas) as accumulating and piling up virtuous and non-virtuous actions, and gives citta, manas and vijñāna as synonyms.

q.t: If the object and the mind were different, there would be a double mind. If the mind were the same as the object, how could the mind perceive the mind? The mind does not perceive the mind.

If the self were distinct from the appropriated aggregates, it would be perceived as something separate from them, just as a cloth is perceived as distinct from a jar. But it is not perceived in this way.

The mind cetas is so called because it accumulates cinoti and piles up upacinoti virtuous and non-virtuous actions, and because it determines niyamayati the capacity to grant the ripening of results. Mind citta, intellect manas, and consciousness vijñāna are synonyms for this same thing.

Artemidorus, Oneirocritica|||Hellenistic.a: Artemidorus says an enypnion arises when passions recur and present themselves to the soul, such as a lover with a beloved or a hungry person eating. He sorts passions into those proper to the body, those proper to the soul, and those common to both. He adds that a dream cannot be judged unless memory holds all of it, and that the dreamer's soul being pleasantly or unpleasantly affected during the dream changes how its outcome turns out.

k.g: a simple dream caused by physical states

q.t: For this is how a oneiros prophetic dream differs from an enypnion vague dream: the former signifies future events, whereas the latter relates to present circumstances.
And the masses see in sleep such things as they wish or such things as they fear. But the wise and those capable of judging them see signs of such things as they intend.

Furthermore, one must consider those dreams whose memory is not preserved in its entirety to be impossible to judge, whether one has forgotten the middle or the end. For a sound interpretation requires one to examine the whole of what appeared to happen; only that which the memory suggests as a complete whole can be truly grasped.

Galen, De placitis Hippocratis et Platon.a: Galen sets out Chrysippus's position that the whole hegemonikon is rational and that the passions occur within the reasoning faculty. He presents Posidonius's report that Cleanthes staged a dialogue between Reason and Spirit (thymos) as two distinct parts of the soul. He also argues that notions and anticipations are activities of reason, and that the soul and reason are not the same thing.

q.t: And when he says they are disobedient and turned away from reason, he expects us not to seek any other faculty in the soul, by the movement of which the passions occur in disobedience to reason; for he claims no such faculty exists, as some philosophers suppose, calling it concupiscible or irascible, for the entire hegemonikon ruling principle of humans is rational.

But Chrysippus neither thinks the passionate part of the soul is distinct from the rational, nor does he exempt irrational animals from the passions, which are clearly governed by desire and spirit, as Posidonius also explains at greater length regarding them.

For the soul and reason are surely not the same thing; furthermore, you indicated through the aforementioned phrase that reason is also one of the things established within the soul; and the soul and what is established within it cannot be the same thing.

Galen, De usu partium (books VIII–IX, XV.a: The one usable page says that the pneuma in the arteries is partly vital and partly psychic, and that the psychic pneuma divides into a sensory and a motive kind. It states the dispute over whether the psychic pneuma and psychic faculty originate in the heart or in the brain as their fountainhead.

q.t: But the matter that is currently in question is whether the psychic pneuma psychic spirit, starting from the heart, is carried up to the brain, stored there, and then from there, as if from a spring, distributed into the nerves.

Marcus Aurelius, Meditations (Ta eis hea.a: Marcus Aurelius writes that perception is dim, the soul is a spinning vortex, and the things of the soul are a dream and a delusion. He names the daimon given by Zeus as each person's own mind and reason. He says things do not touch the soul or enter it, and that the soul is dyed by its phantasiai, so he advises supplying it with chosen thoughts.

q.t: In human life, time is but a moment, substance is in constant flux, perception is dim, and the composition of the whole body is prone to decay. The soul is a spinning vortex, fortune is unpredictable, and fame is a thing without judgment. To put it briefly: all things of the body are a river, and all things of the soul are a dream and a delusion.
The intelligence of the Universe is social. At the very least, it has created lower things for the sake of higher things, and it has linked the higher things to one another.
Things themselves do not touch the soul in any way, nor do they have an entrance to the soul, nor can they turn or move the soul;
From whence a soul was sent to you, clothed with a great mind. These things the father conceived with his mind, and he who is mortal is animated by him.

Every mind understands this God, for he is not without the Intelligible Mind, and the intelligible [original: intelligibile. In Neoplatonic thought, this refers to the highest reality—the world of pure ideas—which can only be grasped by the intellect, not the physical senses.] does not exist without the mind.

Maximus of Tyre, Dissertations (on Socra.a: Maximus reads Epimenides' long sleep through Homer's two gates of dreams, with true dreams passing the horn gate and deceptive ones the ivory. He holds that a pure and sober soul sees clear dreams. He also gives Pythagoras' claim that the soul is immortal and existed before the body, and he describes recollection as the soul following one remembered thing after another.

q.t: For truly, such is the life of men: the soul, while encased in the body and filled with its abundance, barely manages to dream. The work of the souls of the majority is that they enter through the ivory gates.
Again, the sleep itself is forgetfulness, and their resurrection is recollection. And memory is the guardian and the time of those things that were forgotten.

Galen, Quod animi mores corporis tempera.a: Galen treats the ruling part (hegemonikon) of the soul as the part that sees through the eyes, hears through the ears, and remembers, calculates and chooses without using any organ. He compares its action in the body to fire in iron. He assigns sleeplessness and madness to a hotter power and sleepiness and coma to cold causes, and names lethargy and melancholic madness as signs of abnormality in the brain.

q.t: but [the soul] sees through the eyes, and hears through the ears; similarly, however, it remembers, the whole calculates, and chooses, neither using the eye, nor the ears, nor the tongue, nor using other things in any way, but this part of the soul acts in the containing body, just as fire in iron, or the spirit distributed in the body;
For we must attribute sleeplessness and madness to a hotter power as the cause. But we blame cold causes for all things [that are] sleepy and comatose.

Alexander of Aphrodisias, De anima — Gre.a: Alexander of Aphrodisias says intellection is the soul's fitting function and is completed by rest, so the sober think more clearly than the drunk. He says the man, through the soul, grieves, fears, learns and remembers. Imagination is found in animals without reason and is often deceived, while science and intellect are always true. He describes an intellect that comes in from without and is incorruptible.

q.t: Verily, man is delighted and grieves through the soul, he is irascible and fearful, he loves, hates, learns, understands, remembers, and commits to memory, and he does not do these things for any other reason than that he is endowed with such perfection and species.

But indeed, imagination should not be thought to be the same thing as science or intellect. Since science and intellect are always true, but imagination is very often hallucinatory and deceived. Science and intellect, just as prudence, are only in those animals which have attained reason; imagination, however, is observed to be even in those lacking reason.
Moreover, this intellect is generated in us from without and is incorruptible; other acts of understanding also come from without, but they are not in the intellect.

Alexander of Aphrodisias, De anima (with.a: Alexander of Aphrodisias says the soul's work of intellection is completed by rest, and that the man, through the soul, is delighted, grieves, fears, loves, hates, learns and remembers. Imagination, which belongs even to animals lacking reason, is often deceived and has no faith or assent, while science and intellect are always true. The intellect from without, as he reads Aristotle, is generated in us from outside, is separable and incorruptible, and the objects understood become intellects.

q.t: Verily, man is delighted and grieves through the soul, he is irascible and fearful, he loves, hates, learns, understands, remembers, and commits to memory, and he does not do these things for any other reason than that he is endowed with such perfection and species.
But indeed, imagination should not be thought to be the same thing as science or intellect. Since science and intellect are always true, but imagination is very often hallucinatory and deceived.

Moreover, this intellect is generated in us from without and is incorruptible; other acts of understanding also come from without, but they are not in the intellect. But insofar as they are understood, they become intellects.

Corpus Hermeticum (CH I Poimandres; X Th.a: In Book X, Hermes teaches Tat that mind and soul are joined only in an earthy body, with the soul wrapped in vital spirit. At death the mind is separated from the soul and takes a body of fire. A pious soul becomes mind throughout, and mind torments an impious soul with the scourges of its sins. In the Poimandres, man comes from life and light and becomes soul and mind, and the Mind is called Father God.

q.t: And so the mind takes to itself the soul for a wrap; the soul,—for the soul also is in some measure divine,—uses as its wrap the vital spirit; and the vital spirit controls the body.
There is nothing more divine than mind, nothing more potent in its operation, nothing more apt to unite men to gods, and gods to men.
Know it this way: that which in you sees and hears is the Logos Word/Reason of the Lord. But the Mind is Father God.

Kundakunda, Samayasāra|||Indian.a: Kundakunda holds that consciousness is the soul's own nature, and that anger and similar states arise from karma and belong to matter. He describes the soul's attentiveness (upayoga) as shaped by wrong belief, wrong knowledge and lack of self-restraint when joined with delusion. Knowing the pure soul makes the soul pure, and knowing the impure makes it impure.

q.t: Thus, the knower realizes the nature of the soul. But the deluded soul, obscured by the darkness of ignorance and failing to realize the true nature of the soul, mistakes attachment [original: "love"] itself for the soul.

By contemplating the pure soul—which is full of right perception [original: "conation"; darshana] and knowledge—and by not paying attention to the non-self, the soul is liberated from karmas and very soon realizes its own true nature.
The soul, filled with right knowledge, does not mistake what is "not-self" for the self, and does not mistake the "self" for what is not-self; therefore, it ceases to be the "doer" of karma.

Sextus Empiricus, Outlines of Pyrrhonism.a: Sextus Empiricus reports the Peripatetic view that the senses are the instrument and the mind the craftsman. In his account, a sense-affection leaves an imagination in the soul like a footprint called memory, from which the person fashions a mental image. Thought is the soul's capacity and mind its activity. He then argues that thought comprehending the senses would become sense, and that the existence and place of the ruling part is disputed, so judgment is suspended.

q.t: For when the soul is able to make this fashioning—that is, when it is so constituted by nature—it is called thought. But when it is already acting energetically, it is named mind.

For in order for a sense to be apprehended as a sense—that is, as a perceiving thing—the mind itself must become of the same kind as them. For the one who comprehends sight as it sees must, long before that, have become sight; and the one judging hearing as it hears must not be different from hearing.

But if the alteration is different, the mind will not receive the object as it is presented to the senses. Instead, the underlying object will be one thing, and the mental impression arising in the ruling part will be another—which is again absurd.

Umāsvāti, Tattvārtha Sūtra|||Indian.a: Umāsvāti divides consciousness (upayoga) into cognitive application with eight subtypes and perceptive application with four, twelve in all. Sensory knowledge (mati) arises through the five senses and the mind (anindriya), and unfolds in apprehension, speculation, judgment and retention. Each sense has its own object, and scriptural knowledge belongs to the mind.

q.t: The defining characteristic of the soul [Active Consciousness] is consciousness [original: upayoga; the functional manifestation of the soul's innate power of knowing and perceiving].
The four divisions of sensory knowledge are apprehension, speculation, perceptual judgment, and retention.

[Touch] sparshana; the sense of tactile perception, [taste] rasana; the sense of gustatory perception, [smell] ghrana; the sense of olfactory perception, [sight] chakshu; the sense of visual perception, and [hearing] shrotra; the sense of auditory perception — these are the five senses.

Tertullian, De anima|||Early Christian &.a: Tertullian holds that the soul stays in motion during sleep and that dreams arise from ecstasis, which he describes as an excess of sense akin to madness. He says the soul senses corporal things through the body and understands incorporeal things through the animus. He distinguishes the soul as breath (afflatus) of God from spirit.

q.t: We call this power ecstasis a standing outside of oneself, an excess of sense, and akin to madness: thus also in the beginning, sleep was dedicated with ecstasis, and God sent an ecstasis upon Adam, and he slept: for sleep came to the body for rest, ecstasis was added to the soul against rest, and from there arose the form mixing sleep with ecstasis, and nature from form.
For the soul, as it is always mobile and always exercised, never yields to rest, which is obviously foreign to the state of immortality: for nothing immortal admits the end of its work.
But what will sense be if not the intellect of the thing that senses? What will intellect be if not the sense of the thing that understands?

Origen, De principiis|||Early Christian.a: Origen takes up the soul by beginning from the lower things and ascending to the higher, holding that every animal has a soul. He defines the soul as a phantastic and hormetic substance and treats the nature of souls as capable of both good and evil. He describes the soul of Christ as rational and as having the faculty of choosing good and evil. The human mind forms an understanding of God from visible creatures and from the Scriptures.

k.g: the ruling/principal part of the mind

q.t: It is defined in this way: that it is a phantastica imaginative/perceptive and hormetica impulsive substance: which surely fits to be said of all animals, even those that live in the waters; but the same definition of the soul is suitably shown in birds.
That the nature of that soul was the same as that of all souls cannot be doubted; otherwise, it could not even be called a soul if it were not truly a soul.

For regarding God the Father, although no one is able to speak fully, yet it is possible for some understanding to be grasped on the occasion of visible creatures, from those things which the human mind naturally feels; furthermore, it is also possible to be confirmed from the Holy Scriptures.

Diogenes Laertius, Lives and Opinions of.a: In the Pythagorean account the mind and the senses are located in the brain, the soul is nourished by blood, and the veins, arteries and nerves are its bonds. The Stoic report counts eight parts of the soul: the five senses, the seminal reasons, the vocal part and the rational part. Chrysippus is cited for the view that passions are judgments, and Cleanthes and Chrysippus differ on how long souls survive death.

k.g: the leading or ruling part of the soul

q.t: A soul he divides into three parts: into sensation, mind, and anger. Sensation and anger are shared by other living beings, but the mind pertains to man alone.
Zeno the Citiean and Antipater in the books On the Soul and Posidonius say the soul is warm spirit. For by this we are breathing, and by this we are moved.

Perversion arises in the mind from false judgments, from which many passions [original: "πάθη"] sprout, which are the causes of instability. According to Zeno, passion itself is an irrational and unnatural movement of the soul, or an excessive impulse.

Pistis Sophia and the Books of Jeu (Aske.a: The Pistis Sophia describes the psychē soul as bound by the archontes to an antimimon pneuma, the counterfeit spirit, with the moira fate following it. At departure the soul speaks the mystery of breaking the seals, and the bonds and the counterfeit spirit are released. The soul, a power and the counterfeit spirit each perceive according to their own nature, and the counterfeit spirit moves the soul in dreams and in desires of the world.

q.t: And when the psychē soul says the mystērion mystery of the breaking of the sphragis seals, at that hour the antimimon pneuma counterfeit spirit is broken and ceases to be [bound] to the psychē soul.

Eti Also it comes so that it may rest by night and by day, and it moves it in dreams or in the epithymiais kosmou desires of the world, and makes it epithymein desire all the things of the kosmou world.

According to the oikonomia divine arrangement/dispensation that they set within it to give aisthesis perception/sense to the soul, so that it might search for the heights of the Light at all times. And that tebom power acts according to the nature of the soul in every way, and it resembles it. It does not depart from the soul, but it remains within it.

Plotinus, Enneads (IV on the soul; V on.a: Plotinus treats memory of thoughts in this passage. He says the act of the intellect is impartible and remains hidden within, and reason unfolds it into the representative faculty, where the intelligible appears as in a mirror. This transfer and reception into the imagination would constitute memory. He also asks whether one perceiving part serves both sensible and intelligible things, and says we remember with that by which we perceive.

q.t: Perhaps, since reason accompanies the act of the intellect itself, a certain transfer and reception into the imagination will constitute memory.

Porphyry, De abstinentia (animal souls,.a: Porphyry quotes the line "the mind sees and the mind hears" and argues that the impression at eyes and ears produces no perception unless the thinking faculty is present. He cites Cleomenes, whose mind was in the Peloponnese during a performance. He also says sensation is a nail fastening the soul to the body, and that pleasure and pain lead the soul into forgetting its own proper visions.

q.t: For which reason it is said, "The mind sees and the mind hears, but other things are deaf and blind," as the physical state of the eyes and ears does not produce perception if the thinking part is not present.

This nail, through the multitude of things it perceives, penetrates the soul and glues it to the body, fastening it there through enjoyment. For if the senses were not an obstacle to the pure activity of the soul, what difficulty would there be for a person to remain unaffected by the motions of the body even while living within it?

Two springs have been let loose for the binding of the soul in this world. From these, as if filled with deadly drinks, the soul falls into a forgetting of its own proper visions: these are pleasure and pain.

Porphyry, Sententiae ad intelligibilia d.a: In the Epistle to Marcella, Porphyry names the mind (nous) as the temple of God, to be prepared and adorned so that it can receive God. He says the soul is a dwelling place (chōrēma) for gods or for spirits, and that forgetfulness of God admits an evil spirit. Remembering that God stands present as Overseer (ephoros) over all thoughts and actions keeps the inner intent turned toward God.

q.t: But wherever forgetfulness of God enters, an evil spirit must dwell within you; for the soul, as you have learned, is a dwelling place [original: χώρημα (chōrēma)], either for gods or for spirits.

Asclepius (Latin Hermetic dialogue; on t.a: Trismegistus tells Asclepius that the world nourishes bodies, spirit nourishes souls, and sense nourishes the mind. Sense is a celestial gift held by a few, and mixed with the human soul it makes the mind bright. He also says sense differs from intellect, and that people who follow an image without inspecting it by true reason become malicious and take on the habits of beasts.

q.t: The world, therefore, nourishes bodies; spirit, souls; but sense—by which celestial gift humanity alone becomes happy—nourishes the mind. For not all [possess it], but a few, whose mind is such that it can be capable of such a great benefit.

Not all, O Asclepius, have attained true intelligence, but following an image with rash impetuosity, with no true reason inspected, they are deceived, which breeds malice in their minds, and transforms the best animal into the nature of a wild beast, and the habits of beasts.
For this is how intellect differs from sense, that our intellect precedes the intention of the mind to understand and discern the quality of the sense of the world.

Guo Xiang, commentary on Zhuangzi (Xuanx.a: Guo Xiang describes the Sage as "without-mind" (wuxin), whose spirit stays unchanged while the body moves and ten thousand affairs are managed. He says the self of a moment ago is no longer the self of now, since Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things shift at every moment. The world fails to notice this, and he calls the wish to tie down and keep what is encountered ignorance.

q.t: Thus, although he moves his body all day long, his spirit remains unchanged; though he manages ten thousand affairs, he remains tranquil and composed. To see only the form and not reach the spirit is a common failure of the world.
