My 'self' of a moment ago is no longer my 'self' of now; I and the present moment pass away together, yet the world does not realize it.

Iamblichus, De mysteriis (divination, po.a: Iamblichus says enthusiasmos is not a motion of the human mind joined to a daimonic inspiration. A truly possessed mind is not moved, and the inspiration comes from gods. Being held by the divine is the primary cause, and being outside oneself follows it. He holds that divine dreams bring a presence clearer and more accurate than waking awareness. The oikeios daimon binds the soul to the body, directs its life, and supplies the origins of thoughts.

q.t: For it is falsely conjectured to be a motion of the mind together with a daimonic spirit-driven inspiration. For the human mind is not moved, if it is truly possessed, nor does it become an inspiration of daimones spirits, but of the gods.

For it is not possible that the clear presence of the gods should be left behind by the awareness that occurs in the waking state; but if the truth must be told, it is necessary that this presence be even clearer and more accurate than that [waking awareness], and that it brings forth a more perfect understanding.

He binds the soul to the body as it descends, governs its composite animal nature, directs the soul's own proper life, and provides the origins for our thoughts. We deliberate and act according to what he brings to our minds, and he governs human beings until we, through hieratike theourgia priestly divine-working, establish a divine overseer and leader for the soul.

Liezi|||Chinese.a: The Liezi sorts dreams into six conditions: direct, gossip, thought, waking, joy, and fear. It says these are what the spirit communicates, while eight signs are what the body encounters. It ties dream content to bodily states such as strong Yin or Yang, fullness, and hunger. A servant who dreams nightly of ruling a state, and a master who dreams of being a servant, show dreams answering waking circumstances.

q.t: What are the six conditions? One is a direct dream, two is a dreaming of gossip, three is a dreaming of thought, four is a dream of waking, five is a dream of joy, six is a dream of fear. These six are what the spirit communicates.

Only the Yellow Emperor and Rongchengzi, while dwelling on Mount Kongtong, fasted for three months, making their hearts dead and their bodies inert. Slowly, with their spirit's vision, they saw them, like the slopes of Mount Song.

Night after night he dreamed that he was a ruler of a state, positioned above the people, managing the affairs of the entire country, roaming in palaces and towers, and indulging in whatever he desired. His joy was incomparable.

Ge Hong, Baopuzi (Neipian)|||Chinese.a: Ge Hong argues that the hun and po souls are known to everyone as parts of the body, though no one has seen or heard them. He treats the physical form as the dwelling place of the spirit, and compares the spirit to a flame that needs its candle. He adds that when qi grows weary and desires prevail, the essential spirit leaves the body.

q.t: Whether people are wise or foolish, all know that their own bodies possess hun spiritual souls and po corporeal souls. When the hun and po partially depart, a person falls ill; when they depart completely, a person dies.
When the physical form is exhausted, the spirit scatters. When qi vital energy is depleted, life comes to an end.

Īśvarakṛṣṇa, Sāṃkhya-kārikā|||Indian.a: Gauḍapāda's commentary lists eleven senses: five cognitive, five active, and the mind as the eleventh, called the "resolver" saṅkalpaka because it forms intentions. Intellect, ego and mind make up the internal instrument, which grasps objects in all three times and presents them to the puruṣa. Non-perception has eight causes, among them injury to the senses and lack of mental attention.

q.t: It is like a cognitive sense among cognitive senses, and like an active sense among active senses. Why? Because the mind imagines the movement of both cognitive and active senses. Therefore, the mind is of both types.

The cognitive senses, the active senses, the ego, and the mind—all these, having revealed their respective objects to the puruṣa Self/Consciousness, present them to the intellect. They make them exist within the intellect. Because of this, the puruṣa experiences all objects, such as happiness and the rest, which are established in the intellect.
Due to lack of mental attention, such as a distracted person not noticing something clearly performed.

Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra|||Buddhist.a: The sūtra lists the five Dharmas, three Self-natures, eight Consciousnesses, and two Non-selves as containing all the Buddhas' teachings. It states that the world, the triple world, and all forms are Mind-only (cittamātra), and that Citta is pure in its original nature while Manas and the others are not. Through them karmas accumulate and produce two sorts of impurities. It also says the soul sought within the Skandhas is imperceptible to the dull-minded.

q.t: Mahamati, these are the five Dharmas, the three Self-natures, the eight Consciousnesses, and the two Non-selves; all the teachings of the Buddhas are included within them.
To say 'Mind-only' is by mind, is also born of mind; particular forms and figures in all possible varieties, when thoroughly understood, are no more than Mind itself (368).

The Citta [mind or heart] is in its original nature pure, but the Manas [the faculty of deliberation or reflection] and others are not. Through them, various karmas [actions and their results] are accumulated, resulting in two sorts of impurities [or defilements] (754).

Maitreya/Asaṅga, Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra|||.a: The passages say Thought appears as the Phenomenon and that no other Phenomenon exists, whether or not one knows Nothing-but-Thought. They list classes of Thought, including affirmation, condensation and wishing, and set out the Path of Pacification, the Path of Inspection and a Coupled Path joining both. The commentary calls objects mere mental fabrications (jalpamātra) and describes Mind-Only (cittamātra), leading to the non-existence of mind as grasping subject. It also names six kinds of citta: root, following, investigating, determining, conceptualizing and aspiring.

q.t: It is Thought, indeed, which appears as the Phenomenon, and there is no other Phenomenon than Thought; therefore, whether one knows that there is Nothing-but-Thought or one does not know it, Thought is the Phenomenon and there is no other.

By realizing through intellect that there is nothing external to the mind, one then arrives at the non-existence of the mind itself [as a grasping subject]. Having realized the non-existence of both [subject and object], the wise person abides in the Realm of Reality that is free from those movements. (8)

The Vicāraṇā-citta investigating mind is that by which one investigates the meaning and the phrasing. Here, one investigates the meaning through four modes: by counting, by weighing, by examining, and by reviewing.

Patañjali, Yoga Sūtra with Vyāsa's bhāṣy.a: The commentators hold that the mind (citta) does not illuminate itself and is not known by another mind, since that would produce infinite regress and a confusion of memories. They teach that the puruṣa, as citi, knows the states of the mind, which are colored by objects as iron is by a magnet. Sleep (nidrā) is classed as a fluctuation and as a specific perception, shown by recollection on waking.

q.t: This recollection of a person who has awakened would not exist if there were no experience of the perception, and the memories based on it and regarding it would not exist. Therefore, sleep is a specific perception.

If the intellect were known by another intellect, then that intellect, not being self-aware, would be unable to illuminate the other intellect; thus, yet another intellect would have to be imagined to perceive it, and another for that one, leading to infinite regress.

The self-power citi-śakti power of consciousness, which has received a reflection in the mirror of the mind thus affected, experiences the object as being colored by the mind; it does not bestow any manifestness upon the object.

Themistius, Paraphrase of De anima|||Hel.a: Themistius separates imagination from sense: in sleep we imagine and do not sense, and the blind imagine colors. He says sense is mostly true and imagination mostly false, and names four habits that can be true or false: sense, opinion, science, intellect. He describes sleep as the immobility of the common sense, by which we perceive that we perceive, and says the agent intellect, likened to light, makes things understood in act.

q.t: Therefore, while I show that sense is not imagination: in sleep we imagine, in sleep we do not sense, neither in act nor in potentiality.

for we do not see that we see by sight, nor do we declare it by sight, nor by taste do we distinguish sweetness from heat, neither separately nor together by both senses, but by a certain common part which is joined to all the senses, which we simply and properly call the sensus communis common sense.

Therefore, just as the light, by which it approaches the eyes and colors, provides for both sight and colors in act, so the agent intellect, by which the potential intellect is moved, not only ministers to the intellect in act, but also makes the things which were understood in potentiality so that they are understood in act.

Gregory of Nyssa, De hominis opificio|||.a: Gregory distinguishes three kinds of vital faculty: one that is nourished, one that is nourished and perceives, and one that uses reason and is diffused through the others. He holds that the true soul is one, mingled with material nature through the senses. In sleep the mind and senses rest while the nourishing part keeps working, and dream images come from memory.

q.t: For the mind is joined to the human body by a certain temperature through the senses; therefore, with the senses resting from activity, it would be highly consistent that the mind also be idle. One may also perceive this from the argument that sleepers often seem to be engaged in absurd things, and even sometimes in things that cannot happen.
For the true and perfect soul is in reality one, an intelligent thing, not consisting of crude matter, but mingled through the senses with that crude nature.

Just as, therefore, although all men are governed by their own mind, there exist, nevertheless, a few to whom God speaks in an almost familiarly manifest manner: so, while the power of imagining during sleep has been implanted by nature in all equally and without distinction, there are a few from the whole gathering to whom more divine visions of dreams offer themselves.

Gregory of Nyssa, De anima et resurrecti.a: In the dialogue, the soul is said to have a rare and unique nature of its own, independent of the body's coarse texture. The senses give exact knowledge of the outer world and lead to an understanding of the super-sensual world. Life is described as blending with matter by gradation, from inanimate things to sentient to rational beings. Man is created last, taking up every form of life, including that of plants and brutes.

q.t: Our conception is this: the soul exists with a rare and unique nature of its own, independent of the body’s coarse texture. We gain exact knowledge of this outer world from our senses, and these sensory operations lead us to an understanding of the super-sensual world of fact and thought.

Seeing, then, that this life of sensation could not possibly exist apart from the matter which is its subject, and that intellectual life could not be embodied without growing within the sentient, the creation of man is related as coming last, as one who took up into himself every single form of life, both that of plants and that which is seen in brutes.

Pseudo-Macarius, Spiritual Homilies|||Ea.a: The homilies say God made the soul with no vice mixed into her nature, placing in her the laws of the virtues, discernment, knowledge, wisdom, faith and love, along with understanding, thoughts and will. The heart holds many natural thoughts that the understanding, as helmsman, and the conscience rebuke and direct. Since Adam, sin has become a member of the soul. The five rational senses of the soul are called wise virgins when they receive grace.

q.t: For this reason, the soul is a great, wonderful, and divine work: which God has created in such a way that He has mixed no vice with her nature: but He has made her according to the image of the virtues of the spirit: and has placed in her the laws of the virtues, discernment, knowledge, wisdom, faith, love, and other images, according to the image of the spirit.

So the heart has many natural thoughts clinging to it: but the understanding and the conscience rebuke and direct that / and still the natural thoughts that grow in the heart: for the soul has many members / though she is one.

For the five rational senses of the soul, when they have received the grace from above / and the sanctification of the spirit / then they are truly wise virgins / who have received the wisdom of grace from above.

Vasubandhu, Abhidharmakośa with Bhāṣya||.a: Vasubandhu says mind and mental factors are conjoined, being similar in support, object, aspect, time and substance. Ten mental factors, including feeling, volition, contact and concentration, arise with every moment of mind. Volition moves the mind toward an object as a magnet moves iron. The five sense-consciousnesses always carry applied and sustained thought, while the mind, phenomenon and mental-consciousness elements occur in three kinds.

q.t: they each specifically determine aspects of the object such as blue—consciousness cognizes the object, perception grasps it, feeling experiences it, and intention performs the mental act; and those minds and mental factors occur together in mutual similarity.
The definition of volition cetanā mental intention is: the mental factor that moves the mind toward an object, just as a magnet moves iron.

Among the eighteen elements, those with both applied and sustained thought are the five elements of consciousness—eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body. Because they look outward, they are coarse and exist on the level associated with applied and sustained thought; thus they are always associated with them.

Augustine, Soliloquia / De immortalitate.a: In this edition the Soliloquies are addressed to God as a prayer. The speaker asks for a heart, spirit, mind, intellect and reason, and for illumined eyes. The text names God the "Light of the mind" and says that the more a person lies in the darkness of sins, the less they see the snares in their path.

q.t: Give me a heart that thinks of You, a spirit that loves You, a mind that remembers You, an intellect that understands You, and a reason that always adheres to You with sweet fervor; let me love You wisely, and love You with wisdom.
For who shall escape these many snares unless he sees them, and who shall see them unless he whom You have illuminated with Your light?

Augustine, De quantitate animae|||Early.a: Augustine defines the soul as a substance sharing in reason and fitted to rule the body. He argues that it has no length, breadth or height, and that its greatness is a matter of power, shown in its memory of heaven, earth and sea. Reason is described as an aspect of the mind that seeks, while knowledge is the seeing it aims at.

q.t: If, however, you want the soul defined for you and ask what the soul is, I answer easily. For it seems to me to be a certain substance participating in reason, adapted to ruling the body.
Thus, when that aspect of the mind which we call reason strikes upon some thing, it sees, and notes that it is known.
For the soul is by no means to be suspected of being long, or wide, or as if it were powerful.

Evagrius Ponticus, Praktikos / On Though.a: These Antirrhetikos entries each pair a troubling state of the soul with a verse of Scripture. They name vain logismoi that produce fear and trembling and darken the holy light that gives the intellect confidence. Other entries cover logismoi of grief that lead the intellect into the abyss of the dead and impress foul visions on the heart, and demons who speak within the intellect.

q.t: Against a soul not understanding that vain logismoi thoughts generate fear and trembling within it, and darken the holy light that creates confidence in the intellect:

Augustine, Confessiones (Book X on memor.a: Augustine describes confessing to God with the words of the soul and the cry of thought. In Book VII he recalls that he could think of no substance except what is seen through the eyes of the world, and that phantoms clouded the eye of his mind. In Book XI he compares a singer reciting a familiar song, whose sense is stretched between expectation and memory, with God's knowledge of past and future.

q.t: Why do they seek to hear from me who I am, they who do not want to hear from You what they are? And how do they know, when they hear from me about myself, whether I tell the truth, since indeed no man knows what is in man, save the spirit of the man which is in him?
My heart cried out violently against all my phantoms, and with this one blow I tried to drive away the flock of uncleanness hovering around the eye of my mind.

Nor does it happen to You, the unchangeably eternal creator of minds, as it happens to one singing or to one hearing a song, that the affection and sense are distended by the expectation of future sounds and the memory of past ones.

Calcidius, Commentary on the Timaeus (on.a: Calcidius reports Stoic views in which the natural spirit is the soul, divided by Chrysippus into eight parts that include the five senses. He argues that the principal force of the soul sits in the brain, with a second principal part of the sentient soul in the heart. His account of sleep describes the internal fire restrained when the eyelids close, and dreams arising from remnants of the soul's movements.

q.t: And all these things [pertain] to the present; neither does the sense recall so much of the past, nor does it suspect the future. Truly, it is the property of inner deliberation and consideration to understand the passion of each sense, and from those things which they report, to collect what that thing is, and to accept the present indeed, but to remember the absent and [anticipate] the future.

But if they confess that the soul of man is rational, let them believe that God, when men were made by Him, breathed in a divine spirit, by which we reason, and by which we understand, and by which we piously worship God, and there is for us a kinship with divinity, and we are said to be gods, and children of the most high God.

And when the rest is deeper, he says, with the natural spirit having become thicker, we dream nothing, or only something light, uncertain, and perfunctory. But if there are notable remnants of the movements of the soul, of such a kind as they will be, and in which places they will be, such images of visions will be born, pressed, and, because of the significance of the images, residing long in the memory.

Nemesius of Emesa, De natura hominis|||E.a: Nemesius defines memory as the preservation of sensation and of the conception of the intellect, citing Origen and Plato. Things of the intellect are held by accident, through a preceding phantasia. He places the senses in the front ventricles of the brain, the cognitive faculty in the middle and memory in the rear, citing the effects of injury to each. Sensation is defined as a judging of a change in the seats of the senses.

q.t: For the soul perceives through the instruments of sensing those things which fall under the senses, and an opinion is born. But those things which fall under the intellect are produced by the intellect, and this is the conception of the intellect. When, therefore, it preserves the images both of those things it has opined and those which the intellect has grasped, it is said to remember.

For if the front ventricles are damaged in any way, the senses are hindered, but the cognitive faculty remains intact. If only the middle ventricle suffers an injury, the intellect [original: "διάνοια" (dianoia)] is impaired, but the sense organs remain, preserving their natural ability to perceive.
Now, sensation is not a change, but a judging of a change. For the seats of the senses are changed, and the sense judges the change.

k.g: the imaginative faculty of the soul

Augustine, De Genesi ad litteram XII (th.a: Augustine, in Book XII, names three kinds of vision. The corporeal is perceived through the body, the spiritual is an image of an absent body formed like a body, and the intellectual comes from the mind. He calls the spirit a force of the soul lower than the mind, where likenesses of bodily things are expressed, and says prophecy pertains to mental vision. Joseph, who understood the seven ears of grain and the seven oxen, is placed above Pharaoh, who saw them in dreams. A later chapter asks whether the soul, once it has left the body, is carried to bodily places or to places similar to bodies.

k.g: the mental faculty of imagination or illusory form

q.t: There are three kinds of visions. Let us call the first "corporeal," because it is perceived through the body and presented to the bodily senses.
For I judge it to be spiritual, not bodily. But it is carried to spiritual things according to its merits, or to penal places similar to bodies.

Augustine, De anima et eius origine|||Ea.a: Augustine says he does not know how his own soul came into his body and is not ashamed to confess this. He does not defend those who hold that souls are blown into the body from elsewhere. He will accept an answer from canonical books or from reasoning not contrary to catholic truth.

q.t: I say concerning my soul, I do not know how it came into my body; for I did not bestow it upon myself. He knows who bestowed it, whether He drew it from my father or whether He created a new one for the first man.

Augustine, De trinitate (Books X–XV)|||E.a: Augustine says the mind cannot love itself unless it knows itself, and that it gathers knowledge of incorporeal things and of itself as it gathers knowledge of bodies through the senses. He says the mind is a spirit, though the word spirit also names God, the soul, an animal's breath and the imaginations of bodies in a person. When the mind sees itself by thought, it understands itself and begets knowledge of itself, and when it does not think of itself it knows itself as its own memory.

q.t: Therefore, the mind itself, just as it collects knowledge of the bodies of things through the senses of the body, so it does of incorporeal things and itself.

And he says: "in the spirit of your mind," not wishing it to be understood as two things there, as if the mind were one thing and the spirit of the mind were another. But that it is the mind itself, yet not every spirit is a mind.
Therefore, when the mind sees itself by thought, it understands itself and recognizes itself, begets this by its intellect, and by its cognition.

Palladius, Lausiac History (with Vitae P.a: In the first passage a monk finds that dreams cast darkness over his reason. An elder says he has not restrained his mind from the visions within the dreams, and advises vigil and prayer with a sober mind. Six years of sleepless standing leave his desire unconquered. Another passage lists what disturbs prayer: wandering thoughts, memory of kin, and earthly concerns that divide the mind so that it cannot see God. A third account describes a hermit whose mind breaks into thoughts and whose memory is so affected that a woman seems present with him.

q.t: That holy man said to him: "You have not yet restrained your mind from the visions that dwell within those dreams; for that reason you endure these things.

This falling of the mind happens to everyone who has not entirely renounced this world, but hunts to please it. For through many things that he undertakes, bodily and earthly concerns divide his mind; and while he subsequently disputes with the disturbances of his soul, he cannot see God.
The third night followed, and it added a triple evil. For his mind quickly broke into thoughts. His memory was so affected that a woman seemed to be present with him and lying down at the same time.

Buddhaghosa, Visuddhimagga|||Buddhist.a: Buddhaghosa describes how a visible object is cognized in sequence. Subconsciousness ceases, then adverting, seeing, receiving, scrutinizing and determining arise and cease, and apperception follows. Restraint or non-restraint of the sense faculty arises at the moment of apperception, according to whether mindfulness or forgetfulness is present. Another passage assigns conditions to each stage in the five-door and mind-door processes, with eye, forms, light and attention conditioning eye-consciousness. In the base of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, coarse perception is absent and subtle perception remains.

k.g: knowledge of the minds of others

q.t: But indeed, when a visible object enters the avenue of sight, then, on the cessation of the subconsciousness after arising two or three times, the inoperative mind-element (or, the five-door-adverting) arises, accomplishing the function of adverting, and then ceases.

Therefore, the ancient masters stated: "Dependent on the eye, forms, light, and attention, eye-consciousness arises. Dependent on the ear, sounds, the ear-canal, and attention, ear-consciousness arises.

This Jhana, along with its associated phenomena, is not called "having perception" because there is no coarse perception, and it is not called "having no perception" because subtle perception still exists. For this reason, this Jhana is called Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.

Macrobius, Commentary on the Dream of Sc.a: The pages shown from Macrobius deal with the senses and the soul's relation to the body. He holds that the soul is more divine than any body and needs no sensation itself, and that it places a "breathing-space" (spiramentum) in the brain to produce and govern the five senses. Seeing involves sense, reason and memory, and he says the senses depend on reason.

q.t: However, for a man to consist of parts and be a living animal, the soul provides for this by illuminating the body. Furthermore, it illuminates by inhabiting it, and its dwelling place is in the brain.
Because the duty that completes seeing for the purpose of distinguishing form is threefold—sense, reason, memory—sense refunds the seen thing to reason, and the latter remembers what was seen.
Thus it is proven that the efficacy of the senses depends upon reason. Therefore, God the Creator placed all the senses in the head, that is, around the seat of reason.

Pythagorean Golden Verses with Hierocles.a: The commentary says that we ourselves are the mind. The person addressed is a rational soul and a rational substance, and the text separates the soul from the body and from things outside the body. Anger, desire, the senses and the body are called instruments given to a rational existence for use. The text directs trust to right reason alone, which can distinguish what should be fled from what should be followed.

q.t: For both harm the animus mind/soul, and whatever is harmful to the mind becomes useless to us, since we ourselves are the mind. This must be diligently understood, grasping what kind of person you are.

Indeed, all things that are granted for the service and compliance of a rational existence are ours: we are not those things, such as iracundia anger, cupiditas desire, sensus the senses, or the body itself.

Proclus, Commentary on the Timaeus (soul.a: Proclus sets out a series of grades of thought, from the thought identical with the intelligible down to imaginative knowledge, and says that all thought holds the thing known within itself. He places a sensation in the vehicle (ochēma) of the soul that precedes the mortal, organ-bound sensation. The highest and most unified part of the soul is joined to the partial intellect.

q.t: Imagination is a "passive abiding" because it knows whatever it knows as an image, or as a "type of types" and shapes. For that which is common to every form of intellection is this: the yielding up of the very thing known. In this respect, intellection certainly differs from sense-perception.

But there is another sensation prior to this one, located in the vehicle [ochēma; a subtle, "luminous" body that serves as the intermediate carrier for the soul between the physical and divine realms] of the soul, which is immaterial compared to the physical one.
Therefore, it remains that the highest and most unified part of the soul must be established within the act of thinking of the partial intellect, being joined to it through affinity.

Eznik of Kolb, Refutation of the Sects||.a: Eznik states that angels, demons and the spirits of men are incorporeal. He observes that the word for spirit and for wind is the same in Hebrew, Greek, Syriac and Armenian, and he reads the naming of angels as spirits as a reference to their swiftness. God made beings with reason and intellect to receive goodness through their own virtues. The exercise of free will is made the cause of goodness.

k.g: those things which come from the will

q.t: BUT we must also know that angels, demons, and the spirits of men are incorporeal. For of the angels it says: "He made His angels spirits, and His ministers a flame of fire."

And for those endowed with reason and intellect, He ordained that they receive goodness through their respective virtues, but not beauty itself. For He is the giver of beauty, and He made the exercise of free will the cause of goodness.

Claudianus Mamertus, De statu animae|||E.a: Claudianus argues that the soul perceives bodily things through the body and grasps incorporeal things through itself, and he calls the soul's vision intellect. He holds that the senses are distinct from their organs and cannot themselves be sensed. He ties imagination and memory to images the soul has drawn in through the bodily senses.

q.t: The vision of the soul, as has been said often, and it does not weary me to repeat, is intellect. Indeed, corporeal things cannot be understood; they can be sensed by the soul through the body. But just as the soul senses through the body, so it understands through itself, and the substance of things sensed and things understood is vastly different.

For sight is one thing, the eye is another; hearing is one thing, the ears are another; smell is one thing, the nostrils are another; and taste is one thing, the mouth is another. Nor is the hand the same as touch. Therefore, we distinguish hot and cold things by touch, but we do not touch the sense of touching itself.

For whether it imagines for itself those things which it drew through the body, or from those things which it has seen it conjectures and fashions those which it has not seen, it is nonetheless certain that it cannot imagine them within a certain womb of memory except for those things which it received through the body.

Proclus, Elements of Theology and Platon.a: Proposition 184 sorts souls into three kinds: divine souls, souls that turn from Intellect to folly and sometimes perceive by mind and sometimes do not, and souls that remain between, inferior to the divine. The soul moves itself and shares in always cogitating, understanding and perceiving through Mind, which stands before souls, with the One before Mind. The Platonic Theology allows irrational animals with imagination, memory and perception to participate in Intellect, while only rational animals participate in rational soul. It calls reasoning a lesser function of soul and names irrational souls images of souls.

q.t: Every Soul is either divine, or it is that which converts itself from Intellect to folly, or that which always remains between these, but is inferior to divine Souls.

Indeed, the soul itself, on account of the Mind itself, is a participant in always cogitating and understanding—or rather: it is a participant in that faculty through which it always cogitates and understands and perceives things—just as the body, on account of the soul, possesses that faculty by which it moves itself.
As for Intellect, we shall allow not only rational animals to participate in it, but also those irrational ones which possess a cognitive power—I mean imagination, memory, and perception.

Damascius, De principiis (Problems and S.a: Damascius says each of us has consciousness of self, more clearly or more faintly, when we fold back upon ourselves, reflect and examine ourselves. He argues that the non-thinking soul also moves itself toward diverse desires, and that if it moves itself it folds back upon itself and is separable. He adds that all things according to nature are animals and possess a kind of consciousness, very obscure and hidden from our senses. He defines Reason as thinking and thought, the union of the intelligible and the intellectual, with a need that keeps it from being the sovereign Principle.

q.t: Indeed, does not each of us have, more clearly or more faintly, the consciousness of self [1], when he folds back upon himself, when he reflects, when he examines himself, when he stretches the springs of moral life or of knowledge?
For at least all things that are according to nature are animals and possess a kind of consciousness [1], although it is very obscure and hides itself from our senses.

Finally, Reason is thinking and thought; it is the intelligible that which is known by the mind and the intellectual that which pertains to the mind of itself and for itself, and it is the union of the two that is Reason.

John Philoponus, Commentary on De anima|.a: Philoponus distinguishes imagination from sensation by six arguments. The first holds that we have images in dreams while sensation is only potential, so imagination and sensation differ. Sensation does not know its own activity, while the intellect knows its own and that of others. The intellect acts on universals, and sensation concerns the particular and is directed outward. Imagination is intermediate between sensation and thought: it comes from sensation, gives principles to thought, and thought cannot act without it. Thought is quickly deceived, and sensation is not.

q.t: If imagination and sensation were the same thing, then since we experience imagination when we dream, we would also necessarily be sensing at that time. But in fact, we do not sense [while dreaming]; therefore, imagination and sensation are not the same.
Second, sensation does not know its own activity, but the intellect knows both its own and that of the others.

He says that imagination differs from these in that it is intermediate between sensation and thought. For it comes from sensation; for the sensation gives to the imagination, and the imagination, in turn, gives principles to the thought. For without imagination, the thought cannot act.

Boethius, Consolatio philosophiae|||Earl.a: Boethius holds that each cognitive power judges by its own faculty and not by the nature of the thing known. Sense has no power over things outside matter, imagination does not grasp universal species, and reason does not capture the simple form. Intelligence looks from above and knows all of these in one stroke of the mind.

q.t: Do you see, therefore, that all things, in knowing, use their own faculty rather than the nature of those things which are known? And this is not unjust, for since every judgment exists by the act of the judge, it is necessary that each one performs its work not from an alien power, but from its own.
Intelligence, however, exists as a higher eye. For, having surpassed the ambit of universality, it beholds that very simple form with the pure gaze of the mind.

But Reason is only for the human race, just as Intelligence is for the Divine. Whence it happens that this knowledge excels the others, because by its own nature it understands not only what is proper to it, but also knows the subjects of other knowledges.

Simplicius (or Priscian), Commentary on.a: Simplicius takes up whether a dream is an affection of the intellectual or the perceptual part of the soul, since these are the two parts through which one knows. In the commentary on the third book he distinguishes the intellect acted upon by the intelligible from the active intellect within the soul. He holds that the appetitive faculty is always joined with cognition and appears within both reason and the imaginative faculty.

q.t: He asks first by which part of the soul the dream occurs. Since there are two parts of the soul through which one knows, namely the intellect and sense perception, he asks whether the dream is an affection of the intellectual or the perceptual part.

However, he also posits not only the acted-upon intellect but also the active intellect within the soul; for he says it is necessary for these differences to exist within the soul as well. Therefore, he likens the active one in the soul to a habit and a light, so that the intellect above the soul may stand more in accordance with the illuminator.

For even within reason there is a certain appetite, which is boulēsis will/volition, and within the imaginative faculty are the thymoeides spirited and the epithymētikon desiring [faculties]. For it is not possible to desire without cognition, as has been said; for this reason, it exists entirely with some form of cognition.

Cassiodorus, De anima|||Early Christian.a: Cassiodorus says the soul of man is called anima because it is immortal and far separated from blood, and that spirit is spoken of in three ways. He distinguishes soul from mind and understanding, which excel in the soul. He lists five natural virtues of the soul: sensible, imperative, principal, vital and pleasure. He holds that the souls of infants and fools do not grow, and that reason grows in little ones by long meditation.

q.t: But the mind [original: "Animus"] is called ἀπὸ τὰ ἀνέμω from the wind, that is, from the wind, because its thought wanders most swiftly like the wind in rapid motion.

The first is sensitive in both parts, which grants us intelligence and sense, through which we feel all incorporeal things by varied imagination: it also makes the bodily senses thrive, that is, sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch, by which we feel hard and soft, smooth and rough things.
But who does not perceive that the souls of little ones, because of the weakness of the body, can neither explain the offices of the senses nor the ministries of the members?

David the Invincible, Definitions of Phi.a: David lists the cognitive powers as sensation, imagination, opinion, deliberation and intellect, and says imagination makes particular knowledge manifest. One argument he reports holds that the knower, called the self, must change along with a knowable that changes. The definitions define cognition as a movement of the mind into understanding.

q.t: Because it is necessary to know the scientific power of sensation, imagination, opinion, deliberation, intellect, and sensation.
But if the knowable moves, and changes, then it is necessary also for the knower, that is, the self, to be moved with, to be changed with the knowable.
Cognition: the movement of the mind into understanding, from the cognitive which is in another, a cognitive of the world.

Gregory the Great, Dialogi IV|||Early Ch.a: Gregory says dreams arise from various causes, sometimes from thought and revelation together, and that holy men discern whether an image comes from a good spirit or from the deceiver. He infers the life of the soul in the body from the movements of the limbs, and argues the same inference holds for the soul after death from the miracles at the bodies of martyrs. He says the spirit of prophecy does not always illuminate the hearts of the prophets.

q.t: But certainly, since dreams come from such various things, one should believe in them the more heavily the more one cannot easily recognize from what thing they come. But holy men, among the delusions of revelations, recognize distinctly the voices and images with an innermost taste, so that they know what they receive from a good spirit, or what they suffer from the deceiver.

If now you recognize the life of the soul that remains in the body from the movements of the limbs, why do you not also note the life of the soul after the body through the dead bones in the power of the miracles?

For when He gives the spirit of prophecy at one time and withdraws it at another, He lifts the hearts of the prophets on high and keeps them in humility, so that they may discover, when they receive the spirit, what is of God, and again, when they do not have the spirit, that they recognize what they are of themselves.

Ardā Wīrāz Nāmag (Book of Ardā Wīrāz)|||.a: The soul of Vîrâf goes from the body to the Peak of the Law and the Bridge of the Requiter, and returns on the seventh day and night to enter the body. He rises as if waking from a pleasant sleep, with a good mind (Vohûman-mînishn) and joyful.

q.t: 2 and on the seventh day and night it returned, and entered the body. 3 Vîrâf rose up as if waking from a pleasant sleep, 4 good-minded and joyful.

John Climacus, Ladder of Divine Ascent||.a: John Climacus defines a dream as an agitation of the mind while the body is at rest, and a phantasm as a mockery of the eyes in a sleeping mind. He says demons use dreams to show beginners images of their household. Much sleep dulls the soul and produces forgetfulness, while vigils clear the memory, drive away foul dreams and let the monk catch his thoughts. A mind free from every affection of the senses is the contemplation of celestial things perceived by the intellect.

q.t: "A dream is an agitation of the mind" while the body is at rest. A phantasm or vision is a mockery of the eyes in a sleeping mind.
The monk who stays awake throughout the night is a fisherman of his own thoughts. In the tranquility of the night, he observes and catches them with no trouble.
A mind free from every affection of the senses is the contemplation of celestial things which are perceived by the intellect. Silence and stillness are the enemies of vain glory.

Candrakīrti, Madhyamakāvatāra|||Buddhist.a: Candrakīrti holds that memory arises conventionally from its own specific conditions, so it does not prove self-awareness (svasaṃvedana). He applies the dream analogy to the mind: in a dream the eye, its object and the mind generated by it are all false. For the Madhyamika the mind does not exist in a dream, and consciousness is defined by its cognizance of an object.

q.t: Thus, even without self-awareness, memory arises conventionally because it is produced from the specific conditions for the arising of memory.
Just as according to your system, the Vijnanavadin Proponent of Consciousness-Only, external objects like forms are not born in a dream, likewise the mental consciousness is also not born.
A consciousness without an object is impossible, because consciousness is defined by its cognizance of an object.

Isidore of Seville, Etymologiae XI / Sen.a: Isidore says the soul takes different names by function: soul when it gives life, mind when it wills, intellect when it knows, memory when it recollects, reason when it judges, spirit when it breathes, sense when it senses. He denies that the soul is air. He derives mens from knowing or remembering, calls forgetful people amentes, and lists three kinds of vision: through the eyes of the body, through the spirit that imagines, and through intuition of the mind. The praecordia are the places near the heart where sense is perceived.

q.t: Therefore, when it gives life to the body, it is soul; when it wills, it is mind; when it knows, it is intellect; when it recollects, it is memory; when it judges what is right, it is reason; when it breathes, it is spirit; when it senses something, it is sense.

The third type of vision, however, is that which is grasped neither by bodily senses, nor by that part of the soul by which images of bodily things are captured, but through an intuition of the mind by which truth understood is perceived;
The praecordia diaphragm/region of the heart are the places near the heart by which sense is perceived; and they are called praecordia because the principle of the heart and thought is there.

Qurʾān (nafs, rūḥ, qalb; sleep as death;.a: The Qurʾān describes God taking souls at death and, for the living, in sleep, then keeping some and sending others back for a set term. It says God breathed into the first human from His spirit and gave hearing, vision and hearts. In the Joseph narrative a king reports a vision of fat and lean kine, and his chiefs say they cannot interpret dreams.

q.t: God takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die [in their sleep]. Then He keeps those for which He has decreed death and releases the others for a specified term. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect.
from His spirit, and He made for you hearing, vision, and hearts. Little are you grateful.
They said: "A jumble of dreams! And we are not learned in the interpretation of dreams."

Kumārila Bhaṭṭa, Ślokavārttika (Ātmavāda.a: Kumārila places cognition in the soul, which he names as the cognizer and credits with the power of remembering and recognizing past experience. He holds that sense-perception can include specification through memory while remaining dependent on the sense-organs. He argues that the Self, though one, is taken as cogniser and as cognised through its diverse properties.

q.t: Therefore, when the contact of the object with the sense-organ is present, the person—though specifying the object through Memory by means of its own characteristics—comes to have the sensuous perception of that object.
The fact of the word ‘I’ applying only to the Inner Self Pratyagātman is based upon the extreme proximity (of the cognising ‘I’ with the cognised ‘object’).

Xuanzang, Cheng weishi lun (成唯識論) with K.a: The text names the seventh consciousness manas-vijñāna, which deliberates on the eighth consciousness and weighs it to be a "self". The other six consciousnesses discriminate gross objects. Foolish people falsely calculate a real self and phenomena from the appearance and image parts that arise when vasana imprint the base consciousness. In Dharmapāla's interpretation, the body of consciousness is the self-witnessing division, which changes to resemble the appearing and seeing divisions.

q.t: "Measuring" [original: "量"] means to quantify/weigh. It deliberates on the eighth consciousness, weighing it to be a "self." Therefore, it is also called "constantly and precisely deliberating."
Foolish people do not understand that this is only internal consciousness, and relying on it, they falsely calculate that there is a real self and phenomena.
The body of all consciousness is the self-witnessing division [original: "自證分"], which changes to resemble the appearing and seeing divisions [original: "相見二分"] and comes into existence.

Bādarāyaṇa, Brahma-sūtra with Śaṅkara's.a: The commentary says the internal organ antahkarana is called manas, buddhi, vijnana, or chitta, and is called mind by functions such as doubt and intellect by functions such as determination. It argues the organ must be accepted, since otherwise perception would occur perpetually or never. On dreams, it says that if chariots were made by mere will, no one would see an unpleasant dream, and it concludes the dream is māyā-mātra, caused by impressions from waking. On deep sleep, it reads Brihadaranyaka 4.3.21 as naming the individual soul as knower, while the Intelligent Self prajna is the Supreme Lord.

q.t: Within this context, the internal organ antahkarana the inner instrument of the mind which acts as the limiting adjunct of the soul, is described in many ways: as mind manas, intellect buddhi, consciousness vijnana, or thought-stuff chitta. Sometimes it is called "mind" when categorized by its functions such as doubt, and "intellect" when categorized by functions such as determination.
If the creation of chariots in a dream were by mere will, no one would ever see an unpleasant dream. For no one wills something unpleasant for themselves.

Regarding deep sleep, the text says: "This person, embraced by the Intelligent Self prajna-atman, knows nothing at all, neither what is outside nor what is inside" [Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.3.21]. Here, the "person" must be the individual soul because he is the knower; the denial of knowledge is possible only when there is a potential to know the internal and external.

Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra|||Buddhist.a: Śāntideva's chapter on watchfulness says the rules are kept by guarding the fickle thought, which he compares to a young elephant bound by the rope of remembrance. He says all terrors and griefs come from thought alone. The ch. 9 commentary says the intellect (buddhi) cannot be perceived by a previous, later or simultaneous knowledge, and that self-awareness is therefore illogical. It also argues that a Self made conscious through union with consciousness would be destroyed in intoxication or fainting.

q.t: He who would keep the rules must diligently guard his thought; the rules cannot be kept by him who guards not the fickle thought.

First, it cannot be perceived by a previous knowledge, because that previous knowledge has not yet arisen or no longer exists at that time. Nor can it be perceived by a later knowledge, because the object to be grasped is momentary and would have already passed away.
If it is conscious through union with consciousness, then when it is unconscious, it follows that it is destroyed. (66)

Zhouyi Cantong qi (related precursor tex.a: The text instructs the practitioner at midwinter to seal the opening, clarify the heart-mind and preserve silence, so that spirit coagulates and qi gathers. Numinous mercury is attained by emptying the heart-mind and concentrating the spirit. The commentary says the Shishen (discursive spirit) can take shapes and ghost faces to disturb the master of the heart, and the visions dissipate if the master stays unmoved. It gives the example of a snake catcher who dreams of a snake without terror.

q.t: Conceal their outer outlines and sink them deep into the cavernous void. Then the spirit coagulates, the qi vital breath gathers, and the golden liquid forms and crystalizes. This oral secret for cultivating the elixir takes the gathering of vital breath and the coagulation of spirit as its foremost principle.

When we investigate where it originates, it is attained through emptying the heart-mind and concentrating the spirit. Because it issues from one's own heart-mind, it is called numinous mercury, and also termed spiritual mercury.

If the heart wishes to dispel consciousness, the Shishen conscious or discursive spirit still remains. It then transforms into various shapes and images, appearing with the heads of spirits and the faces of ghosts to confuse and disturb the master of the heart.

Śūraṅgama Sūtra|||Chinese.a: The sutra has the Buddha question Ananda about where mind, consciousness and the sense realms originate. Each realm is tested against the sense organ, the object and their union, and none is found to have self-nature. The root of awareness is examined against waking, sleeping, birth and extinction, and the mind's attachment to dharma-dust (mental objects) is described as an internal dust.

q.t: If there is a faculty of discrimination that exists apart from the preceding dusts, then that is your true mind. If the faculty of discrimination has no substance when separated from the dusts, then it is merely the preceding dusts.

As such, Ananda, you should know that this root of awareness does not come from waking or sleeping, does not exist through birth or extinction, does not emerge from the sense organ, and does not arise from emptiness.

Ananda, furthermore, as you understand it, the mind and objects serve as the condition to produce mind-consciousness. Is this consciousness produced because of the mind, taking the mind as its realm, or produced because of objects, taking the objects as its realm?

Śūraṅgama Sūtra (大佛頂首楞嚴經)|||Buddhist.a: The text takes each sense realm in turn and asks whether the consciousness arises from the faculty or from the object. For mind-consciousness it says the faculty has no form and consciousness no function apart from objects. It also says consciousness born from flavor would itself become flavor and could not taste itself. In the meditation section, soul, spirits, willpower, and consciousness are cast aside and secret meanings are heard in empty space. This is called a "good state" and not a holy realization.

q.t: Ananda, if it is born because of the mind, then within your mind there must be thoughts that manifest your mind. If there are no prior objects, the mind has nothing from which to be produced.
If consciousness is born because of flavor, the consciousness itself would become the flavor. It would be the same as the tongue faculty, where it should not be able to taste itself.

Furthermore, using this mind to refine and sharpen both internally and externally, at that time the soul, spirits, willpower, and consciousness [these represent the various aspects of the cognitive mind] are all cast aside, and the body and the rest interact as host and guest.

Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch (L.a: The Platform Sutra says self-nature can contain all ten thousand things and is called the storehouse consciousness. When thought arises it is transformed consciousness, producing the six consciousnesses that go out the six gates and perceive the six dusts. It says one's own mind is the Buddha and nothing outside the mind can be established. "No-thought" means seeing all dharmas with the heart unstained and unattached, and making all thoughts cease is called bondage and a one-sided view.

q.t: Self-nature can contain all ten thousand things, which is called the storehouse consciousness. If thought arises, it is transformed consciousness. It produces the six consciousnesses, exits the six gates, and perceives the six dusts.

Your own mind is the Buddha, so have no further doubts. Outside of the mind, there is not a single thing that can be established. Everything is the original mind giving birth to ten thousand kinds of phenomena.
What is called 'no-thought'? If you see all dharmas things/phenomena but the heart remains unstained and unattached, that is no-thought.

Mālinīvijayottara Tantra|||Indian.a: Verses assign classes of beings to the states: the bound soul sakala to waking, the two unbound souls vijnanakala and pralayakala to dreaming and deep sleep, and the Mantras, their Lords and the Supreme Lord to turya. Another passage traces limited agency (kala-tattva) to the unmanifest, the gunas, the intellect dhi, and ego ahankara, then to the buddhindriyas and karmendriyas. Chapter 15 says bondage and liberation belong to the senses. Senses together with the mind in a pervasive state are called liberated, and senses situated in an object or external place are called bound.

k.g: the state of being conscious but limited
those who exist in the state of dissolution

q.t: The two unbound souls akala [referring to vijnanakala and pralayakala] should be properly known in dreaming and deep sleep. The group of Mantras, their Lords, and the Supreme Lord is remembered as the fourth state turya.
From that very principle of limited agency, the unmanifest was created. From that, the qualities gunas in eightfold form, and from them the intellect dhi. From the intellect, ego ahankara was born.

The wise have declared that both bondage and liberation belong to the senses. When restrained, they lead to bondage [here meaning restricted or worldly engagement]; when released, they lead to liberation.

Theology of Aristotle (Arabic Plotinus,.a: The text describes thought and memory as belonging to the soul's life in the sensible world, with thought as a medium between Intellect and sense. It ranks intellects as divine, human and brutal, each with its own thinking faculty. The rational soul is perfected by the Agent Intellect and depends on the sensitive soul to be stirred toward principles.

q.t: The Soul, turning away from the Intellect Intellect/Divine Mind and descending to this world while speculating on some of its affairs, possesses memory beyond the Intellect. It does not, however, remember higher beings, otherwise it would not have descended here.

For the thinking faculty of man extends the thing perceived by sense to the intellect, which, confirming it, admits it, or, not confirming it, casts it away. And sometimes, having turned toward the sense, it will confirm it, and having returned again to itself, it ruminates within itself many times until it believes the thing is clearly true.

The Intellectual Soul, existing in this lesser world, understands through thought because its intellect, derived from the First [referring to the First Principle or God], is deficient and becomes material, that is, potential. And indeed, the Agent Intellect perfects the Rational Soul when it produces it, just as a father produces a son.

Canonical ḥadīth: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (Kitā.a: The narrations show the Prophet relating a dream seen in sleep and giving its interpretation as religion. Asked about the Rūḥ, the spirit, he answers with the verse that its knowledge lies with the Lord and that people have been given little knowledge. Companions are also shown thinking through a question the Prophet puts to test their knowledge.

q.t: “While I was sleeping I saw (in a dream) that some people were displayed before me wearing shirts, of which some were reaching up to the breasts only, while others were even shorter than that. And ‘Umar bin Al-Khaṭṭāb was displayed before me wearing a (long) shirt which he was dragging.”
Say: Rūḥ the spirit is one of the things, the knowledge of which is only with my Lord. And of knowledge, you (mankind) have been given only a little.
Everybody started thinking about the trees of the desert areas. And I thought of the date-palm tree but felt shy to answer.

al-Jāḥiẓ, Kitāb al-Ḥayawān (animal minds.a: Al-Jāḥiẓ says animals perceive dangers and secure their livelihood by nature, without deliberation, and that some attain in this what a person of careful deliberation does not. He reports an unnamed leader of the dialecticians who held the soul to be of the nature of the breeze. He also attributes desert tales of ghouls and jinn to loneliness, scattered minds and imagining.

q.t: They perceive this by nature without deliberation, and by the sense of the soul without thought, so that the one who reflects may take warning, the one who thinks may ponder, one may remove from himself amazement, and one may know his own measure of helplessness, the limit of his strength, and the extent of the reach of his sight, and that he is a created being, arranged, directed, and facilitated.

When a person feels lonely, the small appears large to them, they fall into doubt, their mind becomes scattered, and their humors are disturbed. They see what is not there and hear what is not heard. They imagine a trivial thing to be something great and magnificent.
Therefore, the soul is of the nature of the breeze; with its corruption, the bodies are corrupted, and with its soundness, they are sound.

al-Kindī, On Sleep and Dreams / On the I.a: Al-Kindī describes imagination (phantasia) as a formative virtue that gives individual forms without their matter when the objects are absent from the senses. He reports that deep thought can suspend the use of sight and hearing in a waking person. On the intellect, he says the soul is rational in potentia and passes to act through the first reason, which is always in act.

q.t: And this virtue performs its operations in the state of sleep and waking. However, in sleep, it is of more apparent operation and formation than in waking.

And the third indeed is that which is to the soul in act, which it has already deposited, wherefore it is found by it when it wishes to use it, and it makes it appear with discovery without anything else from it. Just as writing is to the scribe; for it is ready and possible for him, since he has already stored and fixed it in his soul.

And when the rational form is united with it, then it and the reason are one thing, the rational and the rationalized. The reason and the rationalized are, therefore, one thing from the side of the soul.

Vasugupta, Śiva Sūtra with Kṣemarāja's V.a: Kṣemarāja comments that nothing exists unperceived, so the act of consciousness is the common nature of everything, and the one who perceives is independent in all knowledge and action. He lists the body, life-force, mind, and void as views of the Self held by the worldly, Cārvākas, Vedists, Yogācāra, and Mādhyamika, and says the body and the rest are grasped because consciousness illuminates them. Another passage defines mind mānasa as intention, intellect cetanā as the logical faculty, energy śakti as breath, and the self ātmā as the limited perceiver. When these four are exhausted, the Body of Bhairava appears.

k.g: the level of equality of consciousness

q.t: In this world, because nothing exists that is not perceived [original: achetitasya], the act of consciousness is the common nature of everything. He who perceives is called the conscious one, who is independent in all knowledge and action.

The "mind" mānasa consists of intention; "intellect" cetanā is the logical faculty; "energy" śakti is the breath; and the "self" ātmā is the limited perceiver conditioned by these. When these four are exhausted, meaning they have attained the state of the wonder of consciousness, then the previously mentioned "Body of Bhairava" comes into being.

Rather, it is just as stated: "Consciousness alone." Even when it takes the position of an imagined knower like the body, it shines as the true knower, consisting of unconstructed reflection on the "I."

Vijñānabhairava|||Indian.a: The commentary on verse 138 lists mind as thought, intellect as consciousness, the Shakti identified with breath, and the Self as the limited observer. It says that when these four are exhausted the Bhairava form appears. In the commentary on verse 86, waking, dream and deep sleep are linked to vishva, taijasa and prajna, and objects perceived through the senses are said to be consciousness, like reflections in a mirror.

q.t: The mind, which is composed of thought; consciousness, which is the intellect; the Shakti, which is identified with the breath; and the Self, which is the limited observer defined by these—when this quartet is exhausted and has attained the wonder of pure awareness, then that is the aforementioned Bhairava form, which is "joy in the experience of one's own inner Self."

Furthermore, the light—or illumination—of external objects, which arise from the impressions of the waking state, is the subject of the dream state. Then, again, the darkness—which is the experience of ignorance—rests in the state of deep sleep.
Just as the sun's disk is merely condensed light, so too does consciousness, when thickened, shine as the world; this is the tradition.

Eriugena, Periphyseon IV|||Medieval Lati.a: Eriugena describes sense as a phantasia of sensible things received through the body, and distinguishes exterior sense, aisthesis, with its five instruments, from interior sense. He names nous as intellect, logos as reason, and dianoia as interior sense, and calls these three the essential trinity of the soul in the image of God. He says the soul is whole and indivisible, whole in the senses, in memory, and above memory, and that its different motions receive different names. Intellect contemplates the Creator, reason investigates the reasons of things, and interior sense finds, discerns, and defines them.

q.t: For in that language, nous [original: "νῦς"] is called intellect, logos [original: "λόος"] is reason, and dianoia [original: "διάνοια"] is sense—not that exterior sense, but the interior one. In these three, the essential trinity of the soul, established in the image of God, subsists.

For while it attends to its Creator above itself, and above the intelligence of the whole creation, the intellect, or mind, or spirit is engaged in a contemplative motion. While it investigates the reasons of things in a second, natural motion, it is reason. While it finds them, discerns, and defines them, it is the interior sense.

To conclude briefly: whatever the soul knows uniformly and universally through its first movement (which is the intellect) concerning God and the primordial causes, it fixes in the same uniform and universal way by its second movement (which is reason).

Spanda-kārikā with Kṣemarāja's Nirṇaya a.a: Kṣemarāja describes waking as perceiving objects through the sense organs, dreaming as perceiving objects through the mind alone manas, and deep sleep as a state where mind activity ceases and no object other than the self is perceived. Memory is grouped with dreaming, and intoxication and fainting with deep sleep. On unmeṣa, he says that when focus on one thought closes, all trains of thought are swallowed up and the Supreme arises as spanda pulsation. In sound sleep the all-pervading principle appears as consciousness because the knowable objective world has stopped.

k.g: the subtle body consisting of eight elements

q.t: Due to the closing of that focus, all trains of thought are suddenly swallowed up. It is the arising of the Supreme, which is of the nature of spanda pulsation, which is non-dual like the sun and moon, and which is an otherworldly delight, a different and wonderful state.

Dreaming svapna is the state of sleep in which the person is weary from their external activities. Even though the "play" of the senses like hearing has ceased, the person continues to perceive objects through the mind alone manas.
In the sound sleep this all-pervading principle appears to him as identical with consciousness, owing to the stoppage of the entire knowable, viz., objective world.

Bundahišn|||Zoroastrian.a: In West's translation the soul (rûbân) is created before the body, and the body exists for activity. The first human pair change from plants into human shape when the breath (nismô), identified with the soul rûbân, enters them. The evil spirit and his demons work on the mind: Akoman brings vile thoughts, and Andar restrains the thoughts of the creatures from virtuous deeds.

q.t: it is given into the body so that it may produce activity, and the body is created only for activity; hence the conclusion is this: that the soul rûbân [The immortal part of a person in Zoroastrian theology.] is created before and the body after.
He plants this thought in the minds of men: that this religion of Ohrmazd is worthless, and it is not necessary to remain faithful to it.

(18) And the intellect and the faculty of thought, the body and the soul Ravan [The immortal soul that survives the body.], Paradise Behesht [The "Best Existence" or Heaven.], Hell Dozakh [The place of punishment.], and the future life; and more on that same matter.

5. This, too, that what is produced by the words of Vohûman [Good Mind/Thought, an Amesha Spenta.] is taught by him who shall perform the ceremonial of the sacred beings with the thoughts of Vohûman; even for this reason, because, the mind being with the thoughts of Vohûman, the tongues of the faithful are habituated (khûkînîdakŏ) in the statements of Vohûman.

k.g: one who is pure consciousness but remains limited

q.t: It is you alone who shine in consciousness. Even in the inferior state, whether one thinks "I know this pot" or "this is a pot," in the vision of duality, it would not be possible for the object to shine without the nature of consciousness.

Now, if it is said that knowledge does not belong to the mind, such knowledge is not substantiated, because the mind is an instrument and is insentient. If that is the case, what then is the role of the self here? [107]
If consciousness existed in every individual atom, there would result a multitude of conscious beings. Pots and other objects would not be considered separate from these atoms. [Verse 20]

al-Rāzī (Rhazes), al-Ṭibb al-rūḥānī (Spi.a: Al-Rāzī says passion al-hawa sees only what is to its own advantage and is veiled from what is to its detriment. A person is blinded to the faults of their own soul and perceives their few virtues as much greater than they are. He also says the soul al-nafs loves and attaches to a state from the first impulse, without investigating a higher one. We cannot be certain this attachment comes from the judgment of reason, since it may come from inclination and passion.

q.t: As for passion [original: "al-hawa." This refers to impulsive desires or whims that often lead the soul away from rational judgment.], it sees only what is to its own advantage.

Of these [states], the soul [original: "al-nafs". In this philosophical context, this refers to the self or the human psyche, often viewed as the seat of both desires and spiritual potential.] loves it, prefers it, and attaches itself to it from the very first impulse. This occurs without investigation or thought regarding the state which is more sublime and higher.

al-Rāzī, al-Ḥāwī / al-Manṣūrī (brain, me.a: Al-Rāzī links temperament to mental traits and to sleep. Cold bodies are described as coarse in thought and will, with little wit, few desires and much sleep. Moist bodies sleep much, are dull-witted and quick to fear, while hot bodies sleep little and are hurried. In the chapter on sleep, its benefits include relaxing the body, increasing vision, removing grief, and aiding digestion, while excess causes dullness and increases phlegm and coldness. Sleep after food is said to keep food from leaving the stomach.

q.t: Their actions are sluggish and slow. They are coarse in thought and will, possessing little wit. Their speech and looks are restricted.
Among the benefits of sleep is that it relaxes the body and increases vision. It removes grief which may dull the limbs. it improves digestion and the constitution of the body.

Utpaladeva, Īśvarapratyabhijñā-kārikā wi.a: The commentary holds that in memory the previous experience exists as svasaṃvedana, internal self-awareness, and does not appear as a distinct cognition. It says that unification of the means of knowledge happens through the power of the cognizer (pramātṛ), the conscious subject. All conceptualization is said to be of the nature of memory because it grasps what was already grasped. Citing the Ajadapramatrsiddhi, it states that the functions of mind (manas), intellect (buddhi) and senses are of the nature of consciousness as reflection.

q.t: Thus, this much must be accepted: even at the time of memory, the previous experience exists as an internal self-awareness svasaṃvedana self-cognition and is not manifested as something distinct from the cognition that makes the existence of the memory's form known.

because it consists of grasping what has already been grasped, all conceptualization is of the nature of memory; it only appears as if it does not have that form when it arises colored by the shadow of experience.
the individual soul is in ultimate reality pure existence. Thus, the functions of the mind, intellect, and senses are indeed of the nature of consciousness as reflection.

al-Fārābī, al-Madīna al-fāḍila (Virtuous.a: Al-Fārābī lists the faculties in the order they arise in a human being: nutritive, sensory with its desire or dislike, imaginative, and rational. The imaginative faculty preserves what was depicted from sense objects after they vanish, and composes and separates them, sometimes falsely and sometimes truly. In the chapter on dreams, it stands between the sensory and rational faculties and receives impressions from the five senses while serving the rational and appetitive faculties. A human who receives the Active Intellect through the passive and acquired intellects is a philosopher by what reaches the passive intellect and a prophet by what reaches the imaginative faculty.

k.g: the human mind capable of receiving knowledge
the intellect joined with the Active Intellect
the transcendent intelligence that facilitates human cognition

q.t: Then, another faculty emerges in them, by which they preserve what was depicted in their soul from the objects of sense after they have vanished from the observation of the senses. This is the imaginative faculty power of mental representation.

The imaginative faculty Vorstellungskraft stands in the middle between the sensory faculty Sinneskraft and the rational faculty Denkkraft the power of thought. Now, when all the nourishers of the sensory faculty, namely the five senses, perceive in actuality and perform their work, the imaginative faculty receives impressions from them.

By what flows from it to his passive intellect, he is a wise man, a philosopher, and a perfect thinker. By what flows from it to his imaginative faculty, he is a prophet, a warner of what will be, and an informer of what is now regarding particulars, with an existence through which he perceives the divine.

al-Fārābī, Risāla fī l-ʿaql (De intellec.a: Al-Farabi opens by listing six senses of the name intellect. The first is the sense in which the masses call a man intellectual, tied to good counsel in acquiring what is truly good and refraining from the bad. The others are the intellect speakers invoke when they say it mandates or rejects something, and those Aristotle mentions in the Demonstration, the Ethics, and the Metaphysics.

q.t: Abu Nasr Muhammad ibn Muhammad Al-Farabi said: The name "intellect" is said in many ways. The first of them is the thing by which the masses say of a man that he is "intellectual" ( maskil ).

Yoga Vāsiṣṭha / Mokṣopāya|||Indian.a: Vasishtha teaches Rama that the mind (chitta) is the intellect (chit) exhibiting itself as thought, and that the mind consists of the union of intellectual and vibrating powers. Imagination and volition belong to the mind and give rise to worldly evils unless restrained. Sleeping dreams lie inside the waking dream of the world, and the mind knows things alike in waking and dreaming.

q.t: The breath of life is inert by itself, and its pulsation is the effect and composed of the surrounding air; so the action of the mind, is owing to the force of the intellect; whose pellucidity pervades all nature.
The souls of all living beings are subject to the three states of waking, dreaming, and sound sleep, which are caused by the mind and not by the body.
Learn then this truth from me: this world is a dream, and you and all other men have your sleeping dreams contained within your waking dreams of this visionary world.

al-Niffarī, Mawāqif and Mukhāṭabāt|||Ara.a: Al-Niffarī sorts thoughts into kingdom-like (malakutiyya), domain-like (mulkiyya) and angelic (malakiyya), and adds Satanic thoughts of doubt, polytheism, innovation and denial. The tongues of thoughts are science, interpretation and alteration. In one passage, the intellect is the tool of knowledge, knowledge the tool of gnosis, and gnosis the tool of becoming known, while becoming known and the Stay are not tools. In an address, God tells the servant that between them stands the servant's finding of themself (wajduka bika), and that casting it away leads to being veiled from oneself.

q.t: Thoughts branch out: some are of the hidden kingdom malakutiyya, some are of the manifest domain mulkiyya, and some are angelic malakiyya.
The intellect is the tool of knowledge through which it acts. Knowledge is the tool of gnosis. Gnosis is the tool of becoming known.
O servant, between Me and you is your finding of yourself wajduka bika your self-consciousness or subjective experience; cast it away, and I shall veil you from yourself.

Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, Rasāʾil (epistles on so.a: The Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ define sciences as the forms of known things in the soul of the knower. Teaching is the awakening of the soul that knows in potentiality by the soul that knows in actuality, and learning is the soul's conception of the form of the known thing. Intellectual speech is the soul's conceptualization of meanings within itself and its discrimination of them in thought. The human is defined as a rational, mortal animal, with speech and life from the soul and death from the body. In the animal debate, the five senses report to the mind without being commanded and compare what they perceive when the mind investigates.

q.t: Teaching is the awakening of the soul that is knowing in potentiality by the soul that is knowing in actuality, and learning is the soul’s conception of the form of the known thing.

As for intellectual speech, which is a spiritual, intelligible matter, it is the soul's conceptualization of the meanings of things within itself, its vision of the forms of sensible things in its essence, and its discrimination of them in its thought.

The five senses do not need to be commanded or forbidden when they bring things they perceive to the attention and knowledge of the mind. When the mind focuses on investigating something, the senses—without hesitation or delay—compare it with something else and communicate the result to the mind.

Nemicandra, Dravyasaṃgraha|||Indian.a: Nemicandra gives two views of the soul. From the ordinary point of view it has a period of life, respiration, the five senses and the three forces of thought, word and action. From the realistic point of view it is distinguished by consciousness (upayoga), which is of two kinds, perception (darśana) and knowledge (ṇāṇa). Perception is indeterminate and has four kinds: visual, non-visual, clairvoyant and omniscient. Five-sensed souls are divided into those with mind (samaṇā) and those without (amaṇā), and all beings with one to four senses are without mind.

q.t: Thus, from the ordinary point of view [original: "Vyavahâra Naya"; the practical or conventional perspective], we regard the soul to possess a period of life, during which its characteristics are respiration and the employment of the five senses and the three forces of thought, word and action. But from the realistic point of view [The absolute or essential perspective], the soul is distinguished by its own great quality, viz., consciousness.

The Soul, in its essential nature, possesses perfect and pure Omniscient Perception, which perceives the general existence of all objects existing in the three worlds and across the three periods of time [past, present, and future].
Souls possessing five senses are known to be divided into those with a mind and those without a mind.

Nemicandra, Gommaṭasāra Jīvakāṇḍa|||Indi.a: The Jīvakāṇḍa calls the mind a no-indriya, a quasi-sense, because it lacks the external manifestation of other sense organs. Mental activity and mental knowledge arise in this material mind. Mental knowledge appears in saints with riddhis and is of two kinds, rijumati (simple) and vipulamati (complex). Simple mental knowledge knows what another soul is thinking in the present, while complex mental knowledge also knows what was thought in the past and will be thought in the future. The first can be lost and the second is permanent.

q.t: It is named a no-indriya quasi-sense because it lacks the external manifestation seen in other sense organs. It is within this material mind that mental activity and mental knowledge arise.
