Simple mental knowledge knows the material objects of all three times—past, present, and future—as they are being thought of by a soul in the present moment. Complex mental knowledge knows also what has been thought of in the past and what will be thought of in the future.

al-Majūsī, Kāmil al-ṣināʿa (Pantegni) /.a: Al-Majūsī assigns the senses and phantasy to the spirit in the anterior ventricles, and thought, cognition, foresight, memory and motion to the spirit in the middle ventricle. An obstruction in the middle part destroys thought and cognition, and one in the posterior part destroys only memory. He describes a vital spirit from the heart and an animal spirit from the brain, and sets out vegetative, sensitive and rational souls, with the rational soul's works including intellect and memory.

q.t: It is therefore proven most certainly by what we have said that that spirit which is in the anterior ventricles operates the senses, that is, sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch; and with these it operates athaghil the power of phantasy/imagination, which the Greeks call phantasian imagination. The spirit which is in the middle ventricle operates thought, cognition, foresight, memory, and motion.
The works of the rational soul are cognition, providence, and estimation, doubt, intellect, and memory, and these works belong properly to man among other animals.

For the faculty of imagination sends what it forms and imagines to the intellect. The intellect is the judge and discriminator of the things which it receives from the imagination, whether they are real or from the intellect alone.
As long as there is a spirit in the servant and he is alive, the sensation does not depart from him, because sensation is conjoined with life and the spirit.
There are many theories as to the nature of the spirit, but all who speculate on this subject go astray from the truth, because God has declared that it is beyond human comprehension.
The spirit is two spirits: a spirit by which the creation has life, and a spirit by which the heart has light.

Abhinavagupta, Paramārthasāra (with Yoga.a: The commentary of Yogarāja describes deep sleep as the Prājña state, a mass of knowledge that is still darkened by the impressions of the world's dissolution. It treats the subject in the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) as the knower who takes in objects through the intellect. Perceiving objects while attentive is described as an act of worship that ends in the full "I-consciousness" (pūrṇāhantā).

k.g: the subtle body consisting of eight elements

q.t: Thus, deep sleep is said to be the Prājña state of Brahman, which is consciousness itself. Why? "Due to being a mass of knowledge."

Thus, the wonder camatkāra the bliss of inner resonance that occurs incessantly at the time of accepting each object, which is the blooming of the full "I-consciousness," is itself the worship of the deity of one's own Self. Therefore, objects like sound are the instruments of worship, for one who is attentive at the time of perceiving objects.

However, when the puryaṣṭaka-pramātṛ the subject residing in the subtle body —within the mirror of the intellect, the mirror of reflection—at the time of grasping objects, accepts subjects like sound, it becomes the object of the "I" consciousness, thinking, "I hear."

Abhinavagupta, Parātrīśikā-vivaraṇa / -l.a: Abhinavagupta describes awareness as the illumination of objects, with knower and known arising together through contraction and expansion. The Purusha is held in the middle by four limiting powers: Kala, impure knowledge, Maya and Raga. The text places the knower in the heart and speaks of a liberation while living reached through reflective awareness.

k.g: the state of being a knower

q.t: In this context, awareness is well known as the illumination of objects. An object consists of the nature of both the knower and the known.

Through the form of the Visarga creative emission, which consists of both contraction and expansion, all of this is obtained. The creation of the known is simultaneous with the creation of the knower.

One might ask: the nature of the Subject knower flashes in the heart of everyone, so what is the point of the question? It is true that although it flashes, it has not truly entered the heart in its essential reality.

Abhinavagupta, Tantrāloka (with Jayarath.a: Abhinavagupta's commentary says the reflection of external objects in the intellect is twofold: brought in through the senses, as in direct perception, or not, as in imagination and dreams. The intellect is inert (jada) yet serves as the ground where the soul's self-awareness appears. Intellect, Ego and Mind form the internal instrument (antahkarana), performing knowledge (bodha), assertion (samrambha, "I am this") and desire (sankalpa), which external senses turned inward cannot perform. The text also describes dream and deep sleep as states where time seems extended.

q.t: The reflection of external objects in the intellect is twofold: that which is brought in through the senses, and that which is not. The first occurs in direct perception and similar experiences. The second occurs in imagination utpreksha and related states; the word "and so on" includes dreams.
Knowledge [original: "bodhah"] refers to the mental ascertainment of an object like sound. Assertion [original: "samrambhah"] is the self-identification of the soul [thinking "I am this"].

The phrase "in deep sleep" [original: supte] refers to the state of deep, dreamless slumber. In that state, even if one is in a stupor for only a moment, the prideful thought arises upon waking: "I have been deeply unconscious for a long time."

Śaṅkara (attrib.), Vivekacūḍāmaṇi|||Indi.a: The Chatterji translation says the mind creates the whole phenomenal universe, in dream and in waking alike, including the enjoyer and the objects enjoyed. In dreamless sleep the mind is reduced to its causal state and nothing exists for the sleeper. The Atman is described as the witness of ego and intellect across waking, dream and deep sleep, and as self-cognized because it is known by itself.

q.t: In dreams, where there is no actual contact with the external world, the mind alone creates the entire universe, including the enjoyer and the objects of enjoyment. It is the same in the waking state—there is no difference.

That which clearly manifests itself in the states of wakefulness, dream, and profound sleep; which is inwardly perceived in the mind in various forms as an unbroken series of egoistic impressions; which witnesses the ego, the intellect, and their diverse forms and modifications; and which makes itself felt as Existence-Knowledge-Bliss Absolute—know this Atman as your own Self within your heart. (217)

Gregory of Narek, Book of Lamentations||.a: In Chapter 50 Gregory of Narek's speaker questions whether he can be called rational, a seer, or sentient, having darkened the light in him and closed the doors of his understanding. He says he has died in his soul by his own act. Elsewhere in the prayers he lists wounds of the sense of the heart, doubt, despair of memory, and thoughts that conquer him.

k.g: what one puts in the mind, thought

q.t: How shall I be called a seer, having darkened the light that is in me? And why shall I be reputed as sentient, having closed the doors of my understanding?
Truly, the danger of the confusion of the pains of this hesitation is great, when the body is captured by sins, and the soul has not separated itself from the works of evil;

Druze Rasāʾil al-ḥikma (soul and transmi.a: The exposition compares the Lord to a speaking body in which a subtle spirit is united to a gross body. That body's intelligence directs its actions, and other men know of it only what it manifests through the body. The text says the soul is perceived only by means of the body, and applies this to the divinity made known through the organ of humanity.

q.t: This intelligence is that subtle spirit of which I have spoken, but it only manifests itself through the organ of this gross body. No one can say that intelligence appears otherwise than by means of the body, since it is only by means of the body that the soul can be perceived or seized.

Avicenna, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (brain, inn.a: Avicenna sorts the faculties into psychical, natural and vital, and reports that Galen places the psychical faculty in the brain while Aristotle places the principle of all faculties in the heart. The perceptive psychical faculty divides into outward senses and inward senses, among them phantasy, imagination, memory and the estimative power that judges a wolf to be an enemy. Natural sleep is described as the animal spirit receding with the vital spirit to the interior.

q.t: The psychical faculties comprise two faculties in a genus, one of which is a perceptive faculty and the other a moving faculty. The perceptive faculty is as a genus for two faculties: a faculty perceptive in the outward, and a faculty perceptive in the inward.
But phantasy only places before you what it receives from the senses. And the seat of this power is the middle ventricle of the brain.
It also occurs for rest, so the spirit can gather within itself, where it is nourished, grows, and its substance increases, obtaining a substitute for what was decomposed during wakefulness.

Kṣemarāja, Pratyabhijñā-hṛdaya|||Indian.a: Kṣemarāja defines the mind as consisting of intellect, ego and thought, colored by tendencies toward objects, and as the divine Consciousness in contracted form. He states that liberation arises from correct knowledge of this nature and bondage from incorrect knowledge. Sutra 13 describes the mind turning inward and rising to the position of the perceiver, and sutra 16 names the resulting state liberation while alive.

k.g: the reflective awareness of the Divine
contemplation involving the closing of the eyes or withdrawal of senses

q.t: The meaning is: that which is the mind—consisting of intellect, ego, and thought, which is always colored by tendencies toward objects—is indeed the "Self" of the atomic individual, because it wanders through various forms of existence by relying on the movements of sattva and other qualities, through the concealment of its own nature, which is Consciousness.
Consciousness itself, descended from the state of the pure subject, becomes the mind by contracting into an object.
Upon realizing this, the mind itself becomes Consciousness by turning inward and ascending to the status of the perceiver.

Avicenna, Kitāb al-Nafs (Shifāʾ VI; Lati.a: Avicenna divides the internal perceptive powers into those perceiving the forms of sensibles and those perceiving their meanings. A form reaches the internal sense after the external sense, and a meaning, such as the sheep's perception of the wolf as opposing, is perceived without the external sense. The common sense receives images and the imaginative faculty preserves them. The theoretical intellects rise through material, habitual and actual stages to the acquired intellect (ʿaql mustafād), which comes through conjunction with the Active Intellect.

q.t: As for the meaning, it is that which the soul perceives of the sensible without the external sense perceiving it first—such as the sheep's perception of the "opposing meaning" in the wolf, and the meaning which necessitates its fear of it and its flight from it, without the sense perceiving that at all.
Thus, the common sense is receptive to the image but not preservative of it, whereas the imaginative faculty is preservative of what it has received.
With the acquired intellect, the animal genus and its human species are completed; there, the human faculty comes to resemble the primary principles of all existence.

al-Bīrūnī, Taḥqīq mā li-l-Hind (India: I.a: Al-Bīrūnī reports that in the Indian account the senses bring particular objects to reflection, which passes them to reason, and reason makes them universal and gives them to the soul. A man becomes knowing by inspiration at birth, by inspiration after a time, or by learning. The soul is described as an observer that knows the actions of matter. Al-Bīrūnī sets Greek sayings on the soul and memory beside these views.

q.t: The heart reflects upon what is present and remembers the past. Nature takes hold of the present, lays claim to it as part of the past, and prepares to wrestle with it in the future. Reason understands the nature of a thing regardless of time or date, since past and future are the same to it.
The soul in matter is like the rider of a cart; the senses serve it in driving it according to its desire, and the intellect—which overflows upon it from God, may He be exalted—guides it.
Forgetting is the vanishing of knowledge, and knowing is the soul’s remembrance of that which it had learned before it entered the body.”

Ibn al-Haytham, Kitāb al-Manāẓir (Optics.a: Ibn al-Haytham says sight perceives visible forms and a distinguishing power of the soul discerns them. Recognition occurs only through memory, since sight does not recognize a person seen long before unless it remembers, and he describes it as a kind of syllogism comparing a present form with an earlier one. The essence of a substance is comprehended when the distinguishing faculty finds a likeness among forms resting in the imagination; with no likeness found, the object goes unrecognized.

q.t: Cognition, however, is not perception by sense alone, since sight does not recognize everything it has seen before. If sight perceives an individual and is then separated from them for a long time, and later sees them again without remembering them, it will not recognize them; for it only recognizes what it has known when it remembers.

Therefore, the imagination of visible forms which a person has seen before—and now knows even when they are absent—is proof that the forms of visible things which the eye perceives reach the soul and are shaped in the imagination.

Thus, when the sight perceives a thing, the distinguishing faculty immediately seeks its likeness among the forms existing in the imagination; once found, it recognizes the seen object through it and comprehends its essence.

Miskawayh, Tahdhīb al-akhlāq|||Arabic.a: Miskawayh argues that the soul is neither a body, a part of a body, nor an accident. As evidence he cites its ability to receive image after image without weakening, and its gain in strength with every intelligible it grasps. He names three souls, the animal, the irascible and the rational, and says the rational soul gives humans a share with the angels.

k.g: abstract concepts grasped by the intellect

q.t: We find, however, that our souls accept the forms of all things, in all their variety—both sensible objects and intelligible ones—in their entirety and perfection, without the first form departing, nor being displaced, nor the trace fading.

Therefore, its knowledge is a knowledge not taken from any other science at all; rather, it is from its own self and its substance—I mean the intellect. It does not need anything other than itself to perceive itself.

Since the faculties are three, as we have said, the lowest of them is the animal soul; the middle of them is the irascible [spirited] soul; and the most noble of them is the rational soul. Man only became man through the best of these souls—namely, the rational—and through it he shares with the angels, and through it he is distinguished from the beasts.
I have exhausted myself spending the first half of my life memorizing things, and the second half forgetting them. I studied in Baghdad and left it when my memory was still fresh.
Our ancient God, to whom the forming of desires and the creation of thoughts from imaginings is not difficult, has done this.
Thoughts are a speech that arrives at the conscience dama'ir. It may be an address from an angel, or an address from Satan, or the conversations of the self, or from the Truth—glorified be He.

It is possible that the nafs is a subtle entity placed within this frame, which is the site of defective character, just as the spirit ruh is a subtle entity in this frame, which is the site of praiseworthy character.
Sobriety is a return to sensation after absence, while intoxication is an absence caused by a powerful incoming state.

Solomon Ibn Gabirol — Fons Vitae (Meqor.a: In a dialogue between Disciple and Master, Ibn Gabirol argues that the soul perceives forms through itself because it is simple and spiritual, and the intellect, being simpler, does so to a greater degree. No intermediary lies between a simple substance and the forms it perceives, so those forms exist within its essence. During sleep the soul receives intellectual forms from the Intelligence through the imagination; the rational soul knows the form of truth by nearness to the intellect, while the animal soul only estimates it.

q.t: If the substance of the soul perceives forms through itself on account of its simplicity and spirituality, how much more must the substance of the intellect perceive forms through itself? This is because the substance of the intellect possesses much greater simplicity and spirituality than the substance of the soul.

When the soul raises itself to the Intelligence [original: "intelligentiam", the highest spiritual substance], it grasps those forms through intellectual perception. This means it grasps them through the knowledge of their definitions and what they truly are.
Thus, intelligible things are distinct as far as the intellect is concerned, just in the same way that sensible things are separate as far as the senses are concerned.

Pseudo-Fārābī, Fuṣūṣ al-ḥikam (Bezels of.a: The text holds that the human spirit is one and joined to one body, and that all sensory cognitive faculties serve it. A weak soul occupied with one faculty is distracted from another, and when absorbed in internal cognition it does not retain outer things in memory. The aestimativa perceives intentiones in individual things, such as the enmity a sheep recognizes in the image of a wolf, which external sense perception cannot grasp.

q.t: However, all (sensory) cognitive faculties are servants of this one soul. If the spiritually weak soul is occupied with one of these faculties, it is thereby distracted from making use of another.

The aestimativa perceives within the objects of external sense perception the intentiones intentions/non-sensory meanings present in individual things, which are not perceived through the senses, whether it be that they cannot be perceived at all, or that they are not being perceived at the time of the statement, even if they are otherwise perceptible.

Michael Psellos, De omnifaria doctrina /.a: Psellos describes every soul as divine and as a middle life between indivisible beings and beings divided among bodies. The highest part of the soul is united with the intelligible, and the lowest part communicates with sensible things through the senses and opinions. The text calls the soul rational, places Intellect (nous) above it and the irrational soul after it, and says souls are shut in the body as in a prison until purification returns them to their own power.

q.t: Concerning the "passions" (affections) of the soul: the highest part of the soul is united only with the intelligible [original: "noētois," the realm of pure thought/forms.] and is capable of "seeing" them. The lowest part of the soul communicates with sensible (physical) things, known through the senses and through opinions.

And the soul is properly called the "rational" soul; that which is above the soul is "Intellect" [original: "nous," the highest form of intuitive knowledge.]; that which is after the rational soul is the "irrational soul" and the "image of the soul."
Nor, indeed, are they concerned with the body and things external to the body. Therefore, when you turn back into yourself, look upon the soul living according to its nature.
Imprisoning your five senses is the entirety of the struggle ( mujāhadah ), because the acquisition of all sciences happens through these five doors: seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling, and touching.

In summary, the spirit of the believer is his caller to Paradise, of which it is a sample in the world, and the self is his caller to Hell, of which it is a sample in the world. The governor of the one is perfect reason, and the guide of the other is imperfect desire.

When a man feels desire and passion, he turns to the soul (dil) so that it may guide him to the lower soul (nafs), which is the seat of falsehood. When he finds the evidence of gnosis, he also turns to the soul so that it may guide him to the spirit, which is the source of truth and reality.

Michael Psellos, De operatione daemonum|.a: In this dialogue, demons are bodies of spirit that enter people, fill the passages where the psychic spirit sits, and narrow it, so that the body trembles and the ruling faculties fare badly. They convey shapes and colors from their imaginative substance into our spirit, stirring memories and images of passions, awake and asleep. Marcus states that sensation resides in the spirit within muscle and nerve, so a demon, being entirely spirit, sees, hears, and feels pain through every part.

q.t: Entering into them, they create no small disturbance, as the passages in which the psychic spirit is seated become filled, and the spirit is narrowed and pushed out by the density of the bodies within them; from which it happens that the bodies tremble and the ruling faculties fare badly, and the movements become erratic and faulty.

This is what they say happens even in the souls departing from bodies; for even these communicate with one another without impact. In this way, demons also conduct their conversation, undetected, so that we do not even perceive from where the war against us comes.

And he said, "I am amazed that you are ignorant of this, that in no muscle or nerve does the feeling reside, but in the spirit that exists within them. Wherefore, even if the nerve is compressed, or cooled, or suffers any other affection, the pain is because the spirit transmits it to the spirit;

Milarepa, mGur 'bum (Songs)|||Tibetan.a: Milarepa says no metaphor suits the nature of mind: the sky is a void without awareness, and the nature of mind is a void possessing awareness. Asked about dreams, he calls himself a master of the illusory body who can interpret and transform dreams, and cites the Perfection of Wisdom that dreams are empty, hollow, and deceptive. His songs tell students to realize their sensory perceptions as they are and to see appearances as the Truth Body, since not realizing this is Samsara.

q.t: No metaphor can be found for the nature of mind. If one were to try to find a metaphor for this mind, the sky would not suffice. Why is the sky an inadequate metaphor? The sky is a void without awareness. The nature of mind is a void possessing awareness.

I am a master who has mastered the illusory body. I know how to interpret dreams; I know how to transform dreams; I even have instructions for sealing the reality of dreams with the truth. Generally, I am a master who has realized the nature of dreams.

If you have not experienced the bliss of the five senses, you should not engage in erratic behavior. Until your own sensory perceptions are realized as they are, and until realization has entered into the vast expanse, you should not turn your mind toward its own domain.

al-Ghazālī, Tahāfut al-falāsifa / Maqāṣi.a: In reporting the philosophers' doctrine of dreams and prophecy, al-Ghazali has them say the imaginative faculty imitates what the soul apprehends, so that the example may remain in memory and the dream requires ta'bir. In the same account the prophet's psychological faculty grows strong enough that the external senses do not engulf it. Discussing the First Principle, the philosophers define intellect as an existent free of matter that apprehends itself.

q.t: They claimed that the connection to those souls is accessible, since there is no veil there, but we are preoccupied in our waking state with what the senses and appetites bring upon us. Our preoccupation with these sensory matters diverts us from it. And when some of the preoccupation of the senses falls away from us during sleep, a disposition for the connection appears by it.
If it is stated that it is identical, this would be necessarily false. For each individual is aware of his self and knows that he is not the self of another.

If it is said, “Intellect,” [this] means that He is an existent free of matter. Every existence having this description is an intellect; that is, it apprehends itself, is aware of it, and apprehends intellectually another.

al-Ghazālī, Iḥyāʾ ʿulūm al-dīn (ʿAjāʾib.a: Al-Ghazālī describes the heart as a mirror that accepts traces of knowledge from the Preserved Tablet, with the senses and desires acting as a veil. In sleep the senses leave the heart, the veil lifts, and what falls into the heart is reflected by the imagination in a resembling form, which memory keeps for the interpreter. He names a sixth sense located in the heart, called intellect, light, or heart, and places the true spirit among lordly matters that a light higher than the intellect perceives in Prophethood and Sainthood.

q.t: The meaning of sleep is that the senses leave the heart, so they do not bring to it [information] from the world of manifest creation. When it is free from [the senses] and from imagination, and it is pure in its essence, the veil between it and the Preserved Tablet is lifted.

He called prayer the coolness of his eye and made it the most sublime of beloved things, and it is known that one does not enjoy it through the five senses, but through a sixth sense whose locus is the heart. No one perceives it except he who has a heart.

Nothing of its description is perceived by the intellect, but rather by another light, higher and more noble than the intellect. This light shines in the realm of Prophethood and Sainthood; its relationship to the intellect is like the relationship of the intellect to illusion and imagination.

Anuruddha, Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha|||Budd.a: The Compendium describes cognition through six modes (sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch, thought) and six processes by way of the eye-door, ear-door, nose-door, tongue-door, body-door and mind-door. It states that seventeen thought-moments make up the duration of material phenomena. At the five sense-doors an object's intensity is very great, great, slight or very slight, and at the mind-door the impression is clear or obscure.

q.t: [A single unit of mental activity], termed one thought-moment, consists of three time- [phases], to wit, nascent, static, and arrested.

Honorius Augustodunensis, Elucidarium|||.a: In the dialogue between Student and Master, the soul is formed from spiritual fire and carries the image and likeness of God, which the Master locates in memory, intellect and will. The Master holds that the soul comprehends visible things and cannot itself be comprehended by any visible creature. The body is called the soul's garment, dwelling and instrument.

q.t: Divinity subsists in the Trinity; the soul holds the image of this, for it has memory, by which it recalls past things; it has intellect, by which it understands present, future, and invisible things; it has a will, by which it rejects evil and chooses good.

We read of John, that his soul perceived Christ present while he was still in the womb. Whence it is evident that some souls of infants do not lack knowledge, but because of the weakness of the little body, they cannot exercise the work of God.

The body is also an instrument of the soul, not like a lyre, or a flute, or a carpenter's axe, but it is so united to it that whatever the soul has done, the body is also said to have done; and therefore it is damned with it.

al-Ghazālī, Kīmiyā-yi saʿādat (Alchemy o.a: Al-Ghazālī says the existence of the spirit (ruh) is evident, that it is not body, and that it undergoes no corruption at death, though its essence may not be known. The body needs five external senses and five internal senses: perception, reflection, memory, recollection and imagination, housed in the brain. In sleep the senses close, and a heart free of blameable affections receives forms from the preserved tablet, while the imaginative faculty keeps them.

q.t: Know then, that the existence of the spirit is evident and is not involved in doubt. Still, it is not body, which is found in corpses and in animals generally.
These are five: the faculties of perception, reflection, memory, recollection, and imagination. Their home is in the brain, and each has a specific function, as is well known to the learned.

The heart resembles a pure mirror, you must know, in this particular, that when a man falls asleep, when his senses are closed, and when the heart, free and pure from blameable affections, is confronted with the preserved tablet, then the tablet reflects upon the heart the real states and hidden forms inscribed upon it. In that state the heart sees most wonderful forms and combinations.

al-Ghazālī, Mishkāt al-anwār (Niche of L.a: Ghazālī lists five human spirits, each called a Light: sensory, imaginative, intelligential, discursive and the transcendental prophetic spirit. He ranks them in order, with Sense as the foundation for Imagination, and links them to the Niche, Glass, Lamp and Tree of the Light-Verse. Prophets are said to see concrete objects and the spiritual ideas behind them, and dreams given by inspiration need interpretation.

q.t: The first of these is the sensory spirit. This is the recipient of the information brought in by the senses; for it is the root and origin of the animal spirit and constitutes the differentia of the animal genus. It is sound in the infant at the breast.

Since the lights of the human spirit are graded rank on rank, that of Sense comes first, the foundation for the Imagination (for the latter can only be conceived as superimposed after Sense); those of the Intelligence and Discursive Reason come thereafter.

Scientific knowledge is above faith, and mystic experience is above knowledge. The province of mystic experience is feeling; of knowledge, reasoning; and of faith, bare acceptance of the creed of one's fathers, together with an unsuspicious attitude toward the two superior classes.

al-Ghazālī, al-Munqidh min al-ḍalāl (Del.a: Al-Ghazālī describes man as created empty and simple, gaining news of God's worlds through successive kinds of perception: touch, sight, hearing, taste, then Discernment (al-tamyiz) at about seven years, then Intellect (al-ʿaql). In the doubt episode, his soul compares waking belief to the beliefs held in sleep, and suggests a higher state may relate to waking as waking relates to dreaming. He defines the heart as the spirit that is the seat of the knowledge of God, which has its own health and disease.

q.t: The first thing created in man is the sense of touch. Through it, he perceives categories of existence such as heat, cold, moisture, dryness, softness, roughness, and others. But touch is certainly blind to colors and sounds; rather, they are as if non-existent to the sense of touch.

My soul hesitated for a moment regarding the answer to this, and then strengthened its doubt by reflecting on dreams. My soul said: "Do you not see that while you are asleep you believe certain things, imagine various states, and believe them to be stable and persistent, having no doubt about them while in that state?
By "heart," I mean its true essence: the spirit which is the seat of the knowledge of God, not the physical flesh that we share with the deceased and with animals.

al-Ghazālī, Minhāj al-ʿābidīn|||Arabic.a: Al-Ghazālī classifies thoughts (khawāṭir) occurring in the servant's heart into four types: a direct thought from God, the soul's whim (hawa al-nafs), inspiration (ilhām) from the angel, and whispering (waswasah) from the devil. He calls the soul an enemy that cannot be overcome by total prevention, since it is the mount and the instrument, so it must be trained moderately. He traces every tribulation and sin to the soul, and advises the soul to give up "perhaps" and "if only" because they preoccupy the heart.

q.t: Know after this introduction that thoughts khawāṭir are effects that occur in the servant's heart, urging him toward actions or omissions and calling him to them.

It is not possible to neglect it once because of the tyranny of its harm. Thus you need a way between the two ways to train it and straighten it, according to what it can bear of good deeds, and by which you weaken it and restrain it with caution so that it does not persist beyond it.
Cease saying "perhaps" and "if only," for they offer nothing but the preoccupation of the heart and the wasting of time.

Ibn Bājja (Avempace), treatises on the s.a: Ibn Bājja treats the appetitive soul as having three powers: one tied to imagination, one of the intermediate soul, and one that perceives through speech (al-nutq). The first two are shared with animals and the third belongs to humans only. He calls the soul and its parts the first mover in a human, and the body a collection of instruments. He describes the intellect's movement as a straight line that becomes a spiral once it acquires something of the theoretical.

q.t: The appetitive soul is either a genus for three powers. First is the appetitive power associated with the imagination al-khayal. Through this, the raising of children, the movement toward specific dwellings, familiarity, romantic love, and similar things occur.
The absolute first mover in a human is the soul and its parts. As for the body, it is a collection of instruments, and the totality of the natural instrument is the body.

Once it acquires something of the theoretical, it has divided the line into two halves. It then folds one of the halves over the other, and the intellect's movement shifts from a straight line to a spiral circle.

Hugh of St Victor, De sacramentis I.6 /.a: Hugh of St Victor places the soul between the world outside it and God within it, and assigns it three eyes: the eye of the flesh, the eye of reason, and the eye of contemplation. After sin, contemplation was extinguished and reason became bleary, so it sees doubtfully, while the eye of the flesh kept its clarity. He says man is rational only by the soul, and that each rational spirit is created singly from nothing, with the body formed first and the soul infused afterward.

q.t: And it had received an eye with which to see the world outside itself—those things that were in the world—and this eye was the eye of the flesh. It had received another eye with which to see itself and those things that were within it; this is the eye of reason.

For if man is said to be a rational substance, it is not said on account of the whole, but on account of the soul alone, which is properly said to be a rational substance. For man is rational only by the soul, because it alone has reason or rationality in itself, that is, the capacity for reason.

Again, the Psalmist says, "Who fashioned their hearts one by one." He means by hearts the rational spirits or souls, which He fashioned one by one; for they are not one from another, as appears in bodily birth, but He creates each one by itself from nothing.

Mabinogion (Breuddwyd Rhonabwy, Breuddwy.a: In Breuddwyd Macsen, the Emperor wakes from a dream of a maiden with no lifespan, soul, or life left in him, and every joint full of love for her. For a week he wants only sleep, because sleep shows her to him. In Rhonabwy's Dream, Rhonabwy sleeps on a yellow ox-hide and is given a vision, then wakes on the hide after three nights and three days.

q.t: Nothing could be had from him but sleep; as often as he might sleep, he saw the woman he loved most in his dream. When he was not sleeping, he cared for nothing, for he did not know where in the world she might be.
And as soon as sleep entered his eyes, a vision was given to him: that he and his companions were walking across a plain.
And when he woke, he was upon the yellow heifer skin, having slept for three nights and three days.

Sefer ha-Bahir|||Kabbalistic & Hasidic.a: The passages say the senses are held by the flames, and that all movements and perceptions separate from the light, a burning fire, and spread until they return to the four. Directing the heart toward the letters of the Explicit Name is described as part of the restoration (tikkun). Section 126 states that the treasury of the souls is in the power of the "All", and that souls go out into this world only if Israel is good.

q.t: The senses are held by the flames, and the flames are held in the inheritance. You shall know and understand that what we call "behind" is drawn from the light, which is a precious, burning fire. From it, all movements and perceptions separate, spread, and grow strong until they return to the four.

§ 126 He is the "All" [original footnote 1], and in his power is the treasury of the souls [original footnote 2]. If Israel is good, the souls are permitted to go out to enter into this world; but if they are not good, they do not go out.

Hildegard of Bingen, Scivias|||Medieval.a: Hildegard says the soul vivifies the body and purifies the senses, while the body aids the soul and opens the senses, and the senses touch the soul and entice the body. The soul gives the body two principal powers, intellect and will, which she likens to two arms. The intellect is fixed in the soul as an arm to the body and understands every work of man, and the passages also speak of the soul working through sight, hearing, taste, smell and touch.

q.t: The soul vivifies the body and purifies the senses, but the body aids the soul and opens the senses; the senses, however, touch the soul and entice the body. For the soul provides to the body, just as fire is poured into darkness, two principal powers, namely the intellect and the will, having them as if two arms.
For the soul breathes out through the sense. How? It makes man, while he is living, to be alive, and it glorifies through sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch

Hildegard of Bingen, Causae et curae|||M.a: Hildegard of Bingen holds that the soul originates from God and can see what is true and what is to come while the body sleeps. Its knowledge plays in dreams once the body's many activities no longer hinder it. Dreams can also be clouded by the devil's illusions or by waking thoughts that swell like sourdough. In her account the soul sends a gentle wind from the marrow to give rest, and draws it back to wake the person when discomfort or noise is sensed.

k.g: depressed mind and weakness of the brain

q.t: When God cast sleep upon Adam, his soul meanwhile saw many things in a true prophetic state, because it was then still free from sin. In the same way, the soul of a sleeping person could see many things in true prophecy if that same person were not weighed down by sin.

Because the human being possesses sensation, the soul—which feels these discomforts and sees that its own body is being harmed—gathers its strength, draws back the "wind" it sent out from the marrow, and in this way awakens the person from sleep.

However, if someone was constantly unwise and foolish while in full health because his soul did not fully unfold the wings of the intellect, and then becomes sensible as a sick person, his soul is preparing itself for knowledge and for the paths in another life.

Avicenna Latinus, Liber de anima (Sextus.a: Avicenna, in the Latin text, names the sensus communis as the common center of the senses, from which the nerves derive and which perceives. Imagination, also called the formal faculty or phantasia, retains what it perceives. Learning is described as acquiring the perfect aptitude to connect with the intelligentia agens, the agent intellect, from which forms emanate. The soul is called a substance because it is a form that is not in a subject.

q.t: This faculty is what is called the sensus communis common sense, which is the common center of all the senses and from which the nerves are derived, and to which the senses are rendered; it is truly the one that perceives. But to retain those things which this perceives is the work of that faculty which is called imagination, and is called the formal faculty, and is called phantasia fantasy.

It remains that the intellectual part might be empty, and that to learn is nothing but to acquire the perfect aptitude for connecting oneself to the intelligentia agens agent intellect, until it becomes an intellect, which is simple, and from which the forms emanate in an ordered manner, mediated by the soul in thought.
Therefore, the soul being in the body is not the same as an accident being in a subject. Therefore, the soul is a substance, because it is a form that is not in a subject.

Pseudo-Augustine (Alcher of Clairvaux),.a: The author holds that the soul is one simple essence that takes different names according to its work, such as sense, mind, intellect, reason, memory and will. The soul is rational, desiring and irascible, and its whole essence consists in these powers. Soul and spirit share one essence, with spirit naming its nature and soul naming its giving of life to the body.

q.t: It is called soul while it vegetates, spirit while it contemplates, sense while it perceives, mind while it grows wise, intellect while it understands, reason while it discerns, memory while it remembers, will while it consents. Yet these do not differ in substance, as they do in names, since all these are one soul; the properties are indeed diverse, but the essence is one.
Soul and spirit are the same in man, although one calls it soul and the other spirit. For spirit refers to nature, and soul refers to the vivification.
For it is not a body, nor is it life without sense, such as is in trees, nor is it life without a rational mind, such as is in animals, but it is life, and perpetual life.

Averroes, Colliget (Kitāb al-Kulliyyāt)|.a: Averroes defines sleep as the senses' quietude and their return from their instruments to the internal part of the body, through the return of natural heat. A sleeper with open eyes does not see, since the heat carrying the power of sight has withdrawn through the optic nerve. Dreams are attributed to the imaginative power, which moves the common sense, and that moves the particular senses, so things are sensed as if external. He adds that common people ascribe this to angels or demons.

q.t: We say that sleep is a binding of the quietude of the senses and their return from their instruments to the internal part of the body. These things are known by themselves; therefore, sensible things pass over those sleeping, and they do not sense them.

But in sleep, it happens in a prior mode; the movement begins from the imaginative power through a form received from the outside in the waking time, and that is remote; and therefore it first moves the common sense, and the common [sense] moves the particular senses, and then they will sense things as if they were external;

And here it appears that when a man sleeps while holding his eyes open, he does not see; and if it were not that the heat in which is the power of sight returns through the optic nerve to the internal parts, the sense of sight would not be deprived.

Ibn Ṭufayl, Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān (Philosophus.a: In the passages Hayy concludes that his essence is not the corporeal thing his senses perceive, and he reasons that corruption belongs to bodies, so what is not a body cannot be corrupted. He examines the perceptive faculties, which are sometimes perceptive in potentiality and sometimes in act. The text names the animal soul, the vegetative soul and nature as forms perceived by intellectual speculation, and describes a vision in which the heavens, spiritual forms and his own essence are withdrawn from his memory and thoughts.

k.g: the vital breath or life force

q.t: When he knew that his essence was not this corporeal thing which he perceives with his senses and which its skin encompasses, his body appeared to him entirely contemptible.

These were the first things that became known to him concerning the spiritual world, since they are forms that are not perceived by sense, but are perceived by a certain kind of intellectual speculation.

By "heart," however, I do not understand the body of the heart, nor the spirit which is in its cavity; but by it I understand the form of that spirit which diffuses itself through its faculties in the body of men.

Averroes, Tahāfut al-tahāfut / Faṣl al-m.a: Averroes argues that survival of the soul after death can be shown from the Quranic equation of sleep and death, since the soul's activity is suspended through its instrument and the soul returns on waking. He treats each sense as a distinct faculty with its own object and organ. He assigns the rational soul (nafs natiqa) a practical part and a theoretical part, each with its own virtues.

k.g: the human soul capable of reasoning

q.t: If that were the case, the soul would not return to its original state upon waking. Since it does return, we know that this suspension does not occur because of something that happened to its core substance, but rather it is something that happened to it because of the suspension of its instrument.

For it is obvious that the sense of sight is different from the sense of hearing; that which is perceived by the former is different from that of the latter; the physical organ of one is different from the other; and it is impossible for sight to turn into hearing just as it is impossible for a color to become a sound.

Since the rational soul has two parts—a practical part and a theoretical part—it must be that the first thing required of it is that it exists in its perfection regarding these two faculties, meaning the practical virtues and the theoretical virtues.

Suhrawardī, visionary recitals (Āwāz-i p.a: Suhrawardī describes the Word (the soul) as related both to the Holy Realm and to the body, with five external senses and five internal senses. The internal senses run from the common sense in the front of the brain through imagination and estimation to compositive imagination, called thinking when the intellect uses it. When obstacles weaken, as in sleep or illness, the soul is inspired by a divine matter flowing into the imagination, and a person may see beautiful forms in sleep or wakefulness.

q.t: The first is called the al-hiss al-mushtarak Common Sense. It is a power in the front of the brain where the images of all sensed things gather and are perceived.

Perceiving knowledge without extensive study is not impossible, as you have witnessed the differences in intelligence among your own people. There are those who are dull and cannot benefit from thought, and those with strong intuition who can solve many problems by instinct.

Maimonides — Guide for the Perplexed (Mo.a: Maimonides describes the imaginative faculty as holding memory, composition and impression of sensed things, and as most active when the senses are at rest. An influence flowing into it causes true dreams and prophecy, which differ in degree, not in species. He explains that a human understands in potentiality before understanding and in act after abstracting a form, and that intellect and the understood form are one. He also lists the meanings of nephesh, including sensate soul, blood, rational soul, surviving soul and will.

q.t: You know likewise that it performs its greatest and most noble operation when the senses are at rest and idle from their functions. For then a certain Influence flows into it according to the proportion of the subject's disposition.

For the Intellect is nothing other than the Thing understood. Therefore, in this way it is explained to you that the Thing understood is the abstracted Form of the tree, and that it is the same as the Intellect existing in act, and they are not two things—the Intellect and the understood Form of the tree.
First, it is a general name for the Soul of any living thing endowed with sensation: as in, In which there is a living soul [nephesh] Genesis 1:30.

Chinul, Susimgyŏl and collected works|||.a: Chinul speaks of a True Mind, whose innate radiant awareness he calls numinous brilliance and names the Ordinary Mind. He explains No-Mind as the absence of attachments and stray thoughts inside the mind, and compares it to an empty bottle. A postscript lists five types of mind: the Fleshly Heart, Cognitive Mind, Accumulating Mind, Alaya Mind and Mind of True Suchness.

k.g: the fundamental, enlightened essence of a person
wuxin; a state of mind free from attachment and conceptual thought
yeol-myeong; the innate, radiant awareness of the mind

q.t: Every person possesses a single point of numinous brilliance yeol-myeong; the innate, radiant awareness of the mind. It is as clear as the void and pervades all places.
When I speak of No-Mind now, I do not mean that the essence of the mind does not exist. It is called No-Mind because there are no things [no attachments or stray thoughts] inside the mind.
The Cognitive Mind Thinking mind: Like a wildfire, it suddenly arises and suddenly ceases; it is categorized as deluded thought.

ʿAṭṭār, Ilāhī-nāma|||Persian.a: In the passage on the Ascension of the Messenger, ʿAṭṭār has Muhammad pass beyond body and soul, seeing no intellect or perception, and become selfless before gazing upon the Truth. The call to him is to come to fana, the dying away of the self. In the later passage the six are listed as spirit in the perceptible, the devil in the imagined, intellect speaking of the intelligible, and knowledge seeking the knowable.

k.g: the soul that commands to evil
the dying away of the self

q.t: He passed beyond body and soul, and traveled also; when he became selfless, he gazed upon the Truth.
One is your spirit, and its place is in the perceptible; one is the devil, and its direction is in the imagined.

Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda|||Norse & C.a: Snorri Sturluson says two ravens sit on Odin's shoulders and tell into his ears all tidings they see or hear. They are named Huginn (Thought) and Muninn (Memory), fly out at dawn, and return at breakfast time. The verse quoted in Gylfaginning voices fear for both. The poetic-diction section lists names for the mind, including mood, thought, exertion, memory, wit, nature, temperament, and trust.

q.t: Two ravens sit on his shoulders, and tell into his ears all tidings that they see or hear; they are named thus: Huginn Thought and Muninn Memory. He sends them at dawn to fly over the whole world, and they come back at breakfast time, from that he becomes aware of many tidings; for that reason men call him the Raven-god.
The mind is also called mood, thought, exertion, strength, persistence, memory, wit, nature, temperament, trust.

Ibn ʿArabī, Fuṣūṣ al-ḥikam|||Arabic.a: Ibn ʿArabī holds that whatever is seen in sleep is within imagination, a dream within a dream, which he calls the world of imagination. The interpreter reads a form such as milk as representing knowledge. He says that when revelation came, God veiled the Prophet from the perceived world, and on its lifting the Prophet returned to consciousness at the station of imagination. He states that imagination holds greater authority than the intellects, and that you are an imagination, khayal.

q.t: It is a dream within a dream, and whatever comes from this category is what is called the world of imagination. Therefore, the matter that is itself in one form appears in another form.

Therefore, imaginations were stronger in authority in this existence than the intellects, for the rational person, even if he reaches what he reaches in his intellect, does not escape the judgment of imagination over him.
And the servant, when the matter is as we have established, know that you are an imagination khayal imaginal form, and everything you perceive is the senses.

Heimskringla (Ynglinga saga on Odin's sh.a: The Heimskringla pages shown treat dreams as a way kings gain knowledge of what lies ahead. Halfdan seeks a dream by lying in a pigsty, and Torleiff the Wise interprets it. Olaf falls asleep with a weary mind and is visited by a figure who gives counsel, and a dream of a ladder to Heaven is read by Find as an omen of death.

q.t: One night, after he had long thought of his affairs with great anxiety and toil, and his mind was weary and tired, he fell asleep. Straightaway it seemed to him that a great and impressive man came to stand by his bed, and the King thought that it might be King Olaf Tryggesøn.

The King said, "I thought I was walking up a ladder that stood up into Heaven, and when I had arrived at the highest step, the sky opened, and just as I was to step up into Heaven, you woke me." Find said, "That dream does not please me at this time; it is as if you are marked for death, if it is anything other than sleep-talk."

K. Halfdan never dreamed, and it seemed strange to him. Therefore he carried his counsel to Torleiff the Wise. He told him what he used to do when he wanted to know something in dreams: that he laid himself in a pigsty, and then a dream never failed him.

Ibn ʿArabī, al-Futūḥāt al-makkiyya (imag.a: Ibn ʿArabī places the imagination between the presence of sensible things and the presence of abstract meanings. He assigns it a formative power that works under the rule of the intellect and the wahm, and he says the wahm exercises authority over the intellect. He describes the perceptive power as travelling in sleep, and says certain saints perceive in wakefulness what others perceive in a true dream.

q.t: He made the imagination a presence intermediate between the two ends of the sensible and the meaningful. It is the treasury of the hidden things that the senses perceive.

Likewise in sleep, you see yourself in the highest of the high, and at another moment in the west, and then the west, while you are in a mere span of ground in your bed. This group surpassed others in that what a person perceives in sleep, they perceive in wakefulness.
For the imagination khayal the faculty of imagination, it is the master of the rational soul, for it is derived from it, just as the master is to the servant.

Hadewijch, Visions|||Medieval Latin.a: Hadewijch describes being embraced by Love and lying without consciousness until late in the day. In another vision God takes possession of her soul and leads it before the Holy Spirit, and she receives insight into all things. She then returns to herself and understands what was said. She also records Discerning Reason becoming subject to her.

q.t: But now Love came and embraced me. I lost consciousness and lay there, drunk with unspeakable wonders, until late in the day.
From the one same essence of this countenance, I then received insight into all things and read therein everything that lay before me.

Bartholomaeus Anglicus, De proprietatibu.a: Bartholomaeus Anglicus divides the rational soul into speculative and practical intellect. He holds that it is immortal because understanding does not depend on the body, and that it is passible while joined to the body. Animal spirit is generated in the brain's ventricles, perfecting common sense and imagination, then intellect, then memory. In sleep we behold representations through the spirit, and dreams are sometimes true and sometimes false.

q.t: The rational soul or the intellective force is that which is principal, that is, the speculative intellect and the practical intellect. The speculative intellect exercises contemplation; the practical, in operation.

This animal spirit, therefore, is generated in the anterior ventricle of the brain and is diffused through the organs of sensing. Nevertheless, a part remains in the same ventricles so that it may perfect the common sense and the imaginative virtue.

While waking, therefore, we comprehend the forms of things by sense, but while sleeping, we behold representations through the spirit. Dreams, however, are sometimes true, sometimes false, sometimes tranquil, sometimes disturbed.

al-Abharī, Hidāyat al-ḥikma with Qāḍī Mī.a: The text divides the perceptive power into five manifest senses and five internal senses: common sense, imagination, estimation, memory and the imaginative faculty. It places common sense and imagination in the first cavity of the brain. It argues that the soul needs no bodily instruments for intellectual acts, so intellectual pleasure continues after death. It defines the animal soul by perceiving corporeal particulars and moving by will.

k.g: the faculty that unites all sensations
intentions that are not perceived by the senses

q.t: As for the internal: among them is Common Sense al-hiss al-mushtarak, which is a power arranged in the front of the first cavity of the brain that receives the forms imprinted in the five manifest senses. Imagination al-khayal is a power arranged in the back of the first cavity of the brain that preserves the forms received by the common sense.

As for the first point: the objects of the senses are nothing but specific qualities like colors, tastes, smells, heat, cold, and the like. But the objects of the intellect are the essence of the Creator, His attributes, intellectual substances, celestial bodies, and others.
It is specific to the animal soul, which is a perfection for a natural instrumental body from the aspect of its perceiving of corporeal particulars and its movement by will.

Nikephoros Blemmydes, De anima / Epitome.a: Blemmydes lists the cognitive powers of the soul as intellect, discursive thought, opinion, imagination and sensation. He says opinion can be held with reason or without it, and that Aristotle called the imagination the passive intellect. He also distinguishes a potential intellect, which needs mental images, from an active intellect, and he cites the self-moving soul as the ground of its immortality.

q.t: Sensation is the partial knowledge of what is currently present. I say "of what is present" because it employs the sense-organs, such as sight; it is not able to operate in the same way upon other things [that are absent]. Imagination is the partial knowledge of what is absent; for instance, when having seen someone yesterday, I imagine him today.

Insofar, then, as philosophy is the medicine for the soul's appetitive part and for the potential intellect—which is unable to think without the help of mental images—this appetitive aspect is termed practical.

Experience, therefore, is an unreasoning multitude of memories gained by seeing the same things many times. The empirical doctor, holding in memory a multitude of observations and seeing the same cures many times, uses them without knowing the reason for the healing [original: logon tēs iaseōs].

Vincent of Beauvais, Speculum naturale X.a: Vincent of Beauvais gathers authorities on time and the soul, including Augustine's view that time exists only in the soul, and the claim that sleepers do not perceive time. Another passage argues that the heaven cannot be ensouled, since a soul with diverse powers needs diverse organs. A further passage says the devil imprints images through the humors and does not enter the substance of the soul.

q.t: To which a sign is that the grieving and the sick lengthen time, because of much attention to the motions affected by infirmity and pain. The voluptuous, however, conversely shorten time because of the attention to the motions of delight. Those sleeping do not perceive time at all.

For in the book On the Soul, it is proven that no simple body can be ensouled. And the reason for this is that since the soul has diverse powers, there must be some diversity in the organs, which is perfected according to those distinctions.
He imprints images of delightful things, from which evil thoughts arise while the soul is occupied with them.

Albertus Magnus, De anima / De intellect.a: Albertus Magnus says the possible intellect, moving from potentiality to act, uses reminiscence, sense, imagination and phantasy, taking experience from sense, memory from experiences and the universal from memories. Once it holds science it is the intellectus adeptus and no longer needs the sensible powers. He cites Isaac that the rational soul is the shadow of intelligence, the sensible soul the shadow of the rational, and the vegetative the shadow of the sensible.

q.t: In truth, when the possible intellect proceeds from potentiality to act, it then uses reminiscence, sense, imagination, and phantasy. For it receives experience from sense, memory from experiences, and the universal from memories.
The rational soul is the shadow of intelligence, and the sensible [soul is a shadow] with respect to the rational soul, and the vegetative [is a shadow] with respect to the sensible.

k.g: the innate capacity of the soul to grasp moral first principles

Thomas Aquinas, Summa contra gentiles II.a: Aquinas takes up the question whether the mind is a power of the soul or its essence, with arguments on both sides drawn from Augustine. He argues that intellect differs from sense because intellect knows itself and knows that it understands, and is not corrupted by excellent intelligibles. He holds that the possible intellect is not imagination, since imagination is of singular bodies and intellect knows universals. He cites Augustine that the mind knows itself.

q.t: And therefore, the name of the mind is used in this way in the soul just as the name of the intellect is. For only the intellect receives cognition of things by measuring them as if toward their principles.
The intellect, however, knows itself and knows that it is understanding. Therefore, the intellect and sense are not the same.
But on the contrary, there is what Augustine says in On the Trinity: "The mind knows itself, that it is incorporeal; for if it did not know itself, it would not love itself."

Thomas Aquinas, Quaestio disputata de an.a: Aquinas discusses the agent intellect, which makes things intelligible in potency actually intelligible by abstracting species from matter, and the possible intellect, which is in potency to intelligibles. He holds that man requires a proper intellectual light, while God is the first light illuminating everyone. He notes that sensible operations are exercised through different parts, sight through the eye and hearing through the ears. A further question asks whether the soul is its own powers.

k.g: the intellect capable of receiving knowledge
the active intellect that abstracts universals

q.t: Therefore, I say that just as in natural things there are proper active principles in each genus, and God becomes the agent cause through and common [to all], so also a proper intellectual light is required in man, although God is the first light illuminating everyone in common.
From which it also happens that not all sensible operations are exercised through one part; rather, sight [is exercised] through the eye, hearing through the ears, and so on for others.
Furthermore, the agent intellect is posited for the purpose of making things that are intelligible in potency actually intelligible.

Thomas Aquinas, Sentencia libri De anima.a: Aquinas reports the earlier opinions on the soul, including those of Anaxagoras and Democritus, on whether the soul moves and whether intellect and soul are the same. He discusses the division of the soul into vegetative, sensitive and rational parts, and the appetitive powers. He also treats fantasia in perfect and imperfect animals and its affinity to the intellect.

q.t: But in this he differs, because he did not want everything that moves another to be moved itself. Rather, he said there is one intellect, separate and unmixed, which moves other things without being moved itself.
For the vegetative [is] in plants and in all animals, or in all living things. And the sensitive [is] also in all animals.

It must be said, therefore, that imperfect animals, as is said in the third [book], indeed have fantasia, but indeterminately, because, namely, the motions of fantasia do not remain in them after the apprehension of the sense.

Thomas Aquinas, Summa theologiae Ia qq..a: The Summa's pages ask whether the intellect is a power of the soul, and answer that it is a power, since only in God is understanding the essence. Aquinas holds that the human intellective soul needs a higher intellect to bring it from potentiality to act, and places the agent intellect, which makes phantasms intelligible, in the soul itself. In sleep the reason lacks free judgment, and dreams arise from causes he classes as animal, bodily or spiritual.

k.g: the active faculty of the soul that illuminates phantasms

q.t: But the human intellective soul is said to be intellectual by participation of virtue, in some part of itself, reaching toward the intelligence of truth with a certain discourse and motion of arguing. It also has an imperfect intelligence, both because it does not understand everything, and because in those things which it understands, it proceeds from potentiality into act.

Now, while sleeping, the reason does not have free judgment. For there is no one sleeping who does not attend to some likenesses of phantasms as if they were the things themselves, as is clear from those things which were said in the first part (q. 84, art. 8).

Sometimes, however, the intrinsic cause of dreams is bodily: for from the interior disposition of the body, some motion is formed in the imagination corresponding to such a disposition, just as to a man in whom cold humors abound, it occurs in dreams that he is in water or snow;

Mechthild of Magdeburg, Das fliessende L.a: Mechthild of Magdeburg lists three places where God speaks with the soul: the human senses, the soul itself, and the kingdom of heaven. In the soul God speaks alone, without knowledge of the senses, and the senses cannot perceive the speech. She also reports hearing the Enemy's voice with physical ears and seeing him with spiritual eyes, and he claimed her union with God was a dream. She says a clear soul sees into divine knowledge as a person sees their face in a mirror.

q.t: The second place, where God speaks with the soul, is in the soul itself. Into this place no one can come except God alone. But when God speaks in the soul, this happens without any kind of knowledge of the senses, through a great, powerful, and swift union of God within the soul.
I heard his voice with my physical ears, and I saw a creature with spiritual eyes: black, filthy, and like a gruesome man. Yet I was not afraid of him.

Poetic Edda (Hávamál, Völuspá, Grímnismá.a: The Hávamál stanzas shown speak of the mind as guided by wisdom and as knowing what lies near the heart. They describe the witless man lying awake all night thinking of many things and care-worn at morning. Stanza 96 says the mind alone knows its own spirit.

q.t: The witless man is awake all night, Thinking of many things; Care-worn he is when the morning comes, And his woe is just as it was.
The mind alone knows what lives near the heart, alone it knows its own spirit. [2]

Rūmī, Masnavī-yi maʿnavī|||Persian.a: Rūmī treats ordinary waking life as a kind of sleep, and says the world seems lasting to the sleeper until the last day dawns. He describes intellects as differing in rank, from the sun-like to the star-like, and names the Universal Intellect and the Universal Soul. In the story of Laila and Majnun, wakefulness to the world is said to be sleep to love.

k.g: a Gnostic or one with mystical insight

q.t: Our wakefulness fetters our spirits, Then our souls are a prey to divers whims, Thoughts of loss and gain and fears of misery.
In like manner this world, which is only a dream, Seems to the sleeper as a thing enduring for ever But when the morn of the last day shall dawn, The sleeper will escape from the cloud of illusion;
Know this difference of intellects well in their ranks, from the earth to the sky. There is an intellect like the disc of the sun; there is an intellect less than Venus and a shooting star.

Bar Hebraeus, Ethicon / Book of the Dove.a: Bar Hebraeus describes the mind perceiving the dove, a spiritual nature, through the psychic eye. The mind turns from all other things, and the vision at prayer stupefies it so that the solitary falls to the ground as dead, then rises as the cloud lifts and the eye is enlightened. At the stage of the perfect, the waking person is as if sleeping and the sleeping person is reckoned awake. Later the dove abides in the heart and speaks mysteries to the mind.

q.t: Then he will rise again and prepare himself for vision and little by little the cloud will be removed and the eye become enlightened. At this stage the perfect, when awake, becomes as if he were sleeping; when sleeping, he is reckoned as being awake.

Gertrude of Helfta, Legatus divinae piet.a: Gertrude describes the soul as having a head, which is the will, hands, which are its works, and feet, which are its desires, and she places each in the Lord's heart during the hymn Veni Sancte Spiritus. She commends her senses to the Heart and is promised that they will be enlightened so that others are enlightened through her. The Lord says he gives revelations according to what each person's mind can grasp, using physical parables for the simple and obscure understanding for those of better-grasping intellect.

k.g: the soul's capacity for righteous anger and resistance
the soul's capacity for desire and love

q.t: Through the fourth verse— Accende lumen sensibus Kindle the light of the senses —she commended her senses to the Heart, and thus received this promise: that her senses should be so enlightened that others also should be enlightened through her in knowledge and be ignited in the love of God.

Likewise, the more I communicate my gifts in different ways, the more clearly comes to light the depth of my unsearchable wisdom, with which I answer each one according to what best suits his understanding, and I reveal those things I wish according to what each person's mind can grasp, which I have given him.

Joseph Gikatilla — Sha'arei Orah (Gates.a: Gikatilla says every creature has a living soul according to its kind, supernal or lowly, including the animal soul in man and the higher soul called Neshamah. He states that soul adheres to spirit, spirit to mind, and mind to Prudence (Binah), from which minds fly out, as spirits do from Beauty and souls from Kingdom. He also holds that Thought has no "viewing," no entry, and no limit, so no creature can contemplate matters said to have "ascended in Thought."

q.t: There is no creature in the world that does not have a "living soul" according to its kind. Everything is as it should be: the soul matches the "matter" of the creature—if the creature is supernal, the soul is supernal; if the creature is lowly, the soul is lowly.

The mind (he says), the spirit, and the soul involve and entwine themselves in a mutual bond until they return to the oracle of Prudence. For the soul adheres to the spirit, the spirit to the mind, and the mind to Prudence.
This is because Thought has no "viewing" [it cannot be looked into from the outside] at all, as there is no way to enter it, and it has no end or limit.

Joseph Gikatilla — Sha'arei Tzedek (Gate.a: Gikatilla names three levels of the soul, Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah, and links them to the daily one hundred blessings. If the Nefesh omits blessings, ten fail to reach the Ruach and the "one" fails to reach the Neshamah, which cleaves to the Lord. He assigns the Neshamah to praise of the Name Yah and the Nefesh to prayer, and places all things beneath the Crown within Thought, with the Chariot below Thought.

q.t: In this way, if the Nefesh [Soul] does not bless one hundred blessings every day, ten will not reach the Ruach [Spirit]. And when the Ruach does not receive ten, the "one" will not reach the Neshamah [Higher Soul]. And behold, we are obligated every day to bind the Nefesh to the Ruach, and the Ruach to the Neshamah, and the Neshamah cleaves to the Lord, may He be blessed.
The higher soul (Neshamah) praises the Name Yah [a shorter divine name associated with the higher spheres], while the lower soul (Nefesh) is for prayer.
All things in the world that are beneath the Crown are included in the Thought, and the Thought encompasses them all and surrounds them.

Zohar|||Kabbalistic & Hasidic.a: When people go to bed, their souls depart and wander the world, and the shells of impurity called "human sins" seize the soul and show it false dreams. A vitality from the side of the Nefesh stays in the body and never departs, and the dream is seen from it. Another passage sets out Thought (Machshava), Understanding (Binah) and Knowledge (Da'at) as lights that issue one from another.

q.t: From this vitality that remains in the body, a person sees the dream. For the higher soul has departed and ascended, but the likeness of the body remains.

And Understanding, which emerges from Thought, illuminates that light called Knowledge [original: Da'at], and this is the mystery of what is stated: By His knowledge the depths were broken up (Proverbs 3:20).

Mechthild of Hackeborn, Liber specialis.a: Mechthild of Hackeborn describes God as the soul's sight, hearing, smell, taste, voice, heart, and life. She teaches that occupying memory with earthly things, or turning reason and intellect to earthly wisdom, stains the face of the soul, which is the image of the Holy Trinity. In another vision the soul is a small house within God's heart, its door the soul's desire, its bolt its will, and its chain God's desire, and the soul is called immortal and eternal.

q.t: He is also the soul's hearing, through which it hears his sweet-flowing words, and through which the soul hears the harmony of God himself and all the saints. He is also the soul's sense of smell and the breath breathing into it his own sweetness, by which the soul is made alive forever.

she understood that when a person occupies their memory with earthly things and thoughts, they stain the face of their soul, that is, the image of the Holy Trinity within them. Similarly, when they turn their reason or intellect toward earthly wisdom and curiosity, they defile the face of their soul.

By the door, she understood the desire of the soul to be designated. By the bolt, its will. By the small chain, however, the desire of God, which always pricks the soul's desire and will, and excites and draws it to God.

Angela of Foligno, Memoriale|||Medieval.a: Angela describes the soul receiving knowledge of itself and of God through prayer, and says it loves to the extent that it knows and desires to the extent that it loves. She reports that when God visits the soul, it sees Him without bodily form, and that words and imagination fail her in describing this. In ecstasy the soul is enlightened and understands what it could not grasp by its own powers, and she says the finite soul cannot comprehend even itself.

q.t: enraptured above itself by divine thought and fullness, the soul is transported higher than its own nature, entering into divine understanding more deeply than the nature of things allows, and finds light within this understanding. But the soul cannot explain the knowledge it draws from these sources, because everything it sees and feels is superior to its nature.
the soul swims in joy and in knowledge. Being thus enlightened, it understands the meaning of all the difficult and mysterious sayings of Christ.
My soul then beheld itself in such a way that it could not even understand its own nature.

Cabalistic Disputation on the Soul|||Kab.a: This disputation argues that the intellectual faculty can exist without the phantasy, since the phantasy can exist without the external sense. It cites ecstasy as a state where mind and will operate without the body, and cites Aristotle and Algazel on the agent intellect, which acts as an unmixed soul using no organ. It also assigns Neschamah to the brain, Ruach to the heart and Nephesch to the liver, and sets these beside Plato's parts of the soul.

q.t: Furthermore, the intellectual faculty differs more from the phantasy than the phantasy does from the external sense; because they are sensitive faculties: since, however, the phantasy can exist without the external sense; why then cannot the intellectual faculty exist without the phantasy?
therefore, the intellective soul alone is that which can do these things when it is unmixed and not using an organ in performing its function.
The divine soul dwells in the brain; the living soul bestows dominion and honor in the heart; and the animal soul, which desires to eat and drink, dwells in the liver.

Duns Scotus, Ordinatio / Quaestiones (on.a: Scotus asks whether the intellect is active regarding intellection, citing Aristotle's De Anima on sense as passive and Augustine on awareness (notitia) born from knower and known. He names two extreme opinions, one making the intellect the total cause and one making the object the total cause. He calls the intellective soul the proper form of man, says sensation is organic while intellection is not, and says that in this state we understand no universal without phantasizing its singular.

q.t: Augustine, 9th and 10th books of De Trinitate: every thing that we know generates in us its own awareness [notitia]. For from the knower and the known, awareness is born.
Furthermore, in the third of De Anima, a difference is posited between the intellect and the sense, because an excellent sensible corrupts the sense; an excellent intelligible perfects the intellect.

I say that there is such a connection of that power of fantasy and the intellect in this state, that we understand nothing in the universal unless we phantasize its singular, and there is no other recourse to phantasms except that the intellect understanding the universal imagines its singular

Tripurā-rahasya (Jñāna-khaṇḍa)|||Indian.a: The text and its commentary hold that Consciousness is the Reality of the Self because it is never an object of perception, and everything perceived is non-Self. This Reality is one, follows memory and recognition, and stays uniform through many states, with the world appearing in it as a reflection appears in a mirror. The commentary says the intellect's light depends on the light of consciousness, and that consciousness identified with the intellect takes on delusion, as space in a pot takes the pot's shape.

q.t: Consciousness is the Reality of the Self because it is not an object of perception. Everything else is non-Self because it is an object of perception.
Therefore, O people, abandon delusion and worship Consciousness alone, which shines as the witness of all and the support of all, with a steady vision fixed only on Consciousness. [101]

Just as space, when confined by a pot, takes on the shape of a clay vessel and appears curved, so too the consciousness, when limited or identified with the intellect, takes on the appearance of delusion and the like.

Dante, Convivio|||Medieval Latin.a: Dante, citing Aristotle's On the Soul, gives the soul three powers: to live, to feel, and to reason. Each is the foundation of the next, so reason is found only with the sensitive power, while beasts, birds, and fish have the sensitive power without it. He calls the intellect, the noble part of the soul also called the mind, healthy when body or soul does not impede its operation, which is to know what things are. He describes the intellectual order of the universe as rising by almost continuous grades from the lowest form to the highest.
