q.t: And this sensitive power is the foundation of the intellective power, that is, of reason. And so, in animate mortal things, the reasoning power is not found without the sensitive, but the sensitive is found without this [reasoning], as we see in beasts, birds, fish, and in every brute animal.

Wherefore it is to be known that our intellect, in order to be called healthy or infirm—and I say "intellect," the noble part of the soul, which by common vocabulary can be called "mind"—can be called healthy when it is not impeded by the malice of soul or body in its operation, which is to know what things are.
And therefore, one rises and descends through the intellectual order of the universe by almost continuous grades from the lowest form to the highest.

Meister Eckhart, German Sermons (ground.a: Eckhart says the soul acts through its faculties, namely reason, memory and will, and all outward activity is attached to a medium. In the essence of the soul there is no work, and silence is the place where God the Father speaks the Word. He also describes lower faculties that pass sense impressions upward to the higher faculties of memory, intellect and will, and an outer man and an inner man to whom the soul gives its powers.

q.t: All that it understands, it understands through reason. When it thinks, it does so through memory. When it desires, it does so through the will; and in this manner, it acts through its faculties and not through its essence.
There, it is preserved in the memory, understood in the intellect, and fulfilled in the will. These are the higher faculties of the soul, and they exist as one in nature.
And the powers that the soul has beyond this, which she does not give to the five senses, she gives entirely to the inner man.

Jean de Jandun, Quaestiones super libros.a: Jean de Jandun asks how the intellect understands the intellection of a stone existing in it, and proposes that it does so by the same intellection, which avoids an infinite series of intellections. He says understanding does not exist in the body as in a subject, since otherwise the hand would understand, and that the intellect understands itself without phantasms. He also lists the powers of the soul, including will, agent intellect, possible intellect, common sense, phantasia, cogitativa and the aestimativa in brutes.

q.t: I could thus say that the intellect understands the intellection of the stone existing in it, and not by another intellection, [but by] one simply the same.

If it is cognitive, thus it is the common sense and the phantasia mental imagery faculty, under which phantasia is comprehended the human cogitativa discursive faculty and the aestimativa evaluative faculty in brutes.
But understanding does not exist in the body as in a subject; for either it would exist in the whole body, and thus it is in the hand, and then the hand would understand.

Shabistarī, Gulshan-i rāz (Mystic Rose G.a: Shabistarī answers the first question by defining thinking as passing from the false to the truth and seeing the Absolute Whole in the part. Philosophers name its stages "reminiscence" and "interpretation" and compare the major and minor premises to a father and mother, with the conclusion as their son. On the self, the answer says "I" and "you" are higher than body and soul, which are parts of "me", and that the soul of each creature is hidden within man, the world's soul.

q.t: Thinking is passing from the false to the truth, And seeing the Absolute Whole in the part.
"I" and "you" are higher than body and soul, For both body and soul are parts of "me."
You are the kernel of the world in the midst thereof; Know yourself, that you are the world's soul.

Dante, Commedia (Purgatorio dream theory.a: Dante describes the soul as gathering itself entirely to one faculty, so that time passes unnoticed, and he applies this to the claim that one soul is kindled above another within us. In the Purgatorio the apprehensive faculty draws an image from real existence and unfolds it within the soul, which turns toward it in love. In the Paradiso Beatrice says the human mind grasps through the senses what it then makes worthy of the intellect.

q.t: When, through delights or perhaps through pains, Which any one of our faculties perceives, The soul gathers itself entirely to that one;
The soul, which is created ready to love, Is moved by every thing that pleases it, As soon as it is awakened into action by pleasure.
It is necessary to speak thus to your wit; Since only through the senses does it grasp What it then makes worthy of the intellect.

William of Ockham, Quodlibeta / Reportat.a: Ockham's Quodlibet I, Question XV, argues that our understanding knows sensible things intuitively, because it knows evidently the first contingent proposition about sensibles. He holds that abstractive knowledge of sensibles does not suffice. On the sensitive soul and the intellective soul as one form, he says sensitive sight is received in the body or in a soul distinct from the intellective soul.

q.t: Conclusion. To this question, I say that our understanding does know sensible things intuitively, because our understanding knows evidently the first contingent proposition concerning sensibles; therefore, it has an incomplex conception sufficient to cause this complex conception evidently.

Nikephoros Gregoras, Commentary on Synes.a: The commentary on Synesius sets out a chain of communication from mind to rational soul, to sensitive soul, to the nutritive and augmentative spirit, with the imaginative spirit linking soul and senses. It treats dreams as activity of the imaginative spirit, and says dream phantasiai follow the life of each person. It also discusses the nous in ecstasy and the dianoia in relation to phantasia.

k.g: the imaginative faculty of the soul

q.t: The rational soul communicates with the sensitive, and to the organic senses, through the middle of the imaginative spirit.

And [he calls] the spirit the phantasia; sometimes he calls it the phantastic spirit, sometimes the psychic spirit, carrying the soul around the body, sometimes the spiritual soul, sometimes a common boundary of soul and body.

Henry Suso, Horologium sapientiae / Büch.a: In the dialogue of Truth and the Disciple, every human being has a five-fold "self": being, growth or life, sensation, rational human nature, and one's own person. The soul's blessedness is said to lie in beholding God without a mediator, and Evening Knowledge sees creatures in themselves while Morning Knowledge sees them in God. Chapter 15 says the rational soul is not annihilated in its departure and denial, and remains eternal because of its rational dignity and God-like powers.

q.t: The second he has in common with the plants, and it is called growth, or life. The third, he shares with the irrational animals, and is called sensation. The fourth, he shares with other humans; it is the rational human nature in which all men are equal.

But when creatures are recognized in God, this is and is called Morning Knowledge [original: "Cognitio Matutina"], a clear or morning knowledge, because here the creatures are seen without distinction and without any images within the One, which is God, in Himself.
In this way, the spirit (that is, the rational soul) is not annihilated in its departure and denial; for the soul remains eternal because of its rational dignity and its God-like powers.

Jan van Ruusbroec, Die geestelike bruloc.a: Ruusbroec describes three unities in the human being: a bodily one in the heart, a middle one that is rational and spiritual, and a highest one held essentially in God. He calls the soul "spirit" in the higher unity and "soul" where it gives life to the body and the five senses. He places memory, understanding and will under the unity of the spirit, and names a ground of the mind from which a divine touch wells up.

k.g: the ground or deepest essence of the soul

q.t: This unity we possess within ourselves above the senses and from here come the memory / the understanding and the will and all the power of spiritual works. In this unity the soul is called spirit.
The soul itself is spiritual, rational, and immortal. It also has within itself three powers: Memory, Intellect, and Will, so that it can naturally choose which it prefers, whether good or evil.
This unity of the mind is the scintilla spark and source of the soul, where all the gifts of God provide and infuse a just ascent of virtues according to dignity.

Johannes Tauler, Sermons|||Medieval Lati.a: Tauler lists names for the soul according to its works. It is Anima for the life it gives the body, Geist for its kinship with God as its Grund, and Gemüth for the place where memory, understanding, and will are gathered. Another sermon says the one soul is called soul by its lowest powers and spirit by its highest, and that the understanding keeps searching for the truth of an essence, so that what it grasps of God in this life is more ignorance than knowledge.

k.g: the innermost essence of the soul

q.t: Thirdly, the soul is also called the Gemüth mind or disposition. Now, the mind is a wondrous and very lovely thing, as all the highest powers are gathered therein, namely the memory, the understanding, and the will; and yet the mind is higher in itself and has something more than the mentioned powers.

For according to the lowest powers, where she gives life to the body, she is called by the name "soul." But according to the highest powers, through which she is united with God and beholds Him, she is called "spirit."

When the understanding recognizes the truth of an essential thing, it inclines and turns toward it and desires to rest upon it. Then, through Vernunfft reason, it brings forth its word concerning the thing that is within it.

Longchenpa, Ngal gso skor gsum (Trilogy.a: Longchenpa describes the alaya consciousness as the clear luminosity of a mirror's surface, with the five sense consciousnesses as the reflected images. The mental consciousness and the afflicted mind follow on these. The text asks the practitioner to treat past, present, and future appearances as dreams, so that grasping is released. It gives dream practice in which recognizing "This is a dream" liberates fearful appearances and makes the dream clearer.

q.t: For example, when seeing form: the alaya consciousness remains in the clear luminosity without grasping at the object, and the eye consciousness arises as the aspect of seeing the form. When these two are placed and then cease, the aspect that arises in an instant thinking "it is a form" is called the "mind" or "thought."

The mind is without an object to focus on; it is the state itself, like the vast sky. Awareness, free from the duality of the "lake of memory," dawns naturally as empty, clear, and free from conceptual complexity.

By sleeping in the state of thinking, "This is a dream," for those with stable meditative absorption samadhi meditative concentration, the luminosity that is clear and without center or edge will arise. Even if it is not stable, the dream will be clearer than before and easy to recognize.

Mādhava, Sarva-darśana-saṃgraha|||Indian.a: In the Bauddha chapter, Mādhava presents the view that intellect is its own object, self-subsistent and luminous, and that the apparent gap between perceiver and perceived is an illusion like seeing two moons. The Śaiva chapter treats the soul (paśu) as the knower of the body and rejects its identity with the body on grounds of memory. The Patañjali chapter compares the understanding to iron affected by magnet-like objects, and places the modifications in the understanding.

q.t: The identity of the perceiver and the perceived can be inferred thus: that which is known by any cognition is not separate from that cognition (just as the soul is not separate from the consciousness of the soul), and "blue" or other momentary objects are known through cognition.

We must not agree with the Chárvákas [3] that the soul is the same as the body; if that were true, we could not account for memory, as there is a proverb that one man cannot remember what another has seen.

Therefore, the "modifications" belong to the understanding, not to the soul. So says the Śruti [the sacred texts], "Desire, volition, doubt, faith, lack of faith, firmness, lack of firmness—all this is only the mind."

Theologia Deutsch|||Medieval Latin.a: The Theologia Deutsch says the human soul has two eyes, one for seeing into eternity and one for seeing into time and created things. The two cannot work at once, so the left eye must be as if dead when the right eye looks into eternity. Knowledge, reason, and will are given so that reason may teach the will that neither comes from itself. The inner human is taught by God and orders the outer human.

k.g: the physical body and social self
original: icheit; the state of being an "I

q.t: Now, the created soul of a human also has two eyes. One is the possibility to see into eternity. The other is to see into time and into the creaturē created things, to recognize distinctions therein, as was spoken before, and to give life to the body.
See, knowledge and reason are created and given along with the will so that reason may teach the will, and also itself, that neither knowledge nor will comes from itself.

Also, one should note that God's commandment, and his word, and all his teaching, belong to the inner human the spiritual self or soul, concerning how he may be united with God. And where that happens, there the outer human the physical body and social self is well ordered and taught by the inner one, so that one needs no outer commandment or teaching.

Guillaume de Deguileville, Pèlerinage (d.a: In this passage the Pilgrim sees a great turning wheel with a smaller wheel inside it turning the other way. A butterfly turning on top of it represents the soul or spirit. Grace of God tells the Pilgrim that, as God's image and creature, the Pilgrim came from Him. The wheel's circular movement is said to return directly to its beginning.

k.g: common sense; the faculty that unites sensory inputs

q.t: And if it had not been for a papillon butterfly, representing the soul or spirit that turned around on top of it, I would have easily thought that the said wheel was the one Ezekiel saw, one within the other, as he says.

Ibn Khaldūn, Muqaddima (prophecy, dreams.a: Ibn Khaldun describes the human soul as connected below to the body, from which it gains sensory perception, and above to the angelic horizon, from which it gains unseen knowledge. The external senses ascend through the common sense and the imagination toward the rational faculty. He holds that sleep, soothsaying and spiritual discipline each lift the veil of the senses for a moment, and he sorts dreams into true visions, interpretable ones and confused ones.

k.g: a faculty that perceives sensory data like sight, sound, and touch simultaneously
the subtle vapors thought to animate the body

q.t: Indeed, every person has seen in their sleep things that were verified in their waking life, time and again. It has become certain to them that the soul perceives the unseen during sleep, and this is inevitable.

It is veiled from the latter by being immersed in the body, the senses, and their preoccupations, because the senses are always drawing it toward the manifest, due to the initial bodily perception it was created with.

The first of these is the common sense a faculty that perceives sensory data like sight, sound, and touch simultaneously, which is a faculty that perceives sensed objects—visible, audible, tangible, and others—in a single state.

Catherine of Siena, Dialogo della divina.a: Catherine describes the soul as made in God's image with three powers: memory, intellect and will. Affection moves the intellect, and the intellect in turn feeds affection. She calls the intellect's sight the "eye of the intellect" and says self-love clouds it, while free will chooses where the soul plants its tree. In the Eucharist passage, the senses of the body are deceived, and the sense of the soul perceives through the eye of the intellect with faith as its pupil.

q.t: For this tree has within itself reason, if free will wishes to use it, and it has the eye of the Intellect which knows and sees the truth, provided the fog of self-love does not obscure it.

The soul cannot live without love, but always wants to love something, because it is made of love: for by love I created it. And so I told you that affection moved the intellect, as if to say: "I want to love, because the food upon which I nourish myself is love."

Who is it, then, that tastes and sees and touches this sacrament? It is the sense of the soul. With what eye does the soul see it? With the eye of the intellect, if the pupil of most holy faith is within it.

Cloud of Unknowing / Walter Hilton, Scal.a: The passages divide the soul's powers into three principal ones, Mind, Reason, and Will, and two secondary ones, Imagination and Sensuality. Reason and will work in spiritual matters without help, while imagination and sensuality work in the body through the five senses. Mind is called primary because it contains the other powers and the things they act upon. A note traces this scheme to Richard of St Victor and Augustine.

q.t: Within yourself in nature are the powers of your soul: which are these three principal ones: Mind, Reason, and Will; and secondary: Imagination and Sensuality.
The mind is called a primary power because it spiritually contains within itself not only all the other powers, but also all the things upon which those powers act.

Karma Lingpa, Bar do thos grol (Zhi khro.a: The Bardo Thödol passages speak of transparent awareness and of the self-liberation of hatred, pride, and attachment into wisdoms. One passage says thine own consciousness is shining, void, and without birth or death, and that recognizing the voidness of one's intellect is Buddhahood. A translator's note separates rig-pa, consciousness in its purest aspect, from shes-rig, the consciousness of phenomena. A ritual passage lists fundamental, mental, afflicted, body, eye, ear, nose, and tongue consciousness.

q.t: Hum Svah. Transparent awareness, the body of light; the single, brilliant, sparkling chain; the empty essence of shifting thoughts; the self-radiant clarity of the nature of emptiness; the unceasing compassion of clarity.

Ha! To Gauri, in whom the fundamental consciousness [the alaya-vijnana or storehouse consciousness] is transformed, I fulfill the sacred bond! To Chauri, in whom the mental consciousness is transformed, I fulfill the sacred bond!
Thine own consciousness, shining, void, and inseparable from the Great Body of Radiance, hath no birth, nor death, and is the Immutable Light—Buddha Amitābha.⁴

Julian of Norwich, Revelations of Divine.a: Julian writes that God dwells in the soul and the soul dwells in God, and that the soul is made to be God's dwelling place. She saw no difference between God and our substance, though the substance is a creature in God. She says the sense-soul of this passing life does not know what our Self is. Full knowledge of the Self comes only at the last point, and clear sight of God follows clear sight of the Self.

q.t: We ought to rejoice highly that God dwells in our soul, and we ought to rejoice much more highly that our soul dwells in God. Our soul is made to be God’s dwelling place, and the dwelling place of the soul is God, Who is uncreated.

But our passing life that we have here in our sense-soul does not know what our Self is. When we verily and clearly see and know what our Self is, then shall we verily and clearly see and know our Lord God in fullness of joy.

For it is His good pleasure to reign in our Understanding blissfully, and sit in our Soul restfully, and to dwell in our Soul endlessly, working us all into Him; in which working He wills that we be His helpers, giving to Him all our attention, learning His teachings, keeping His laws, desiring that all be done that He does; truly trusting in Him.

al-Ījī / al-Jurjānī, al-Mawāqif with Sha.a: The commentary reports a dispute over dreams. Abu Ishaq calls the dream true perception. The Mu'tazilites call it false imagination because the conditions of perception are lost in sleep. The Ash'arites say perception during sleep is contrary to custom (khilāf al-ʿāda), and that sleep is an opposite to perception. For the intellect, al-Ashʿarī defines it as knowledge of some self-evident truths, called the "Intellect in Habitus." al-Baqillani adds the necessity of what is necessary and the course of natural habits. A further passage says man in reality is the rational soul (al-nafs al-nāṭiqa), a separate subsisting substance, and the body is its instrument.

k.g: the human soul capable of speech and logic

q.t: Professor Abu Ishaq said: The dream is "true perception" without a doubt. There is no difference between what a sleeper finds within himself during sleep—seeing visible things, hearing audible things, tasting flavors, and other perceptions—and what a person who is awake finds in their wakefulness.
Sheikh Abu al-Hasan al-Ash‘ari said: "It is the knowledge of some self-evident truths." We have called the knowledge of that "some" the "Intellect in Habitus."

The body is merely an instrument for its actions. The soul is a separate, subsisting substance jawhar mujarrad for which there is no path to annihilation. When the body is annihilated, that soul remains and its attachments are severed, so it returns to the world of separate entities alam al-mujarradat as it was before the body.

Sāṃkhya-sūtra with Aniruddha and Vijñāna.a: The commentary treats waking, dream and deep sleep as modifications of the intellect (buddhi). The self (puruṣa) is their witness and is devoid of those states. Waking is the intellect taking the form of objects through the senses, and dream is a similar modification born only from latent impressions (saṃskāra). Deep sleep is divided into partial and total dissolution. In the partial kind the intellect becomes pleasure, pain and delusion, which allows the waker to recall "I slept happily." The text names the intellect as the substrate of all saṃskāra, since the blind and deaf could otherwise not remember what they saw or heard. Perception is described as pure consciousness delimited by the reflection of a mental operation colored by the object.

q.t: There, the "waking state" is the modification of the intellect into the form of objects through the senses. The "dream state" is a similar modification born solely from latent impressions saṃskāra.

The intellect alone is the substrate of all subliminal impressions, not the eye and the others, nor the ego or the mind. This is because it is impossible for the blind, deaf, and others to remember things previously seen, heard, and so on.
Therefore, pure consciousness, delimited by the reflection of the mental operation colored by the object, is what we call perception.

Tsongkhapa, Lam rim chen mo / chung ngu.a: Tsongkhapa lists stages of settling the mind, including close placement, disciplining, pacifying, one-pointedness, and placement in equilibrium. Sinking from lethargy or sleep is met by the perception of light or by inspiring subjects, and excitement by reflection on impermanence. Right Mindfulness guards against sinking and excitement. In the emptiness practice one abandons memory and mental engagement, and views things as like an illusion, a dream, or the moon reflected in water.

k.g: the innate belief in a permanent, independent self

q.t: If the mind becomes sunken due to lethargy or sleep, one should apply the perception of light or reflect on the qualities of the Buddha and other inspiring subjects to uplift the mind.

Specifically, if the mind is excited or if one fears it will become excited, one should direct the mind to objects that produce weariness, such as impermanence; this is the cause of calm abiding. If the mind sinks or if one fears it will sink, one should direct the mind to objects that produce joy; this is the cause of intensification.
Having abandoned all memory and mental engagement, one should abide one-pointedly in the state of emptiness. While abiding there, one should not let the continuum of the mind become distracted.

Paul of Venice, Expositio super libros D.a: Paul of Venice follows Aristotle and the Commentator on the agent and possible intellect, treating both as powers of the intellective soul. The passive intellect is named as the imaginative, fantastic, or cogitative power in man. He holds that the intellect cannot understand or remember without a phantasm, so it does not remember after the death of man.

q.t: Whence, the agent intellect is the power of the intellective soul making all things. The possible intellect is the power of the soul receiving all things.

Fourth proposition: act and potency are the differences by which the agent intellect and possible intellect are distinguished, because the possible intellect is pure potency for receiving intelligibles. The agent intellect, however, is pure act, not receiving these things.
The human intellect is immaterial, incorporeal, and unmixed. The intellect understands all material forms, and it is immaterial and unmixed.

Tsongkhapa, Drang nges legs bshad snying.a: Tsongkhapa takes up whether memory can arise if self-awareness (svasaṃvedana) does not exist. A quoted verse says memory comes from what experienced the object, and the thought "I saw it" belongs to worldly conventional terminology. The text explains that the earlier perception of blue and the later memory engage the same object, so the memory "I saw it" arises. A second passage describes a position that rejects the foundation consciousness (ālayavijñāna), the afflicted mind (kliṣṭamanas) and self-cognition. Accepting the foundation consciousness would let object-appearing representations ripen from latencies without external objects.

q.t: Because memory arises from that which experienced the object, and this memory is not something other than me, therefore the thought arises: I saw it. This too is the way of worldly conventional terminology.

Therefore, he also does not accept the alayavijnana foundation consciousness. If that were accepted, then even without external objects, one would have to establish the arising of representations appearing as objects from the ripening of its latencies; thus, there would be no purpose in asserting external objects.

Svātmārāma, Haṭhapradīpikā|||Indian.a: Svātmārāma lists many names for samādhi, including Unmani, Manonmani, Amanaska and Turya, and defines it as the union of Self and mind, or of individual and Supreme Soul. He places the mind as master of the senses, the breath as master of the mind, and dissolution (laya) as master of the breath, with dissolution resting on inner sound. The commentary adds that a steady mind steadies the breath and the vital seed, and that the dissolved mind sees no duality.

k.g: the fourth state of consciousness beyond waking, dreaming, and deep sleep

q.t: Just as salt [original: Saindhava] attains oneness when joined with water [original: Salila], so the union of the Self [original: Atman] and the mind [original: Manas] is called Samadhi.

The mind, or the internal faculty, is the "lord" or the driver of the senses, such as hearing and the rest. The "lord" of the mind is the breath. The "lord" of the breath is dissolution—the melting away of the mind.

Root: Making the mind supportless Niralamba [a state where the mind does not lean on any external or internal object of thought], one should not think of anything at all. He remains fixed like a pot in the outer and inner space [original: vyoman]. || 50 ||

Nicholas of Cusa, De visione Dei / Idiot.a: In De visione Dei, Cusa writes that the eye is not seen by sight, nor the ear by hearing, and so the mind is even less seen by the intellect. The goal of the intellect is what it understands by not understanding. Another passage says the vision of our mind is in itself, and the vision of our senses is in signs. The chapter list of De mente describes the mind as a living substance created in a body, a living description of eternal wisdom, and an image of the eternal application. It says the mind measures all things and exerts the forms of things from itself by assimilation.

q.t: For if the eye is not seen by sight, nor the ear by hearing, then even less is the mind seen by the intellect. Therefore, that which makes the intellect, or which is its goal, is not the thing it understands; nor can that which it does not understand at all be its goal.
The vision of our mind is in itself; the vision of our senses is in signs. And it is that very Power than which nothing is more powerful.
How the mind is a living substance created in a body. And concerning the manner how. And whether reason exists in brutes. And how the mind is a living description of eternal wisdom. Chapter five

Jacobus de Clusa (de Paradiso), De anima.a: Jacobus de Clusa describes death as the soul's separation from the body. The soul's natural appetite for the body is broken, and it does not know where it will be led, since it had no existence before infusion. The vital spirits thicken and fail, so the vegetative and sensitive powers cannot operate. The soul can do nothing without them, even in acts of the intellectual power, and the text compares it to a harpist whose strings are destroyed. On purgatory, the text holds that these souls are not yet blessed and are alienated from intuitive cognition. They may know a diminution of their pains, and angels may reveal the prayers offered for them.

q.t: And the powers of the soul, both vegetative and sensitive, are rendered instrumentally unable to operate, because the soul cannot do anything without them, even in the acts of the intellectual power.

To this, it must be answered that although souls in heaven know the prayers of the living made for their honor from the mirror of the Trinity and divine cognition, it is not to be believed that it is in a similar way for souls in purgatory, because they are not yet blessed, and they are still alienated from that cognition, at least the intuitive one.

Therefore, the powers being destitute, the soul cannot linger in the body, just as a harpist cannot play when the strings are destroyed, and it disposes the body toward another form through elemental qualities, for example, toward putrefaction.

Jacobus de Clusa, De animabus exutis a c.a: Jacobus de Clusa says that at death the vital spirits fail and the instrumental powers of the soul, vegetative and sensitive, cannot operate. Citing Aristotle's De Anima, book three, the text says the soul can do nothing without them, even in acts of intellect, since anyone thinking must contemplate phantasms. A story of a damned theologian who appears to a bishop states that the dead do not lose intellect and memory. The same story says the pain and anxiety of the damned are so great that they retain nothing in memory except the sensation of pain.

q.t: Thence the vital spirits through which the soul operates in the body grow thick and fail, and the instrumental powers of the soul, both vegetative and sensitive, are rendered unable to operate, because the soul can do nothing without them, even in acts of the intellectual power, according to the third book On the Soul [Aristotle's De Anima]. It is necessary for anyone thinking to contemplate phantasms.
Furthermore, there is such great pain and anxiety in the damned that they retain nothing at all in memory except the sensation of pain.

Jāmī, Lawāʾiḥ|||Persian.a: Jāmī distinguishes self-annihilation from annihilation of annihilation. In the first, the Very Being so overpowers the inner man that no consciousness of anything beside Him remains. In the second, no consciousness remains even of that unconsciousness. The text says consciousness of annihilation is incompatible with annihilation. Another passage says the speaking soul (nafs-i nāṭiqa), when illuminated by images of the Divine Truths, becomes as if it were the whole of existence. It adds that most people cannot distinguish themselves from the body, and quotes Rumi: "you are only your thoughts."

q.t: Self-annihilation consists in this, that through the overpowering influence of the Very Being upon the inner man, there remains no consciousness of anything beside Him. Annihilation of annihilation consists in this, that there remains no consciousness even of that unconsciousness.
O brother, you are only your thoughts; As for the rest, you are but bones and fiber.

Johannes Treviensis, Oratio de immortali.a: Johannes Treviensis argues from reason that the mind is simple, has no contrariety in itself, and so cannot perish by the action of contraries. When the mind reflects on itself and its own operations, which suit no material sense, it must be removed from matter. The oration points to martyrs whose minds persisted whole under torture and to philosophers who weakened the body to strengthen the mind. It describes contemplative happiness, following Aristotle's Ethics, as the activity of the intellect formed by the habit of wisdom regarding God and the separated substances.

q.t: This is clear even from the fact that when the mind reflects upon itself and its own proper operations—acts which are not fitting for material senses—it must be removed from all matter. For it understands not only all other things but also itself, and its own thoughts are not those of material things or senses.

To this we add that when bodies are tormented by tortures and pains, the mind often persists whole and most lively, as is seen in the martyrs who, in the very heat of their torments, with their bodies almost exhausted, persevered with the most upright mind and a sincere and most constant soul.

But contemplative happiness is the activity of the mind or intellect, formed by the habit of wisdom regarding the most noble objects, namely, God and the separated substances, which he maintains in the tenth book of the Ethics to be the highest and perfect human happiness.

Ficino, Theologia Platonica de immortali.a: Ficino calls corporal life the continuous act of the soul and the intellectual life the perennial act of the divine intellect joined to the soul. God ignites sparks of things to be known in the soul. He argues that sense does not reach insensible things and imagination is ignorant of universals, so the mind alone holds the power that considers being. He calls this an excellent imagination and an intellectual sense. A mind left pure, with imagination, sensation, and generation erased, would be an angel, and truth remains other than the mind.

k.g: an intelligible form or mental image

q.t: And just as the soul sows the seeds of things to be generated into corporal life, so God ignites the sparks of things to be known in the soul. Corporal life is the image of the rational soul. The intellectual life of the soul is the image of the life and mind of God.

Since sense does not reach insensible things, nor perceive anything more common than the general class of sensibles, and the imagination is ignorant of universals, that power will be the mind alone. Therefore, in the substance of the mind there will be a power of distinguishing all sensible things, just as there is in the imagination; which will certainly be able to be called an excellent imagination and an intellectual sense.

Imagine again that your mind grows so much over the soul that, with the remaining parts of the soul pertaining to imagination, sensation, and generation being erased, the whole soul is one mind and nothing else: this mind, being left alone and pure, will be an angel.

Giovanni Pico, Oratio, Conclusiones and.a: These pages give Pico's theses on the soul and intellect. He states that the soul always understands itself and thereby understands all beings in a certain way, and that it understands nothing in act and distinctly except itself. The rational part is called possible intellect, agent intellect, or intellect in habit, according to its condition. The agent intellect makes pre-existing species actually knowable, as light makes colors actually visible.

q.t: The soul always understands itself, and by understanding itself, it understands all beings in a certain way.

Just as light does not make colors colors, but makes already pre-existing colors (potentially visible) actually visible, so the agent intellect does not make species when they were not there before, but makes actually knowable species that were pre-existing in potentiality.

Ficino, De vita libri tres|||Renaissance.a: Ficino defines the spirit as a vapor of the blood, pure, subtle, warm, and lucid, made from the subtler blood by the heart's heat. It rises to the brain, where the mind uses it to exercise the internal and external senses. He orders the chain as blood serving spirit, spirit the senses, and the senses reason. He also says the phantasia is troubled by images and cares through waking, and the quiet of night settles it. The soul is master and king of the body, and the body's health depends on the soul's.

k.g: the vital energy or animating force
the spirit responsible for sensory and cognitive functions

q.t: An instrument of this kind is the spirit itself, which among physicians is defined as a certain vapor of the blood, pure, subtle, warm, and lucid. And, recreated from the subtler blood by the very heat of the heart, it flies to the brain; and there the mind uses it diligently to exercise the senses, both internal and external.

This distraction and perturbation is entirely contrary to subsequent contemplation, which demands a tranquil and serene mind. Only in the quiet of the night is that agitation finally settled and calmed.

For it is not right to cultivate only the servant of the soul, that is, the body, while neglecting the soul, the master and king of the body: especially since it is the opinion of the Magi and Plato that the whole body so depends upon the soul that unless the soul is in good health, the body cannot be in good health.

Colonna, Hypnerotomachia Poliphili|||Ren.a: In Colonna's narrative, sleep occupies the eyes of the speaker while the mind and the vigilant spirits stay apart from it. Polia's Idea is described as deeply impressed in Poliphilo and sculpted within. Poliphilo says the sights he saw stay in his intellect and fresh memory, depicted and indelible. Polia, in her own account, describes a vigilant, regulating, thieving imagination that let her do in his absence what she could not do in his presence.

q.t: Now the damp eyes, closed a little between the reddening eyelids, without lingering between bitter life and sweet death, were occupied and oppressed by a sweet sleep, which with the mind and with the loving and vigilant spirits does not remain united, nor participate in such operations.
Nor do I feel a lethargic passion. But I hold it all well preserved within my intellect and most fresh memory, depicted and indelible.

By such accidents, already inclined and greedily immersed in the extreme leagues of love, with the vigilant, regulating, and thieving imagination, I operated with him absent that which I could not, nor knew how to, do presentially.

Guru Nānak, Japjī / Ādi Granth|||Indian.a: The hymns shown address the mind directly, calling it wandering, quarrelsome, foolish or fickle, and telling it to meditate on the Name and take up the word of the Guru. The self-willed Manmukh burns in the poison of ego, and Maya leads the mind astray in doubt. The Guru brings the five senses under control, and the mind that was withered and parched comes to drink the elixir. The pages shown are hymns from the Ādi Granth outside the Japjī.

q.t: By meeting with the true Guru, the wandering mind is stopped; it returns and dwells in its own house [Metaphor for the soul returning to its natural, divine state.].
The Guru has come to me, O my soul, and all my five senses have come under control. Within me, the Guru has instilled the Word, O my soul, and the True Guru is known as the Eternal One.
My mind is satisfied by the Guru’s Name, O my soul; the arrogance of my mind is erased.

Śiva Saṃhitā|||Indian.a: The Śiva Saṃhitā says the one soul in a dream creates many objects by willing, and on waking only the one soul remains. The universe is likened to this, and to a rope seen as a snake and a shell seen as silver. The commentary says the world is born from consciousness and, if held to be true, is conceptualization. The yogi who renounces mental constructs sees the Self within the Self, forgets the world, and delights in samadhi.

q.t: As in a dream the one soul creates many objects by mere willing; but on awaking everything vanishes but the one soul; so is this universe.

This entire world of moving and non-moving beings is born from consciousness. If the world is considered true, then this is the imagination. If it does not exist, then only that one Consciousness exists, and nothing else.
The yogi practitioner of yoga, having renounced all mental constructs, sees the Self within the Self.

Svapnaśāstra / Svapnādhyāya (Sanskrit dr.a: The text says dreams arise when all the senses are at rest and the mind stays active among objects of thought. It sorts dreams into those with auspicious results and those with inauspicious results, and lists images for each. Dreams of the sick, suspicious, worried, lustful, or overexcited bear no fruit. After a significant dream one should not fall back asleep.

q.t: when all the senses are at rest, but the mind is not at rest and remains active among objects of thought, it enters into dreams of various forms.
One who is sick, suspicious, overcome by worry, afflicted by lust, or overly excited—the dreams of such people never bear any fruit.

Gianfrancesco Pico, De imaginatione (wit.a: Gianfrancesco Pico says the human soul is joined to the body as its form, and is not submerged in it as souls without intellect are. He reports Themistius, for whom the passive intellect is the sensible phantasy and the possible intellect is not bound to an organ. In that account men do not remember after death because the passive intellect is abolished with the body. He also notes that sense, affected by a more vehement sensible object, is weakened and misses lesser ones.

q.t: It is therefore proper and most peculiar to the human soul, among those forms joined to perishable bodies, to be joined to the body as its form, and furthermore not to be immersed in it in the manner that those souls are submerged which are not endowed with intellect.

For that [passive intellect] in Themistius is the sensible phantasy, gifted with the name of "intellect"; but the possible intellect, which also has the name "of power," is properly the intellect, not bound to an organ;

Again, when he treats of the difference between the intellect and the sense, he teaches that the sense, having been affected by a more vehement sensible object, is weakened, so much so that it does not perceive lesser sensible objects.

Pomponazzi, Tractatus de immortalitate a.a: Pomponazzi holds that the human intellect has two aspects: as intellect it knows the universal, and as human it perceives the universal only within the singular. The phantasm moves the intellect, and understanding is a kind of being acted upon, so the soul never understands without a phantasm. He says the intellect requires the organ as object, not as subject.

q.t: For the human intellect possesses two aspects: that it is an intellect, and that it is human. Insofar as it is an intellect, it knows the universal; but insofar as it is human, it is unable to perceive the universal except within the singular.

The thing that moves the intellect is the phantasm, as is clear from Book 3 of On the Soul. Therefore, it does not understand without a phantasm, although it does not "know" in the same way that the imagination does.
For in every cognition, no matter how abstract, the mind forms for itself some corporal image [original: "idolum," here meaning a mental representation].

Nifo, De intellectu / De immortalitate a.a: Nifo, answering Pomponazzi, says the soul needs the phantasm to acquire intelligible species and, while in the body, afterward as well, as sight needs a wall to perceive colors. He says the intellectual soul remains after death as intellect or intelligence, because as soul it has no proper operation. He also separates faculties, which flow from the soul's essence, from habits, which are acquired through acts with the body and remain after death.

q.t: We have also said that it, after the species are acquired while it is in the body, needs the phantasm in the way that sight, in perceiving colors, needs a wall; for just as colors cannot be without a wall, so universals cannot be without phantasms, which are singulars imagined or existing in the body.

From which it is clear Aristotle did not deny the soul remains after death: but only asserted it does not remain, because it is a soul, since it (as soul) has no proper operation. It remains, however, as an intellect, and as a perfect intelligence: which afterward no longer needs the body.

Indeed, faculties are in the soul without the body, since they flow from the essence of the soul, which is simultaneously rational and sensitive. Habits of the soul cannot exist without the body, since they are not acquired by it except from frequent acts, which do not exist without the body.

Wang Yangming, Chuanxilu|||Chinese.a: In letters to Lu Yuanjing, Wang Yangming says the mind keeps self-awareness whether it is excited or calm, because the natural, clear realization of its original nature remains present. The observing mind and the disorderly mind are parts of one self, and a temporary stop would be a dead stop. He holds that freedom is the mind's original state and that self-possession and carefulness express it. Treating them as two divides the mind and causes internal conflict.

q.t: The mind that maintains self-awareness is not agitated, because it possesses a natural, clear realization of its original nature, and therefore its emotions have not been stirred. As soon as agitation and excitement are present, the mind becomes disorderly and unruly.
If the mind constantly maintains true self-awareness, it will be simultaneously active and tranquil. Heaven and earth endure precisely because they are always in motion and yet always at peace.

Such a person fails to realize that freedom is the mind’s original state, and that self-possession and carefulness are the manifestations of that freedom. To treat them as two separate things, and thus divide the mind when using it, causes internal conflict.

Pomponazzi, De naturalium effectuum caus.a: Pomponazzi holds that the imaginative and cogitative powers, when strongly fixed on something, command the spirits and the blood, so that health, sickness and even death can follow from the mind. He treats visions as arising in rapture and ecstasy, in sleep, and in waking states where the internal powers send images to the external senses. Morning dreams are said to be truer than others. He also discusses how mental images and species are produced in the soul.

q.t: For the operations of living beings, whether they belong to the nutritive power [the biological function of growth and sustenance] or the sensitive power [the faculty of sensation and movement], are immediately carried out through the spirits and the blood, acting as their own proper instruments. These instruments are naturally suited to be moved by and to obey the imagination and the desires according to their command.

From this, it follows that the nature of the body is entirely subject to the movements of the soul. For this reason, the human face displays most certainly both the clear signs of the mind’s inclinations and the indications of individual emotions.
Wherefore, since everything that exists is either sensible or intelligible, the human soul—because it comprehends both, namely sense and intellect—will itself be all things.

Agrippa, De occulta philosophia libri tr.a: Agrippa describes light from God passing down through the mind (mens) into reason and then into the idol of the soul, where it becomes imaginable. The idol holds phantasy and the sense of nature, and it is affected by celestial influences, while the mind stands above fate. He also treats prophetic dreams as arising from the fantastic spirit and intellect together, and he gives the world and the celestial bodies souls that share in reason and mind.

q.t: The human soul consists of mind, reason, and the idol: the mind illuminates the reason, the reason flows into the idol, and all is one soul.

I say, however, the idol of the soul is that vivifying and ruling power of the body, the origin of the senses, through which the soul itself unfolds its powers of sensing in this body: it senses corporeal things through the body, moves the body through space, rules it in place, and nourishes the body in the body.
just as seeing dreams is from the strength of the imagination, so understanding them is from the strength of the intellect.

Paracelsus, Astronomia magna (Philosophi.a: Paracelsus places the soul's seat and throne in the heart, at the middle of the human, and says it must be cleansed of all that is contrary to God. A spirit from Heaven, called an eternal light in everyone, gives understanding of the Kingdom of God; without it, understanding is earthly. A person tinctures the soul by choice, and fruits and works make it manifest. An inner angel carries messages between the person and God, faster than thought.

q.t: Regarding this, take note now of the seat and throne of the soul: namely, that it sits in the heart in the middle of the human, and it consumes the spirits given to it, which possess knowledge of good and evil.

Namely, this is through a spirit that is from Heaven, as we possess it, and it is that which returns again to the Lord; it is an eternal light within all of us. Now, in that same spirit, we have understanding alone, so that when we hear of the Kingdom of God, we understand it through him.

Rather, if a thought occurs to our mind, it has already traveled toward God and back again. Thus, because God wishes to dwell in us, it is proper for us to act in the spirit, which should act from us toward Him.

Paracelsus, De occulta philosophia (drea.a: Paracelsus says certain harms and illnesses arise through belief, thought, and imagination, which he calls the creative power of the mind. A person burdened with melancholy and evil imaginings should be kept in cheerful company so those thoughts are forgotten. In time of plague, he writes, imagination travels from house to house and land to land, and only resistance by imagination helps. He adds that a sleeper as rational as one awake could question the Evestrum, a spiritual double, and be told the truth.

k.g: the creative power of the mind
the soul, heart, or internal disposition

q.t: But regarding this path: it is only through the power of belief, through thought, and through imagination the creative power of the mind to manifest reality that certain harms and illnesses arise.

For in this, the imagination is so fast, evil, and wonderful, that it travels not only from one house to another, from one street to another, or from a named city to another, but from one land to another.

For if it were possible that a person in sleep were as rational as when awake, and such an Evestrum appeared to him, and he asked it about whatever he wished, the truth would be indicated to him about every matter, of which it is not fitting to speak further.

Cardano, De immortalitate animorum (with.a: Cardano names the mind and intellective soul as the immortal part of a person and lists its five habits: prudence, art, science, intellect and wisdom. He argues that the intellect does not wear away with age, and that the natural philosophers he cites hold the soul to be one. He describes sleep and waking through the joining or separation of three principles: the mind, the internal sense and the external sense.

q.t: This, however, is that the mind will know itself, what it is and whence it set out; for the immortal nature is the mind and the intellective soul.

From its operation, moreover, it is demonstrated in two ways: first, because it is always being perfected and never grows old; but the other powers do not act thus: indeed, memory, which seems the most excellent of the internal senses, the more it holds, the less capable it is of holding more.

Sleep, therefore, is the fettering of the mind with an impediment to both senses. Wakefulness, however (I speak of in man), is the freedom of the mind, whether the senses be shrouded or the senses themselves be free.

Popol Vuh|||Native American & Mesoameric.a: The creators judge that the first four men, who know and see everything, are equal to them, and the Heart of Heaven casts a mist over their eyes. Their sight clouds like a breathed-on mirror, so they see only what is near, and their wisdom and understanding are lost. Their wives are given to them while they sleep, and they find them on waking.

q.t: Immediately, a mist was cast into their eyes by the one who was the Heart of Heaven. Their sight was clouded like a mirror that is breathed upon; their eyes were blurred. Thus they could only see what was near, and only those things were clear to them.

Renaissance ars memoriae (Grataroli, Bru.a: Grataroli gathers definitions of memory from Aristotle and Plato, places its seat in the third ventricle of the brain, and separates memory from reminiscence, which recovers what has been forgotten. He links the working of the memory to the temperament of the brain and spirits, and lists foods, habits and cares that harm or strengthen it. Bruxius, in the second edition, calls memory the mother of the Muses and defends an artificial memory built on images.

q.t: Memory is that by which the mind recalls those things which have been. Or, it is a firm perception of the disposition of things and words of the mind. Or (as Aristotle opines) it is the imagination which remains from those things which the senses had detected.

Memory, however, is the retention of images previously perceived by the soul, which, nevertheless, is not useful unless it retains all of them, and restores them in the order in which it conceived them.

If, therefore, you wish to excel in the memory of good things, take care diligently that you understand the certain reason of that which is to be learned. For reason is an indissoluble bond of truth and memory.

Cantares Mexicanos and Nahuatl poetry (w.a: The songs speak of the soul as something that lives on earth for a short time and wishes to keep living after death, and they call earthly life a dream and a fleeting illusion. The singers describe memory and thought as capacities that can be turned toward the heavens, and the poet works "in spirit" on songs heard from the divine. Brinton's vocabulary glosses yollotl as heart, mind, soul.

q.t: But what can I truly speak of here regarding the Giver of Life? We only dream. We are plunged in sleep. I speak here on earth, but we can never speak in worthy terms in this place.

Unless my memory turns toward divine things, it will hardly be possible to reach those heights and witness the wondrous sights in heaven, which bring joy to the sweet heavenly birds before the face of the Lord of the Near and Close.

Why should we remember, while the soul is still alive, that our souls must be scattered here and there? Why remember that we are to be destroyed on earth wherever we go? It is better to hide from this thought and turn away from it.

Cardano, Somniorum synesiorum libri IV||.a: Cardano explains dreams through the movement of the spirits, with sleep as their rest and waking as their vehement movement. He distinguishes five orders of the mind in relation to understanding, and places ecstasy between waking and sleep, with hearing remaining in it. He says the active intellect can bring forgotten dreams back to memory.

k.g: the faculty of the mind that actualizes potential knowledge

q.t: Indeed, ecstasy is intermediate between waking and sleep, just as sleep is between death and waking or life.

But indeed, it was seen in the book on the Immortality of the Soul, that sleep is the rest of the spirits, while wakefulness is their vehement movement: and a dream is a certain trembling and imperfect movement of them. Therefore, all dreams occur when the spirits are moved lightly.

The soul at first sees true dreams, since it is aided by the mind from the lightest motion of the spirits; for it can neither foresee the future with great motion, nor understand at all without motion.

Weyer, De praestigiis daemonum|||Renaiss.a: Weyer, citing Augustine and Aristotle, treats the imagination (phantasia) as a faculty that varies while thinking or dreaming and takes on forms like bodies. People withdrawn from their senses see images of the living and the dead, and on waking believe they were with them. Images remain when objects are absent, and the humors and spirits carry them. Demons can move the humors and bring images to the organs in sleep or waking, and those affected hold the forms to be real.

q.t: A similar thing also happens when men are withdrawn from their bodily senses more deeply than if they were sleeping, and are occupied by such visions. For to these people, images of both the living and the dead appear.

By this same reasoning, demons are able to move the humors of the internal and external senses, and thus bring certain images to the organs as if they were occurring from the outside, whether we are asleep or awake.

In this way, he introduces certain appearances into the appropriate sensory organs just as if they were actually occurring externally—not only to those who are sleeping, but also to those who are wide awake. Thus, certain things are thought to exist or happen externally which, in truth, neither exist nor happen, and often have no existence in the natural world.

Lavater, De spectris, lemuribus et magni.a: Lavater holds that nearly all reported specters are imaginings of the mind. He names the melancholic, people with great headaches or bodily diseases, those who pass sleepless nights, and those of a disturbed mind as subject to seeing and hearing things that no one else perceives. He also separates phantasm, a vision of what does not exist, from fantasy, which concerns what exists.

q.t: In the first place, no one can deny that men who are sad and melancholic—either by their natural temperament or because of great calamities they have suffered—imagine wondrous things for themselves.

a phantasm [original: "phantasma"] is an imagination, a form, or a vision of that which does not exist, such as those things which people seem to see while sleeping; however, a fantasy [original: "phantasia"] is only of that which truly exists.

Huarte, Examen de ingenios|||Renaissance.a: Huarte treats the intellect as an organic power that has its own instrument in the brain. He cites Galen on illness that spoils the brain's temperament, where the intellect's works are lost while memory and imagination stay firm. He says the three front ventricles serve discourse and philosophy, with intellect, memory, and imagination united in each. Imagination is born of heat, and frenzy, madness, and melancholy are hot passions of the brain.

q.t: Of this, experience is seen in one thing, and Galen notes it, that, when in infirmity the temperament and the good composition of the brain is spoiled: many times the works of the intellect are lost, and those of the memory and of the imagination remain firm: which could not happen, if the intellect did not have for itself a particular instrument outside of that, which the other powers have.

The three ventricles, which are in front, I do not doubt that nature made them for nothing other than to discourse and philosophize. Which is proved clearly: because in great studies and contemplations, that part of the head always aches which corresponds to these three concavities.

From heat, which is the third quality, the imagination is born: because there is no other rational power in the brain, nor any other quality that can be assigned to it; furthermore, the sciences that belong to the imagination are those which those who rave in their illnesses speak of, and not those which belong to the intellect and the memory.

Reshit Chokhmah|||Kabbalistic & Hasidic.a: The text says the soul has five parts, the nutritive, sensory, imaginative, appetitive and intellectual faculties. They are one soul divided by function, and all serve the intellect. The imaginative faculty paints the forms of felt things after they leave the senses, and through it a person sees true and false dreams. Samuel is cited as saying that prophecy comes when the soul strips off its senses and physicality, helped by music and joy. Sorcery is said to be healed by nullifying the imagination in the soul.

q.t: But the imaginative faculty is what paints in the soul the forms of things that are felt, even after they have departed from the senses. This faculty is what combines and exchanges some things with others. This is the faculty through which a person sees true and false dreams.

Samuel said that through the expansion of the soul and the nullification of its external sensations and senses, it strips itself of physicality. Then it is a spiritual entity and attains better things than it had attained while it was in the body.

And many have been healed in this way, for the intellect and the thought that prevail over the body and the power of imagination will put the act to rest, and the matter will return to its own essence.

Pūrṇānanda, Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa|||Indian.a: The commentary identifies the Great Principle (Mahat-tattva) with Buddhi, and says it consists of the three qualities (Sattva, Rajas, Tamas) and the Inner Instrument (Antahkarana). The Sharada-Tilaka names that Instrument as Manas, Buddhi, Ahamkara and Chitta. The Mindless State (Unmani) is described as the state where the mind's "mind-ness" no longer exists and it seeks no external objects. In the Yoni Mudra the sensory gateways are closed and breath and mind are joined, and Shruti is cited for the claim that restraining breath restrains the mind.

q.t: The Great Principle, however, consists of the three qualities and the Inner Instrument Antahkarana. The qualities consist of Purity, Passion, and Inertia Sattva, Rajas, Tamas. Regarding the Inner Instrument, the Sharada-Tilaka states: "The Inner Instrument of the Soul is proclaimed to be the Mind, Intellect, Ego, and Consciousness Manas, Buddhi, Ahamkara, Chitta."
Therefore, the essence of the Mindless State is the achievement of a total absence of mental activity—the state where the mind no longer seeks to grasp external objects.

The sacred Scripture Shruti confirms that the mind's stability is gained through such a Seal. It explains that the mind naturally wanders among worldly objects like a restless swan; by restraining the breath through this practice, the mind itself is brought under restraint.

Sahagún, Historia general de las cosas d.a: Sahagún's text reports that the ancients spoke of death as an awakening from a dream. The dead were addressed with "wake up, it is beginning to dawn" and were called teotl, spirit or god. In the Nahuatl description of the good noble maiden, inner qualities appear as qualnamilice (she has good thoughts) and chipauaca iollo (she has a clean heart).

q.t: For which reason the ancients said that when men died, they did not perish, but that anew they began to live, almost as if awakened from a dream, and they returned as spirits or gods.

The good noble maiden: caocquauztica she is very dignified, macitica she is complete, atzoio she is clean, ateuhio she is dustless, qualnamilice she has good thoughts, chipauaca iollo she has a clean heart, tlatlacatl she is a true person, tlacatl person, tlacamelauac she is a straight person,

Bright, A Treatise of Melancholie|||Rena.a: Bright holds that the soul is simple and everlasting, and that its faculties are essential to it. In his account the bodily organs, which he calls ambassadors and notaries to the mind, deliver corrupt reports in melancholy, while reason itself reasons correctly from what it is given. He also argues from dreams that the soul can perceive while the outward senses sleep.

q.t: Even when dreams are merely fancies [products of the imagination], the object—whether caused by a poor diet or the physical condition of the body—is perceived by the mind alone. During this time, the outward senses are in a deep sleep.

For the madman, whatever kind he may be, concludes as logically from what fantasy [the faculty of the mind that forms images of things not present] provides through conceit [a thought, idea, or mental image] as the wisest man does.
For it is most manifest that because of its simple nature, the soul cannot contain any mixture. It cannot support diverse things.

Hayyim Vital — Etz Chaim (Tree of Life)|.a: The pages shown give a philosophical psychology of one human soul with five faculties, among them the Sentient, Imaginative and Rational. They describe a material intellect that perishes with the body and an acquired intellect, emitted from the Active Intellect, that remains after death. The Active Intellect is also said to bestow prophecy, vision and dream on a prepared rational soul.

q.t: Know that the soul is singular in the human species—it is the human soul—yet it possesses many powers and performs many functions within the body according to the instruments through which it operates. These are five faculties: the Nutritive Faculty, the Sentient Faculty, the Imaginative Faculty, the Appetitive Faculty, and the Rational Faculty.

However, the sechel hiyuli material/potential intellect is the intellect born with a person. It is the capacity that prepares them to receive conceptual knowledge. This intellect is a power within the body and is not distinct from it; therefore, it perishes with the destruction of the body.

This is because the Active Intellect is intellect in act constantly and is not otherwise, and it bestows upon the rational soul constantly according to its preparation, its purity, and its freedom from bodily thoughts and false imaginations.

Renaissance Aristotelian De anima commen.a: These commentaries give arguments that the intellect cannot understand without conversion to phantasms. They cite Aristotle, the soul's union with the body, the impairment of understanding when the organ of phantasy is corrupted, and the agent intellect's action on phantasms. Another passage says the intellect uses memory and other powers to collect the universal and later has no need of them. The rational soul is described as one substance that gives the vegetative and sensitive operations, and no bodily organ is the organ of the intellect.

q.t: Because the Philosopher [Aristotle] says that to understand is to contemplate phantasms. Therefore, it cannot understand without conversion to phantasms.
For the intellect uses memory and other powers to collect the universal, which is the principle of art and science, of which it later has no need once it has attained it.
Thus, the rational soul vegetates and gives sensation everywhere through the body of man, because no bodily organ is the organ of the intellect and reason in which it exercises its operations;

Bruno, De imaginum, signorum et idearum.a: Bruno cites Aristotle's De Anima to hold that human understanding is either imagination or not without imagination, so the intellect sees only through a likeness, image, shape or sign. Forms pass from the senses into the inner faculties. He sets sense, imagination, reason, intellect and the divine mind in a graded order as acts of one simple essence.

q.t: Thus, whether the mind is searching, discovering, judging, arranging, or remembering, it must not wander away from the mirror, nor should it act without images.

Therefore, we recognize that we cannot perform any operation suited to our nature without certain forms or figures. These are conceived from sensible objects through the external senses and are then placed and organized within our inner faculties.

Sense, which is now reason, argues within itself, and in the intellect it notices that it is arguing. Sense, which is now intellect, understands within itself, but in the divine mind, it contemplates its own understanding.

Perera, De magia, de observatione somnio.a: Perera lists four causes of true dreams. The first is a predominating bodily humor, and the second is a vehement disturbance of the mind such as love, hope, fear, or hatred. He says the sleeping mind receives what is presented without examination, and is readier to believe divine things than the waking mind, which weighs everything by reason. Citing Iamblichus, he places divine dreams near the beginning or end of sleep. God can calm the humors and animal spirits and purge the imagination.

q.t: The second cause of dreams looks to some vehement and excited affection and disturbance of the mind, I mean love, hope, fear, and hatred. For those who love ardently frequently dream of their loves; those who fear are often troubled by threatening and terrifying sights in their sleep.
But in sleep, the mind of man receives the things presented to it without examination, being more prepared and prompt to believe and obey the things given divinely.

He can, at any time—indeed even without time—suddenly calm the agitation of the humors, quiet the tossing of the animal spirits, purge the imagination, enlighten the mind, and appropriately prepare the soul for perceiving divine dreams.

Wright, The Passions of the Minde in Gen.a: Wright defines the passions as internal acts of the soul bordering on reason and sense, pursuing good or fleeing ill and causing alteration in the body. When a passion holds the soul, the imagination gives the understanding only what feeds the passion, like green spectacles, and shows the object fairer than it is. The will is said to have affections like the sensitive appetite, and the appetite often draws the will to follow its pleasures.

k.g: the concupiscible power or coveting faculty

q.t: for whatsoever we understand, passeth by the gates of our imagination, the cousin-german to our sensitive appetite, the gates of our imagination being prevented, yea, and well-nigh shut up with the consideration of that object which feedeth the passion, and pleaseth the appetite;

Theſe paſſions then be certaine internall actes or operations of the ſoule, bordering vpon reaſon and ſenſe, proſecuting some good thing, or flying some ill thing, cauſing therewithall some alteration in the body.
finally, as our wit understands whatsoever our senses perceive, even so our will may affect whatsoever our passions do follow:

Xingming Guizhi (Aims of Nature and Life.a: The compendium arranges consciousness in nine layers, using the image of wind, ripples, waves and sea. The Ninth, Amala-vijnana, is named the White and Pure Consciousness. It assigns the Hun cloud-soul to breath and the Po white-soul to essence, with the Po tied to seeing and hearing. Quoting Heze, it describes the mind as empty and quiet yet able to know.

q.t: The Sixth Consciousness is the ripples. The Seventh Consciousness is the waves. The Eighth Consciousness is the Sea of the Heart.
The Po white-soul is the spirit of the essence. It has both empty and solid aspects. It is that which the ears and eyes use for seeing and hearing.
The essence of the mind can know. This knowing is the mind itself. The mind is fundamentally empty and quiet, supremely void and supremely spiritual.

Fludd, Utriusque cosmi historia — tracta.a: Fludd holds that the mind remembers and understands itself, and that it assimilates to things: by essence to the earth, by imagination to water, by reason to the air, and by intellect to the firmament. He calls the soul always moved, a rational intellect and intellectual spirit. He argues it is immortal because understanding is a rational operation that no bodily organ determines, and because it naturally desires blessedness. In the astrology section the human mind is called a living ray of God, which the stars as ministers cannot act upon.

q.t: Thus, through its essence, it is assimilated to the earth; through imagination, to water; through reason, to the air; and through the intellect, it is assimilated to the firmament.
Furthermore, since understanding is a rational operation of the soul that does not depend on the body—because no bodily organ determines it—it is certain that the soul itself is incorruptible.
But because the human mind is like a living ray of God himself, the celestial ministers can no more act upon it than they can upon the ordainer himself, namely God.

Academic disputationes de anima, de imag.a: The disputation places the dream in the sensitive faculty, where common sense, phantasy and memory concur, since a dream happens in sleep. Phantasy is named the efficient cause and is said to work at night, stirring the species perceived in wakefulness through spirits and vapors. Animals dream too, though man dreams more distinctly because of thinner vapors and sharper internal senses. The intellect is admitted to a share in ordering dreams, and by day the external senses pass species to the internal senses.

q.t: This is the phantasy, which is not only busy in the daytime, but also diligently performs its duty at night, and wandering here and there at will, excites, outlines, and represents the species perceived in wakefulness by means of the concurrence and agitation of spirits and vapors, so that they become more evident.

Otherwise, we willingly grant that the intellect is not to be excluded from the elaboration of dreams. For such a discourse, such a disposition of orations is not to be ascribed to the sensitive soul, but rather to the intelligent soul.
By day, the senses of the external man are most busy and industrious, while they receive the species of sensible objects in the outer part of the body and transmit them to the internal senses.

Boehme, Vierzig Fragen von der Seelen Ur.a: Boehme places the soul in the inner principium, ruling also the outer. The heart is the seat of the fire-smith, and the head holds the mind and the five senses, which arise from five spirits of understanding. The outer being reaches the soul only through imagination, and the body is called the soul's mirror and dwelling-house. The spirit is said to hold all understanding and knowledge and to be able to enter God. It can also change itself through imagination without its knowledge.

k.g: the power of forming mental images or creative desire
the breathing of the soul into the body
the doctrine that the soul is transmitted from parents to children

q.t: But the true fire-smith in the centrum sits in the heart and conducts his rule with the spirit in the head, where he has his council chamber as the mind and senses, and the five prince-counselors as the five senses, which arise from the five spirits of understanding, as we have mentioned in the third, second, and first books.

And we give you to understand that the spirit can change itself in this time of the body, which happens without its knowledge through the imagination, as through the lust-seeking, where the desiring figures such a shape in the soul's will, as the lust is toward the evil or good.
for in the spirit lies all understanding and knowledge; it has the senses and the noble life, which unites itself with GOD, and is so subtle that this spirit can and may enter into GOD.

Campanella, De sensu rerum et magia|||Re.a: Campanella calls the soul God sends into us the mens (mind) and the soul shared with beasts the spiritus (spirit). Man is said to be composed of flesh, spirit and mind. Sensation is defined as the perception of an affection together with a judgment about the object causing it. Memory is called an anticipated sensation and discourse a sensation of the similar within the similar. The soul is described as a warm, thin, mobile spirit, and dreams are said to arise from internal causes, waking motions left in the spirit, God, or intelligences.

q.t: The soul, therefore, which God sends into us is called the mens mind, but that which we have in common with beasts is the spiritus spirit.

For as we explained in the booklet on dreams, dreams arise either from internal affections and causes, or from motions occurring during waking time and left behind in the spirit, or from God, or from intelligences.
Therefore, if sensation is an affection, and all elements and elemented things suffer, then all things feel.

Burton, The Anatomy of Melancholy|||Rena.a: Burton describes memory as a register of sense impressions, seated in the back of the brain and called on by imagination and reason. Sleep binds the outward senses and the common sense, while imagination and reason stay free, which is why dreams arise, varying with humors, diet, actions, and objects. The Rational Soul is defined as a spiritual substance moving itself and divides into Understanding and Will. Imagination, taking objects from the senses or memory, may misjudge or exaggerate them and pass them to the heart, seat of the affections.

q.t: The imagination [original: "Phantasie"] alone is free, along with its commander reason, as appears by those imaginary dreams which are of various kinds: natural, divine, demonic, etc.
It is divided into two chief parts, differing in function only, not in essence: the Understanding, which is the rational power of comprehension; and the Will, which is the rational power of action.

In brief, the process is as follows: an object to be known comes to our imagination through the outward senses or memory (residing in the front part of the brain). The imagination, by either misunderstanding or exaggerating the object, immediately communicates it to the heart, which is the seat of all emotions [original: "affections"].

Descartes, Traité de l'homme (De homine).a: Descartes names four causes of the ideas formed on the gland in waking or sleep: the force of the soul, the action of the spirits, external objects, and the vestiges of memory. During sleep the soul usually has little power over its own attention, though in the morning it can reason well for short intervals. He argues that the seat of the soul cannot be the whole brain, since all remembered ideas would then be present to the Mind, and he says memory impressions help shape the ideas formed on the gland.

q.t: The ideas which are formed upon the gland while waking or while sleeping cannot have more than four causes, which we have already indicated several times, namely the force of the soul, the action of the spirits, the action of external objects, and the vestiges of memory.
Nor is the entire brain the seat, for otherwise we should have to have all the ideas that are hosted in our memory perpetually present to our Mind, that is, to perceive them.

For if the figure of some particular object is imprinted much more distinctly than any other at the location in the brain toward which this gland is precisely leaned, the spirits tending toward there cannot fail to also receive its impression.

Descartes, Meditationes de prima philoso.a: Descartes holds that nothing can exist in the mind as a thinking thing without the mind being conscious of it. He says the mind begins to think and is conscious of its thinking from infancy, even where memory does not retain it, and that we are always conscious of its acts but of its faculties only in potentiality.
