He separates imagination from pure intellection using the triangle, the chiliogon, and the pentagon. Imagining needs a particular contention of the mind that understanding does not.

k.g: I think, I am, I am a thinking thing

q.t: That nothing can exist in the mind, insofar as it is a thinking thing, of which it is not conscious, seems to me self-evident, because we understand nothing in it, when viewed in this way, that is not a thought or dependent upon a thought.

For example, when I imagine a triangle, I not only understand that it is a figure encompassed by three lines, but I simultaneously view these three lines as if present with the eye of the mind, and this is what I call imagining.

Descartes, Les passions de l'âme|||Renai.a: Descartes distinguishes perceptions that have the soul as cause, such as perceiving one's own volitions and imaginations, from those caused by the body. He defines the passions of the soul as perceptions, feelings, or emotions referred to the soul and produced, preserved, and strengthened by movements of the spirits. He also separates purely intellectual joy, which the soul excites in itself, from the joy that is a passion, and says that while the soul is joined to the body the imagination makes a brain impression that accompanies intellectual joy.

q.t: Those which have the soul as their cause are the perceptions of our volitions, and of all the imaginations or other thoughts which depend upon it. For it is certain that we cannot will anything without perceiving at the same time that we will it.

After it has been thus considered in what way the Passions of the soul differ from all its other thoughts, it seems to me that they can be defined in general as: Perceptions, or feelings, or emotions of the soul, which are referred specifically to it, and which are produced, preserved, and strengthened by some movement of the spirits.
In truth, however, as long as the soul is joined to the body, it can hardly happen that this intellectual joy does not have as a companion that joy which is a Passion.

Isaiah Horowitz — Shnei Luchot HaBrit (T.a: Horowitz states that the Kabbalists count five levels of the soul: Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah, Chayah, and Yechidah. He says the vital soul is sustained by physical food and the emanated, spiritual soul by conceptual and intellectual matters. The soul's power first expands in Thought, then becomes Wisdom and intellect, and the soul endures in the individual while the body endures only as a species.

k.g: a high level of the soul

q.t: It is known to the Kabbalists that the levels of the soul are five: Nefesh vitality, Ruach spirit, Neshamah breath/soul, Chayah living one, and Yechidah singular one.
The vital soul is sustained by physical food and drink. However, this emanated and spiritual soul is only nourished by conceptual and intellectual matters.
In truth, the first expansion of the soul's power is in Thought; from Thought, it becomes Wisdom and intellect.

Annambhaṭṭa, Tarkasaṃgraha|||Indian.a: Annambhaṭṭa defines the soul (ātman) as the substratum of knowledge, of two kinds: the Supreme soul, God, and the individual soul, which is distributed to each body, all-pervading, and eternal. Mind (manas) is the organ by which pleasure and the like are perceived, one for each soul, atomic in form, and eternal. The commentary says mind is atomic so that sensations are not simultaneous. Imagination (bhāvanā), the cause of memory, is a quality residing only in the soul, and memory is correct or incorrect according to its source.

k.g: The eight starting with understanding are the specific qualities of the Soul

q.t: The organ which is the cause of the perception of pleasure, &c., they call the Mind manas. And it is innumerable, for this reason, that one remains with each Soul. It is in the form of an atom, and is eternal.
Imagination ( bhávaná mental representation ), the cause of memory and arising from notion, resides only in the Soul.
But this definition is common to beasts and plants, and therefore he has stumbled onto another: The Soul is the principle by which we live, feel, move, and understand.
To be plain then, this principle is the Soul of the World [original: "Anima Mundi"], or the universal spirit of Nature.

When the soul looks on one hand at the filth and death of the body, and on the other hand at the excellence and perpetual happiness of the spirit, it desires to be connected with the latter (by the arrangement of the divine breath).

Hobbes, Leviathan (Part I, Of Man) with.a: Hobbes holds that dreams are imaginations of sleepers, drawn from what the senses once received. In sleep the brain and nerves are numbed, so dreams arise from agitation of the inner parts of the body, and different disorders cause different dreams. Hobbes defines reason as the reckoning, by adding and subtracting, of the consequences of agreed general names, and treats the train of thoughts as bound to earlier sense.

q.t: The imaginations of those who sleep are what we call dreams. These also—like all other imaginations—have existed before, either entirely or in pieces, within our senses.

But just as we have no imagination of which we have not formerly had a sense, either in whole or in parts, so we have no transition from one imagination to another of which we have never had the like before in our senses. The reason for this is as follows: All fancies are motions within us, relics of those made in the sense.
Reason, in this sense, is nothing but the reckoning (that is, adding and subtracting) of the consequences of general names agreed upon for the marking and signifying of our thoughts.

Now, our Sages of blessed memory referred to this physical carrier by the name "spirit" ( ruach ), because it is a fine spiritual thing while yet being physical. They referred to the divine matter—that is, the intellect carried upon it—by the name "soul" ( neshamah ), because it is emanated and goes forth from Him, may He be blessed, as a breath goes forth from the mouth of a man.

All these types of dreams are from the power of the koach medameh imaginative faculty, which by itself creates combinations and imagines images, and they all speak vanity and falsehood. This happens during sleep because then smoke and vapors rise from the estomcha stomach to the brain, and then the imaginative faculty mixes and confuses things.

This evidence invalidates the notion that the acquisition of wisdom and knowledge depends on the body and soul together. If so, all of man's acquisition of wisdom and knowledge is due only to the soul, and the body has no part in this, except as a tool for the artisan—and the existence of wisdom and knowledge is impossible in the dead.

Charleton, Physiologia Epicuro-Gassendo-.a: Charleton states that the faculties of an animal, with human ratiocination excepted, are identical with its spirits, the most subtle and active part of its materials. He compares the faculty to a fountain with its chief residence in one part of the body, and the spirits to streams or rays spreading from it to other parts.

q.t: Now, what more pregnant argument than this can the most circumspect desire, in order to their conviction, that the faculties of an animal (we exclude the rational faculty of man from the sphere of our assertion) are identical with its spirits, i.e., the most subtle, most free, and most movable or active part of its materials?

Dārā Shikūh, Sirr-i akbar (Persian Upani.a: The Oupnek'hat sets out the waking state, the state of sleep and the state of sak'hepat, deep sleep, and links them to the worlds of nasout, malkout and djabrout. In sak'hepat the djiw atma, the individual soul, becomes one with the pram atma, the supreme soul. The text also describes the senses, heart, intellect and individual soul being drawn back, step by step, into the âtma.

q.t: Afterwards, they cause the heart to be destroyed within their intellect; and they cause the intellect to be destroyed within the djiw âtma individual soul; and they cause the djiw âtma to be destroyed within the collection of souls collective consciousness; and they cause the collection of souls to be destroyed within the âtma.
It is necessary that you recognize the knower, the act of knowing, and the thing known as one.
Afterward, in the time which is sak'hepat [original: sak'hepat, referring to sushupti, or deep, dreamless sleep], in that time he perceives (grasps) absolutely nothing.

Henry More, The Immortality of the Soul.a: Henry More holds that sensation arises when motion passes from the object to the organ and is conveyed by the soul's presence there, with the spirits as her immediate instrument. He places imagination mainly in the finer animal spirits of the brain's fourth ventricle, and he argues that dreams vary with the dominant humour of the body. He also argues against a single Soul of the World on the ground that memory requires a prior perception by the same soul.

k.g: a hypothesized fluid in the nerves responsible for motion and sensation
the faculty that unites the inputs of the five senses
the Anima Mundi, a universal spirit animating all nature

q.t: For what are dreams but the imaginations and perceptions of someone asleep? Yet these steal upon the soul or rise out of her without her consent.

For it is clearly true that a person is most properly whatever it is that perceives [original: "animadverts"; the faculty of conscious awareness and attention] within them; for that is an operation that no being but oneself can do for them.

Whatever it is, that which sends and directs them must have animadversion [The faculty of conscious awareness or the power to take notice.]; and whatever has the power of awareness also has memory and reason.

Glanvill, Vanity of Dogmatizing / Lux Or.a: The sections on the true notion of a Spirit argue against the Nullibists, who place the mind nowhere, and against the Holenmerians, who place the soul whole in every part of the body. The author holds that the mind is somewhere and has some amplitude, and that thoughts are modes of a lasting soul-substance. A spirit is defined as an immaterial substance naturally endowed with life and the ability to move, divided into intellectual, sensitive and vegetative kinds.

q.t: I cannot help but conceive an Idea of a certain Extension, infinite and immoveable, and of necessary and actual Existence. This I most clearly perceive was not drawn in by the outward senses, but is innate and essentially inherent in the Mind itself.

To this you may add that the human soul is a permanent being, while its thoughts are in a state of flux or constant succession. How, then, can the substance of the soul be its successive operations? If the substance of the soul were to constantly end or perish with every new thought, I ask you, what would happen to memory?
For physicians and anatomists unanimously declare that they have found by very solid experiments that the soul perceives only within the head, and that outside the head there is no perception.

Willis, De anima brutorum (with Cerebri.a: Willis describes man as sharing a corporeal soul with animals, formed from vital blood and animal spirits, and an immaterial, immortal understanding soul with the angels. He assigns imagination, memory and appetite to the cerebrum and ascribes involuntary actions to the cerebellum. He treats sleep, wakefulness and memory as conditions of the same parts of the brain.

q.t: Furthermore, the human mind looks upon itself by a reflexive action. It thinks about its own thinking. By doing this, it acknowledges its own existence, which cannot be perceived by the senses or the phantasy.

For it seems that imagination is a certain undulation of the animal spirits, begun inwardly in the middle of the Cerebrum, and from there expanded everywhere toward its circuit; on the contrary, the act of memory consists in the regurgitation of the spirits from the exterior circuit of the cerebrum toward its middle;
For dreamers imagine that they are performing physical movements which they are actually not doing at all; but sleepwalkers are physically moved, yet they are not aware of it.

Malebranche, De la recherche de la vérit.a: Malebranche calls the understanding the passive faculty of the soul by which it receives ideas and modifications, and he says the senses and imagination are the understanding perceiving through the organs of the body. He holds the mind to be limited, able to know only a few things distinctly at once, and he compares it to a piece of wax taking on shapes. Spirits know truth through union with the Word, the universal Reason of spirits.

k.g: hypothetical physiological fluids responsible for sensation and motor movement

q.t: From this we ought to conclude that it is the understanding which perceives, since its only business is to receive the ideas of objects. For the soul to perceive an object and to receive the idea that represents it is one and the same thing.

But as I am assured that no one has any knowledge of his soul except by thought, or by being inwardly conscious of what passes in his mind, I am certain that if anyone would reason about the nature of the soul, he ought only to consult that internal sensation which constantly represents him to himself as he is.
The spirit cannot know the truth except through its natural and necessary union with Truth itself. It can only be reasonable through Reason.

Christian Knorr von Rosenroth — Kabbala.a: The compendium lists Zohar sayings that place the Psyche, spirit and mind in a chain, and others on dreams and on souls before birth. Its commentary sets out five degrees of the soul: Nephesch, Ruach, Neschamah, Chaijah and Jechidah. It also describes intellection as a generation, with the intelligible object as father, the power of understanding as mother and the act of intellection as son.

q.t: The Psyche lower soul is attached to the body; and the spirit to the psyche; and the mind to the spirit: Like the light of a lamp, which adheres to the wick, with the flame always ascending.

Therefore, the power of understanding, like a mother, through the intellectual form as seed, understands and generates intellectual and internal intellection as a son; with the help of the Father, in whose place is the intelligible object which, either immediately or by means of an idea, is the fundamental cause of cognition or intellection.

And Briah indeed is in the place of the head—for this, because it contains the senses, both internal and external, is the supreme and most excellent part of the human body, the vessel and dwelling place of the rational soul, and through this, of the intellect; and it rules and governs the remaining members, and directs them through suitable means to their end and their ultimate perfection.
Thought, therefore, is the essence and nature of myself, or of my mind, or of that which is in me besides the body.
The very first thing that occurs to me concerning myself is this: I Think, as I also observed above. I see that thought is so connected to me that I cannot exist without it, as far as I know myself.

Hence, during sleep, by the force of the union still enduring, languid, interrupted, involuntary, and fleeting thoughts are excited in the mind, which seem either to be almost non-existent or entirely absorbed.

Spinoza, Ethica (Parts II–V)|||Renaissan.a: Spinoza holds that the idea of the Mind is united to the Mind as the Mind is united to the Body, and that Mind and its idea are one thing conceived under Thought. Whoever knows something knows that they know it, and so on to infinity. He describes a linking of ideas that follows the order of the body's affections and each person's habit, as when a Roman hears the word apple and thinks of the fruit. He denies a free power to suspend judgment, citing dreams, where judgment is suspended only when one dreams that one is dreaming.

q.t: For as soon as someone knows something, by that very fact they know that they know it, and at the same time they know that they know that they know, and so on to infinity.
And thus each person, according as they have been accustomed to join and link the images of things in this or that way, will fall from one thought into this or into another thought.

And we experience this daily in our dreams; I do not believe there is anyone who thinks that while dreaming they have a free power to suspend judgment on the things they dream about, or to ensure that they do not dream what they see themselves dreaming.

Cudworth, The True Intellectual System o.a: Cudworth divides life, or internal self-activity, into a kind that acts with express consciousness and self-awareness and a kind that acts without it. He holds that perfect knowledge requires consciousness and self-perception, and that no organization of matter could produce them. In sleep and dreams he finds the soul shaping its own thoughts without always being conscious of doing so.

q.t: It is this consciousness that makes a being present with itself, attentive to its own actions, or observant of them, perceiving itself to do or suffer, and having a fruition or enjoyment of itself.

But just as nothing can be more prodigiously absurd than to attribute infallible omniscience to every atom of matter, it is also directly contradictory to suppose perfect knowledge, wisdom, or understanding exists without any consciousness or self-perception. Consciousness is essential to cogitation [original: "cogitation"; thought or the act of thinking].

There is also another more interior kind of plastic power in the soul (if we may call it that) by which it is formative of its own thoughts [original: "cogitations"], which the soul itself is not always conscious of. For example, when in sleep or dreams, the soul frames conversational discourses [original: "interlocutory discourses"] between itself and other persons in a long series, with coherent sense and appropriate connections.

Sefer Refu'at ha-Nefesh (Healing of the.a: The passage is a prayer in which the speaker entrusts spirit and body to God in sleep and in waking. Nearby hymns speak of the soul's gathering at death, evil spirits removed from the enclosure of the soul, and angels of peace guiding it to rest.

q.t: Into His hand I will entrust my spirit when I sleep and when I wake, and with my spirit, my body; the Lord is with me, and I will not fear.

Estonian folk-belief and magical song (B.a: The dream-omen list assigns outcomes to dream images: a wolf, the dead, thunder, water, blood, a snake and a black horse each foretell a particular event, such as illness, death or a change in weather. The idiom list uses meel, mind, in phrases such as mind in the throat for great need and nine minds for fickleness. Hingede-päew, Soul Day, is described as a day when the souls of the departed may walk and are invited by name at first cock's crow to a meal.

k.t: miks sa oma meele metsa lükkasid?
k.g: why did you push your mind into the forest?
my mind was right in my throat

k.t: ära sa pea enesele üheksa meelt
k.g: do not hold nine minds for yourself
one soul coming, the other going

k.t: hing aga luie, or kontide, wahel
k.g: the soul is only between the bones

q.t: Dreaming of a wolf means having dealings with Germans; being with the deceased in a dream or hearing from them signifies a change in the weather; hearing thunder in a dream means an imperial command; being in water or having to do with it threatens illness to the dreamer himself or to another person about whom he has dreamed at the same time.

nüüd tema meel on perses peast now his mind is in the backside out of his head he is foolish — mull oli meel õige kaelas my mind was right in my throat I was in great need — ära sa pea enesele üheksa meelt do not hold nine minds for yourself do not be fickle

The souls of the departed are permitted to walk about on this day; therefore, a meal is prepared for them, to which they are invited by name at the first cock's crow while the household members go outside.

Kirk, The Secret Commonwealth of Elves,.a: Kirk writes that a seer is first wrapped in a trance, a transport and a kind of temporary death, as if stripped of body and senses, and that this places no obstacle on the intellect. The text describes souls that have not reached rest and wish to reveal a murder or a treasure, and says the fairy folk have more refined bodies and intellects than humans. In an account from around 1676, a treasure appeared first to the imagination and then an audible voice named the place to the waking senses.

q.t: Similarly, our seer is wrapped in a trance, a transport, and a kind of temporary death—as if stripped of his body and all his senses—when he is first made a participant in this curious piece of knowledge. However, this does not create any obstacle or strain on a person's intellect.

It is not at all likely that their own apprehension or the strong imagination that puts the "animal spirits" [In older medicine, the fluids in the nerves that caused movement] to work to move the body could preserve it from sinking into the depths or falling headlong while asleep any better than when awake, as the body is just as heavy as before.
The appearance of a treasure was first represented to their imagination, and then an audible voice named the location to their waking senses.

Aubrey, Miscellanies; Beaumont, Treatise.a: These collections describe spirits entering souls: a good spirit raises a holy soul to the light of wisdom, and an evil spirit incites a wicked one to crime. Dreams are said to come from angels or from God, and divine dreams are known by a settled determination of the understanding. Cardano, quoted on ecstasy, places it between wakefulness and sleep, with visions clearer than dreams and hearing still possible.

q.t: For when a good spirit passes into a holy soul, he elevates it to the light of wisdom. But an evil spirit, infused into a wicked soul, incites it to theft, murder, lust, and all the typical works of evil spirits.

He observes that God rules in the understanding of wise and virtuous men and powerfully inclines it to a belief and resolution, even though the understanding does not see reasons in the object that are altogether proportionate to the effect it feels in the soul; so the extraordinary determination of the understanding is an evident proof of the divinity of the dream.

Ecstasy is a middle state between wakefulness and sleep, just as sleep is between death and wakefulness or life. Visions in ecstasy are more certain than dreams—clearer and more evident. Those caught in an ecstasy can hear, which those who are sleeping cannot.

Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā|||Indian.a: In the Fourth Lesson, Gheraṇḍa teaches pratyāhāra, in which the Chitta is withdrawn from sights, praise or censure, smells and tastes and brought under the control of the Self. The Seventh Lesson describes Samadhi as separating the Manas from the body and uniting it with the Paramatma, and lists a sixth form reached through Mano-Murcha Kumbhaka, the swoon of mind. In Sukshma Dhyana, the awakened Kundali joins the Atma and leaves the body through the eyes.

k.g: the latent spiritual force at the base of the spine

q.t: Let one bring the Chitta under his control by withdrawing it, whenever it wanders away drawn by the various objects of sight.
Separate the Manas from the body, and unite it with the Paramatma Supreme Self. This is known as Samadhi or Mukti liberation from all states of consciousness.

When by a great good fortune, the Kundali is awakened, it joins with the Atma Self and leaves the body through the portals of the two eyes; and enjoys itself by walking in the royal road (Astral Light). It cannot be seen on account of its subtleness and great changeability.

Mahāmudrā instruction manuals (Bhutanese.a: These manuals search for the mind and report that it cannot be found: it cannot see itself, and the Ratnakuta Sutra says it is not found in past, future, or present. They teach that thoughts arising as memories can be recognised in their own nature, like a wave that is not other than water. Awareness and emptiness are called inseparable, and that inseparability is named the nature of the mind.

q.t: If the object and the mind were different, then the mind would become two. However, if the object itself is the mind, how could the mind see itself? The mind cannot see the mind.

Within the state where the essence of one's own mind remains as self-knowing and self-luminous, various thoughts—whether good, bad, or neutral, or whether subtle, medium, or coarse—arise and move as memories.
Because these two are inseparable, it is called the inseparability of awareness and emptiness. This very inseparability of awareness and emptiness is the nature of the mind.

German Traumbücher of the 18th century (.a: The Traumbücher say that dreams differ according to the nature and inclination of the dreamer. Those burdened by black bile have very bad dreams and lovers have sweet ones. They also treat dreams of kings and princes as a separate class, and report a dream taken as divine that led a sick man to a remedy and recovery.

q.t: However, the distinction of all dreams reveals itself according to the nature and inclination of the object. Hence, those who are burdened by black bile harbor very bad dreams, whereas those of the enamored are sweet, according to the common proverb: "The delirious and the lovers fashion their own dreams" [original: "Delirantes & amantes sibi somnia fingunt"].

That the Holy Spirit says of kings and princes that they would have princely and royal thoughts, Isaiah 32:8, and hold them in high regard; that may well also apply to their dreams; for according to the man, so is his strength, Judges 8:21, of which Richter writes as follows:
When he awoke, he held both to be entirely a divine dream, which was by no means to be dismissed, so he did as instructed and recovered to great astonishment.

k.g: the theory that soul and body run in parallel without causal interaction

Moshe Hayyim Luzzatto — kabbalistic disc.a: Luzzatto describes the Emanated Intellect as a simple intellect with no composition, neither a body nor a force in a body, and unchanging. He says it exists in the speaking soul and in the living soul of one who merits it, and that souls are capable of reaching it. On sleep, he says the thoughts that come while sleeping depend on the nature of the body and on one's affairs and customs before sleep, and he compares thoughts to a scribe recording the day.

q.t: Because the Emanated Intellect is a simple intellect, it contains no composition at all; it is not a body, nor is it a force within a body. Rather, it is a simple intellect that does not change at all.
During the day, a person thinks of various ideas, and sleep reflects upon these during the day and night. The thoughts recall one's daily activities, as a scribe records his affairs for that day.

Wolff, Psychologia empirica / Psychologi.a: Wolff holds that the soul has perceptions of itself only through its own modifications, and that being conscious of things perceived together is the same state as distinct perceptions. Apperception arises from the clarity of partial perceptions, and attention, memory and reflection concur in thought. He also derives imagination, dreams and memory from prior sensation, and ascribes memory and intellect to spirits.

q.t: It is well known that we are conscious of the things we perceive and of ourselves when we are awake and when we dream. Therefore, the soul is in a state of distinct perceptions when we are awake and when we dream (§. 13).
Attention and memory concur in the act of apperception. For when the soul is conscious of itself and of the things it perceives, it reflects upon the total whole (§. 23).

Spirits enjoy memory. For every spirit is rational (§. 623), and is thus endowed with reason (§. 451). Since reason would belong to a spirit in vain unless it could actually use it (§. 452), the use of reason cannot be denied to it.

Andrew Baxter, An Enquiry into the Natur.a: Baxter argues that our ideas have no parts, yet we are conscious of perceiving parts, so an extended sensory exists outside the mind. He holds that the soul is always awake and perceiving, even in deep sleep, since an impercipient soul would be dead. Thinking, for Baxter, is active perception, and he denies matter any perceptivity.

k.g: the act of willing or choosing

q.t: If our ideas have no parts, and yet if we perceive parts, it is plain we perceive something more than our own perceptions. But both these are certain: we are conscious that we perceive parts when we look upon a house, a tree, a river, or the dial-plate of a clock or watch.

If it were then an impercipient substance a thing incapable of sensing or perceiving for four or five hours together, it would have to be completely dead. If it were not, let anyone tell me what life is, or what it consists of.

And lastly, thinking could never be produced from such perceptivity. Thinking implies active perception, or activity joined with perceptivity. For this reason, although irrational animals are percipient and also active in willing motion, they lack the other species of activity: the spontaneous direction of their perceptive capacity towards and through their past perceptions.

Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature (Book I.a: Hume names memory and imagination as the two faculties that repeat impressions, and separates them by the force and vivacity of their ideas. He treats belief as the vivacity of the perceptions that memory and the senses present. In the conclusion of Book I he founds memory, the senses and the understanding on the imagination, and describes the self as a succession of perceptions.

q.t: The faculty by which we repeat our impressions in the first manner is called the MEMORY, and the other is called the IMAGINATION. It is evident at first sight that the ideas of the memory are much more lively and strong than those of the imagination, and that the former faculty paints its objects in more distinct colors than any which are employed by the latter.

Thus it appears that the belief or assent [original: "assent"; the mental act of accepting something as true] which always accompanies the memory and the senses is nothing but the vivacity of the perceptions they present. This quality alone distinguishes them from the imagination.
Therefore, the memory, the senses, and the understanding are all founded on the imagination—specifically, on the vividness [original: "vivacity"] of our ideas.

Swedenborg, De anima (Rational Psycholog.a: Swedenborg says the ideas of the imagination enter through the senses and are held in memory, while the order of the memory's parts comes from the pure intellect, which is the soul. He says the ideas used in thought are produced by the mind itself and that thought is perfected as it nears the pure intellect. He calls the mind the soul or life of the intellect and the intellect its body, and he says the mind's loves begin every act of thought.

q.t: Such an arrangement and ordering of the parts of the memory does not come from the senses, but from the pure intellect, and thus from the soul—which is the order, the love, the truth, the law, and the rule of its own system.
Furthermore, thought can be perfected and elevated as it approaches the pure intellect, but imagination is perfected only through sensory experience—either our own or that of others.
The mind is therefore the very soul or life of the intellect. The intellect may be compared to the body of that soul.

Swedenborg, Journal of Dreams (Drömboken.a: Swedenborg records that he held two distinct thoughts at once, one occupied with others and one of the temptation, and that thoughts he had fixed in his mind long before were reproduced. He writes that the will has chief direction over the understanding, and that thoughts fly in with inhalation and are expelled and rectified with exhalation. He reports being granted faith without reasoning, after which he saw his confirmatory thoughts beneath him and laughed at them.

q.t: It was wonderful that I was able to have at one and the same time two thoughts quite distinct from one another,—the one for myself, which occupied entirely the thoughts of others; and at the side of this the thoughts of the temptation, in such a manner that nothing was powerful enough to drive them away.

When we inhale the breath the thoughts fly in from the body, and when we exhale the thoughts are as it were expelled and rectified, so that the very thoughts possess their alternations of activity like the respiration of the lungs.

At last it was granted me by the grace of the spirit to receive faith, without reasoning, an assurance of it. I then saw my own confirmatory thoughts as it were beneath me; I laughed at them in my mind, and still more at those thoughts which offended and opposed them.

Calmet, Dissertations sur les apparition.a: Calmet discusses whether thought could belong to matter, and judges that view to contain greater absurdities than the ones it tries to avoid. He lists melancholy, anger, frenzy, fever and weakened senses as causes of imagining, seeing and hearing what has no basis in reality. He cites Aristotle on the internal senses in sleep and Augustine on images formed in the soul, and assigns most apparitions to the force of the imagination.

q.t: Can one doubt that among all the alleged apparitions of which we hear, the imagination alone produces all those that do not come from Angels and blessed Souls, and which are not the result of human malice?
we see clearly that an infinite number of images are excited in our soul, representing to us what has struck our eyes or our other senses; we experience this every day and at every hour.

When a living man appears in a dream to another man, we do not say that his body or his soul appeared to him, but simply that such a person appeared to him. Why then can we not say that the dead appear without bodies and without souls, but simply that their figure presents itself to the mind and imagination of the living person?

La Mettrie, L'homme machine|||Renaissanc.a: La Mettrie says the word soul should name only the part that thinks within us, and that thought develops visibly with the organs. He cites philosophers who hold that thought is a faculty of feeling and that the rational soul is the sensitive soul applied to ideas. He offers as proof that thought is extinguished when feeling is, as in apoplexy, lethargy and catalepsy. He compares the imagination to a bird on a branch, and calls attention the mother of the Sciences.

k.g: Swiss-style dreams; meaning drifting thoughts or daydreams

q.t: The SOUL is therefore only a vain term for which one has no Idea, and which a good Mind should only use to name the part that thinks within us.

Moreover, how many excellent philosophers have demonstrated that thought is only a faculty of feeling, and that the rational soul is merely the sensitive soul applied to contemplating ideas and reasoning! This would be proven by the mere fact that when feeling is extinguished, thought is as well, as in apoplexy, lethargy, catalepsy, etc.

It is true that such is the vivacity of the springs of the imagination that, if attention, that key or mother of the Sciences, does not intervene, it is scarcely permitted to do anything but traverse and graze over objects.

Lenglet Dufresnoy, Traité historique et.a: The treatise sorts visions into corporal, spiritual or imaginary, and intellectual kinds, and assigns each a different degree of certainty. It holds that the external senses and the imagination can both err. Its notes and quotations link some apparitions to troubled senses, frenzy and sleep, and cite Cardinal Bona on the discernment of spirits.

q.t: The external senses often deceive, when on their simple report one claims to know & penetrate an object entirely, because the different situations of this object represent it in different ways, sometimes even very opposite ones.

The spiritual or imaginary visions or apparitions are those whose impressions are made on the imagination independently of the external senses. (4) They sometimes happen to persons who are sleeping; then they are regarded as dreams.

There are some whose senses are (3) troubled, like the frenetic and other furious people, who have during their waking hours visions exactly like dreams. They speak alone as if they were with people actually present, and they speak with the absent as if with the present, whose resemblances they see, whether they be living or dead.

Helvétius, De l'esprit|||Renaissance & E.a: Helvétius takes the word mind in two senses: the faculty of thinking, and the assemblage of a person's thoughts. He traces errors of judgment to the passions and to ignorance of facts or of the meaning of words, and concludes that all men essentially have a sound mind. He measures the extent of a mind by the number of its ideas and combinations, and treats a new idea as a relationship newly perceived between objects.

q.t: The other is the faculty of preserving the impression that these objects have made upon us; it is called mémoire memory: and memory is nothing other than a continued, but weakened, sensation.
Memory is the warehouse where sensations, facts, and ideas are deposited, the diverse combinations of which form what is called mind.
These principles once admitted, nothing prevents me now from advancing that judging, as I have already proved, is properly nothing but feeling.

Swedenborg, De coelo et inferno (with De.a: Swedenborg calls thought the internal vision of the mind and perception an internal hearing, and says both require internal organized substances. After death the spirit keeps a human form and senses, and the external or natural memory remains, though it reproduces only spiritual things joined to natural ones by correspondence. Spirits joined to a person suppose that person's memory and thoughts are their own.

k.g: the faculty of desire and intent

q.t: Now, thought is internal vision, or the sight of the mind, just as perception is internal hearing; and these cannot exist without internal organized substances as their proper subjects.

Although the external or natural memory remains with man after death, things merely natural are not reproduced therein in the other life, but only such spiritual things as are adjuncts to the natural by correspondence.

Now these spirits know nothing of their being in the person, but all the time they are with him, suppose his memory and thoughts are their own; neither do they see him, for the things in our solar world are not objects of their sight (201).

Reid, An Inquiry into the Human Mind on.a: Reid describes sensation, memory and imagination as distinct operations of the mind. Sensation compels belief in present existence, memory belief in past existence, and imagination carries no belief. He says the faculty of smelling differs from the sensation, and the mind differs from the faculty, since the mind stays the same individual being when the faculty is lost. He holds that the mechanism of the mind's perception is beyond comprehension and finds no purpose in supposed images in the brain.

k.g: the mere act of understanding a concept without judgment or belief
the assumed seat of sensation in the brain

q.t: I am conscious of a difference in kind between sensation and memory, and between both and imagination. I find this also, that the sensation compels my belief of the present existence of the smell, and memory my belief of its past existence.

The faculty of smelling is something very different from the actual sensation of smelling; for the faculty may remain when we have no sensation. And the mind is no less different from the faculty; for it continues the same individual being when that faculty is lost.

If any man will shew how the mind may perceive images in the brain, I will undertake to shew how it may perceive the most distant objects: for if we give eyes to the mind, to perceive what is transacted at home in its dark chamber, why may we not make these eyes a little longer-sighted?

Richard, La théorie des songes|||Renaiss.a: Richard holds that remembering on waking that one has dreamed leaves no room to doubt that the soul is a spirit. Dreaming is defined as awareness of one's dreams and of the soul's continuous action, while reason and its related faculties stay suspended during them. The imagination is described as the place where the soul forms images by imprinting them on the fibers of the brain, with its strength set by the brain's disposition and its activity by the soul.

k.g: hypothetical fluids once thought to carry sensory/motor impulses through nerves

q.t: Recalling therefore upon our waking that we have had such or such a Dream, or at least that we have dreamed; there remains no room for us to doubt that our soul is truly a spirit; this is the noblest destination that one can give to Dreams.
For the imagination, properly speaking, should only be considered as the place where the soul forms images of objects, by imprinting them upon the fibers of the brain.

Moses Mendelssohn — Phädon oder über die.a: In Mendelssohn's dialogue, Socrates and his friends treat the soul as a thinking being whose actions are feeling, thinking and willing. Concepts begin in sensory perception, and the faculty of thought is the source of comparison and composition. The speakers grant that sleep, fainting, dizziness and ecstasy can remove clear consciousness for a time, and ask whether self-awareness and memory continue after death.

k.g: the faculty of forming mental images and concepts
indivisible substances, referring to the soul as a monad that cannot be decomposed

q.t: If that which happens to it afterward is to concern us, and is to excite fear or hope in us already here below: then we ourselves, who are conscious of ourselves here, must still retain this self-awareness in that life and be able to remember the present.

If it is to be present, it must act and suffer; if it is to act and suffer, it must have concepts: for feeling, thinking, and willing are the only actions and sufferings that can belong to a thinking being. Concepts always take their beginning from a sensory perception, and where should sensory perceptions come from, if no instruments, no limbs of the senses are present?

The faculty of thought, and this alone in all of nature, is capable of actually producing comparisons, connections, and juxtapositions through an internal activity: therefore the origin of everything composite, of numbers, magnitudes, symmetry, harmony, and so forth, insofar as they require a comparison and juxtaposition, must be sought solely and exclusively in the faculty of thought.

Mesmer, Mémoire sur la découverte du mag.a: One passage describes waking as the state in which external sensory activity predominates and sleep as the state in which the internal sense predominates, with dream and somnambulism lying between. Another says that in the sleep called somnambulism a person can exercise mental and movement faculties with greater perfection than when awake, through an internal mechanism of the nervous system. The Commission text quotes the ancients on the faculty of the soul they called 'phantasia', imagination, and its empire over the body.

q.t: Waking, however, is the state in which the isolated external sensory activity acts predominantly and is decomposed and imprinted into thoughts and sensations in the internal sense; just as sleep is the state in which the original activity of the internal sense is the predominant one before external sensory perceptions.
For it can be observed that, in sleep, a human being can often exercise all their faculties—both mental and those of movement—with even greater perfection than when awake.

Let one read what the ancients wrote of this faculty of the soul, to which they gave the name of phantasia imagination, & of its empire over the body, & one will see of how many very extraordinary & singular effects it can be the cause, in how many respects it can change, in the end, our physical manner of being, & the ordinary exercise of our functions.

Kant, Kritik der reinen Vernunft|||Renai.a: Kant says the thought that representations belong to me is the same as connecting them in one self-consciousness, and that this unity of apperception is the highest principle of human knowledge. Being conscious of oneself as thinking gives no knowledge of oneself, which requires an intuition of oneself determined by the function of thought. In man, self-consciousness needs internal perception of a given manifold, called sensibility, and its form is the representation of time.

q.t: The thought that the representations given in intuition belong all of them to me, is therefore the same as that I connect them in one self-consciousness, or am able at least to do so; and though this is not yet the consciousness of the synthesis of representations, it nevertheless presupposes the possibility of the latter.

I do not know any object by merely thinking, but only by determining a given intuition with respect to that unity of consciousness in which all thought consists; therefore, I do not know myself by being conscious of myself, as thinking, but only if I am conscious of the intuition of myself as determined with respect to the function of thought.

The consciousness of self (apperception) is the simple representation of the ego, and if by it alone all the manifold (representations) in the subject were given spontaneously, the inner intuition would be intellectual.

Philokalia (hesychast anthology)|||Byzan.a: One set of sayings in the anthology places the soul in the body, the Mind in the soul and Reason in the Mind, and says God is perceived through them. Evagrius teaches that demonic thoughts bring images of sensed things into the soul and shape the mind, and that divine radiance appears to the ruling faculty only when it is stripped of worldly images. The Ascetic Discourse describes a sensation of the mind, a tasting by which the mind receives the consolation of the Holy Spirit.

q.t: For just as the body, when tasting earthly delicacies, has an unerring experience of the sensation, so also the mind, when it triumphs over the "wisdom of the flesh," is able to taste the consolation of the Holy Spirit without error.

I do not say that all memories of such things come from demons, for the mind itself is naturally inclined to bring up images of past events when moved by a person's own will. However, those memories which stir up anger or desire contrary to nature are demonic.

The soul exists within the body, and within the soul is the Mind; and within the Mind is Reason. Through these, God is perceived and glorified, and He makes the soul immortal, granting it incorruptibility and eternal delight.

The soul is never indifferent, not even in sleep, toward the changes occurring in its body; rather, it directs its attention to everything that causes impressions from outside into the body and also what causes them from within.

In sleep, however, the external sensations rest; the person knows nothing of them. Through this silence of the senses, the ideas in sleep obtain such great light that the sleeper is not capable of distinguishing them from sensations.
That we do not remember our dreams after waking, as stated before, comes from the fact that we do not have the attention necessary for thoughts when we wake.

Puységur, Mémoires pour servir à l'histo.a: Puységur reports that people in the magnetic state remember what occupied them in the natural state, while the natural state holds no memory of the magnetic one. He attributes this to an additional sense and compares it to a blind man given sight. He also divides an act into thought, will and action.

k.g: a sleep-like state induced by magnetism
crisis (the state of magnetic healing sleep)
the ability to perceive things through internal mental sight

q.t: They can, with SIX SENSES (if one may put it that way), remember the sensations that the enjoyment of the first five provided them, whereas with five senses they cannot trace back to ideas formed with six.

I distinguish the same transition in me within the most ordinary and common action: I see a book on a table; immediately my thought is occupied with it, my will is then to take it, and immediately I seize it.

Although a somnambulist magnetic sleepwalker, this man still retained all the memories of his waking state conscious condition. It therefore took a new effort on my part to submit him entirely to my will, and this I accomplished promptly.

Schelling, Von der Weltseele (with Syste.a: Schelling defines self-consciousness as the act by which the thinker immediately becomes his own object, and says subject and object of thought are one in it. He calls this act absolutely free. He names internal sense as that within the Self which senses with consciousness, and treats the thing in itself as ideal activity hypostatized.

k.g: ideelle Thätigkeit; the mind's internal power to think and perceive without boundaries
Anſchauung; a direct, non-rational perception or "beholding" of an object
Begräntztheit; the state of being restricted or having a boundary, which is necessary for consciousness

q.t: For what we call "internal sense" is nothing other than that within the Self which senses with consciousness.
Self-consciousness is the act by which the thinker immediately becomes his own object, and conversely, this act and no other is self-consciousness.

Gallerie der neuen Propheten, apokalypti.a: In the Wenzel volume, dreams have several sources: the blood, food, temperament, external impressions, the imagination, and the soul's own inner power. Dreams in which understanding and reason act are said to let the soul examine truths and their connections. Morning dreams are named as a favourable time, when the soul is not led astray by the vapors of the stomach.

q.t: Not all dreams arise from the blood, from consumed food, from temperament, or from external impressions during sleep; in not all is merely the imagination alone active; one also has those to which the soul itself gives existence through its inner power.

There are dreams where the soul, entirely withdrawn from the world and entirely independent of the body, acts not as a soul [meaning the inhabitant of an organic body] but as a spirit, for whom time, space, past, future, and language are nothing.

Maine de Biran, Oeuvres philosophiques (.a: Maine de Biran says that in complete sleep the exercise of the will and the feeling of the moi are suspended, while animal sensibility and motility continue. He holds that every sleep is filled with dreams and that memory of a dream means the sleep was not perfect. He adds that each faculty carries its own testimony, and that a subject, the moi, is needed to collect it.

q.t: Indeed, it can be said, and this objection has already been made to me by a profound metaphysician who knew the theory I am developing today: without the action of the will, there is no effort of attention; without some effort of attention, there is no memory; now, if, in sleep, the action of the will is suspended, how does any memory of certain dreams remain?

Each of our faculties carries with it its own authority or the evident proof of its testimony. The senses of perception testify to the presence of their object. Memory testifies to the presence and previous existence of the object it recalls.

In complete sleep, and when all exercise of free activity is suspended, the feeling of the moi self is, by that very fact, also suspended. Animal sensibility and motility can still be brought into play by different organic causes, without the person being present.

Hegel, Phänomenologie des Geistes (with.a: Hegel sets out stages of spirit as consciousness: consciousness in general, self-consciousness, and reason as their unity. Sensory consciousness is the immediate certainty of an object. Premonitions, dreams, somnambulism and animal magnetism belong to a sphere where spirit fluctuates between nature-spirit and rational reality, and the soul there sees only its own particular inwardness.

q.t: Consciousness is, 1) first of all, immediate; its relationship to the object is therefore a simple, unmediated certainty of that object. The object itself is defined as a "being," but one reflected into itself, and further defined as an immediate individual — sensory consciousness.

Spirit is therefore consciousness in general, which encompasses sensible certainty, perceiving, and understanding in itself, insofar as it holds fast in the analysis of itself the moment that it is for itself objective, existing reality, and abstracts from the fact that this reality is its own being-for-itself.

However, because only the latter possesses true universality—namely, that of thinking—that expansion of "sympathetic life" which comes to representation is strictly limited to a particular circle. What this soul sees and foresees is only its own particular inwardness, not that of the universal essence.

Jung-Stilling, Theorie der Geisterkunde|.a: Jung-Stilling says the human soul is present throughout its body and perceives with self-consciousness through the organs, and that it reflects and chooses with freedom of the will. Natural sleep is a release of the soul from the nerves of the five senses, during which the soul keeps acting, and a dream is remembered when it impresses the inner sensory instruments. After death the soul remembers its earthly life completely, no longer perceives the sensory world as present, and perceives the spirit-world.

q.t: The human soul is present everywhere within its body. It perceives everywhere with self-consciousness, as permitted by the organs of the body. It sees with the eyes; it hears with the ears; it smells with the nose; it tastes with the tongue and the palate; and it feels with the entire skin, the whole surface of the body.

Natural sleep is also a type of this release; when the organic machine of the body—or more accurately, the nerves—grow weary to a certain degree, the human soul releases these instruments, insofar as they belong to the five senses: for through these alone does our consciousness in the sensory world [original: Sinnenwelt] arise—yet for itself, the soul acts constantly.

It remembers its earthly life perfectly from beginning to end. It thinks of those it left behind, and it can imagine the world of the senses quite clearly, but it no longer perceives that world as present at all. In contrast, it now perceives the spirit-world and its objects.

Deleuze, Histoire critique du magnétisme.a: Deleuze draws a line of demarcation between sleep and somnambulism, and between the sensations of somnambulists and dreams. Ideas had in sleep and remembered on waking are, he says, only dreams. He reports somnambulists who speak of their waking self and their somnambulist self as two different people, citing Mademoiselle Adelaïde le F., who had no idea of the self properly speaking.

q.t: All the ideas that one has had while one was sleeping, and that one remembers while awake, are only dreams. Thus, far from the observation of the phenomena of somnambulism leading to a belief in dreams, it tends to destroy this belief; it even explains why some doctors celebrated in antiquity asserted that, during sleep, the soul was more enlightened and that it foresaw the ills with which the body was threatened.

The somnambule magnetic sleepwalker described a state she knew perfectly; she saw and felt the effects of magnetism; she accounted for all the sensations she had experienced; she compared her state of somnambulism magnetic sleep to her waking state; she neither imagined nor conjectured, she observed; and as nothing distracted her attention, she reported everything with accuracy and clarity.

Hammer-Purgstall, Geschichte der Assassi.a: Hammer-Purgstall treats the intoxication of hashish pastilles as a substitute for heavenly joys, and derives the name Hashishin, 'herb-users', from their consumption. He ties the drug's appeal to the imagination of the Arab and the indolence of the Turk. Elsewhere the Sheikh is called the soul of the order, who steers the consciences of the initiates.

q.t: Even today, Constantinople and Cairo show what an incredible appeal opium derived from hyoscyamus henbane has on the sleepy indolence of the Turk and the fiery imagination of the Arab, and it explains the fury with which those youths sought the enjoyment of these intoxicating herbal pastilles ( hashish ), and into which they were transported by them, becoming capable of undertaking anything.

The recruiters, or the actual initiates, worked on the minds and directed the arms according to the commands of the Sheikh, who, as the soul of the organization at the center of power, calmly steered the consciences and the daggers from his mountain fortress toward the goals of his ambition.

Faria, De la cause du sommeil lucide|||M.a: Faria calls thought an effect of the soul that cannot belong to matter, and describes it as the memory of the past and a conjecture of the future. He defines imagination as reproducing ideas of objects as present, and memory as recognizing them as ones perceived formerly. He calls lucid sleep a state of dreaming whose intuition is mixed and presents objects under images.

k.g: a state combining direct intellectual perception with sensory content

q.t: Thought is, without dispute, an effect of the soul, and whatever the materialists may say, we shall victoriously prove that it can in no way belong to matter. It is therefore evident that if thought has no boundary in space that can circumscribe it, the human soul has none that can circumscribe it.

Memory, which in this definition seems to be confused with imagination, is essentially distinguished from it; because it is only a faculty of recognizing reproduced ideas as being the same ones the mind perceived formerly. Memory can therefore exist without the imagination; but the imagination never without memory.

It is therefore clear that the intuition of epopts is the same as the intuition of those who dream, and that consequently it can only present objects to them under appearances; that is to say, under images that depict and represent them.

Schopenhauer, Die Welt als Wille und Vor.a: Schopenhauer says intuition arises when the understanding applies the causal nexus to sensory sensation, with the imagination supplementing the impression. He finds dreaming close to madness because memory is not fully available while the other mental powers act. He calls clairvoyance a veridical dreaming (Wahrträumen) whose objects appear to the intellect intuitively, and says ordinary dreams lack its relation to the real world.

q.t: Rather, empirical reality, and thus experience, is already given in intuition itself: yet intuition can only come about by applying the knowledge of the causal nexus (which is the sole function of the understanding) to sensory sensation.
It thus seems indeed that in dreams, while all mental powers are active, memory alone is not fully available.
The objects of this dreaming therefore present themselves to the intellect intuitively and in the flesh, just like our ordinary dreams, which is why somnambulists speak of "seeing" them.

De Quincey, Confessions of an English Op.a: De Quincey holds that forgetting is impossible for the mind, since a veil may fall between present consciousness and the inscriptions on the mind, and the inscription remains forever. He calls the dreaming faculty the tube through which man communicates with the shadowy, and says opium strengthens it. He also describes verses read once reviving in memory when he lies awake.

q.t: Of this, at least, I feel assured, that there is no such thing as forgetting possible to the mind; a thousand accidents may and will interpose a veil between our present consciousness and the secret inscriptions on the mind; accidents of the same sort will also rend away this veil.

The machinery for dreaming planted in the human brain was not planted for nothing. That faculty, in alliance with the mystery of darkness, is the one great tube through which man communicates with the shadowy.
Still it is a fact, that this pertinacious life of memory for things that simply touch the ear without touching the consciousness, does in fact beset me.

Herbart, Psychologie als Wissenschaft|||.a: Herbart argues that we cannot feel our feeling or think our thinking directly, and that the perception of the Ich requires a foreign point of attachment. He calls a pure Ich impossible and criticizes treating the faculties of the soul as predicates of the I. He says older and newer masses of ideas let a deeper-lying I judge inclinations.

q.t: If only it were true that we could so directly, immediately, feel our feeling, or will our willing, or think our thinking! Then we would also be able to see our seeing, and in the same way listen to our hearing, taste our taste, and smell our smell.

The latter case occurs where one makes the so-called faculties of the soul predicates of the "I"; in common speech: "We have reason, we have understanding, we have a will, we have sensibility," and so forth.

In these very strongly mythological opinions, there is this much truth: that in the course of years, a difference of older and newer masses of ideas (41.) is accustomed to develop, by virtue of which the inclinations and desires excited at any given time encounter, as it were, a deeper-lying I within, to which they serve as a spectacle, so that they are presented and judged by it.

Kerner, Die Seherin von Prevorst|||Moder.a: Kerner records Friederike Hauffe's statements, made while sleep-waking, that soul (Seele) and spirit (Geist) are distinct. In deeper states the spirit has the upper hand and thinks from the pit of the stomach, while the large brain is felt very little. She describes the spirit separating from the soul and nerve-spirit, the two speaking like different persons. Her sister reports seeing a spirit's shadow with her inner self, and Kerner relates apparitions to dreams, sleep and death.

q.t: In the fully waking state, one feels the spirit only very little, just a bit. But for a person as they are in this world, the soul must rule the most.

In this state, spirit and soul speak with each other like two different persons. However, the spirit knows nothing at all of the rest of the world; it knows only of itself, and everything else is of no concern to it.
I did not see it, and yet I did see it. It felt to me as if there were thoughts within this shadow that then communicated themselves to me and evoked a feeling of compassion within me.

Kalevala|||Slavic & Finnic.a: In the passage, a speaker preparing to ski to the forest spirits' home says his mind moves and his thoughts incline toward the hunting grounds of other men and the remote forests of the heroes.

k.g: a figure of sleep and dreams

q.t: From there the wilderness glows, From there the blue thing shines; To there my mind moves, 145. My thoughts incline, To the hunting grounds of other men, To the remote forests of the heroes.

Colquhoun, Isis Revelata; Townshend, Fac.a: The author uses consciousness as a general expression for every act and state of the mind, and treats sensation, perception, attention and reflection as forms of it. In mesmeric sleep the sleeper wakes with no recollection yet may have been thinking, observing and speaking. The sleeper remembers earlier sleeps in the next one, has a double or divided consciousness, and may lose the sense of identity.

q.t: A sensation of which the mind is not conscious is no sensation at all. We cannot feel without perceiving, nor can we perceive without, in some degree, paying attention to what we perceive.
It is only an "unconscious" state in relation to his ordinary waking condition; the sleeper may have been actively engaged in thinking, observing, and speaking throughout the entire period of sleep.
However, when he is next put to sleep, he perfectly remembers everything that occurred, not only in the last sleep but in all previous sleeps.

Ennemoser, Geschichte der Magie|||Modern.a: Ennemoser calls the human soul an indivisible unity of spiritual powers: sense, understanding, self-conscious mind and will. Quoting Paracelsus, he has imagination arise from the heart as a material seed, strengthened by faith. Van Helmont, after taking aconite, felt and thought in the stomach region, and concluded the soul is not fettered to one organ, with memory in the head and feeling in the stomach.

q.t: The human soul is an indivisible unity of spiritual powers. The sense, which in subjective feeling and representation unfolds itself within, comprehends the external objective world, which the understanding and the mind in self-consciousness again shape into a unity; from which, on the other hand, the subjective impulse and conception in the will come forth again objective in revelation.

Every imagination of man comes from the heart, for this is the sun of the microcosm; and out of the microcosm proceeds the imagination into the great world. Thus the imagination of man is a seed, which is material. Determined imagination is a beginning of all magical operations.

From this extraordinary phenomenon, Van Helmont concludes that the soul is not necessarily fettered to one organ or another of the body, and that it can, like a permeating light, diffuse itself through all, without any medium being necessary.

Crowe, The Night-Side of Nature|||Modern.a: Crowe attributes ordinary dreams to light or interrupted sleep, in which some parts of the brain rest less than others, and compares dreaming to delirium. He suggests the spirit does not sleep, so deep sleep may bring clairvoyant perception. He notes that memories do not carry between sleeping and waking, and he separates mind, soul (anima) and spirit.

q.t: Everyone will recall how often, at the moment of waking, we are not only aware that we have been dreaming but also conscious of the subject of the dream—yet we try in vain to grasp it. It eludes us and is gone forever the moment we have entered a state of complete wakefulness.

If dreaming were like thinking, the explanations might be quite satisfactory; but the truth is that dreaming is not thinking in the way we think while awake. Instead, it is more like the thoughts of someone in a delirium, a state of intense mania, or a chronic condition that causes sensory illusions [original: "sensuous illusions"].

By a temporary pressure on the brain, the mind is certainly not destroyed [original: annihilated], but its expression through the brain is suspended. The source of these expressions is the soul, or anima [Latin: life-force or soul], which contains the life that prepares the "temple" of the body for its divine inhabitant, the spirit.

Reichenbach, Der sensitive Mensch / Phys.a: Reichenbach holds that somnambulism develops with repetition: ideas strengthen, concepts and judgments form, and the somnambule becomes a sensible person in the state of sleep. In somnambule sleep memory is sharpened and recovers forgotten things and languages, though most of it is lost on waking. He describes somnambule sleep as deeper than ordinary sleep, and discusses sensitive people who walk while asleep, avoid obstacles, and wake on arrival.

q.t: But if the state recurs often, the same ideas repeat themselves, strengthen through the coalescing of the similar, gain space in the soul, and reach height in consciousness; they then become clearer and clearer, concepts are abstracted, judgments are made, conclusions are drawn, and the somnambule is no longer a dreamer, but a sensible person in the state of sleep.
The capacity for memory is then sharpened and increased, so much so that one remembers things that occurred and entire languages, etc., that one had completely forgotten in waking life.

They act with a certain consciousness, pursue their goal systematically, recognize obstacles on the way; they avoid them with an awareness of the difficulty and come to themselves as soon as the travel destination and travel purpose are reached. This state is therefore neither ordinary sleep nor is it somnambulism.

Fechner, Zend-Avesta (with Nanna, Über d.a: Fechner holds that a soul must be able to feel and desire, and that a sleeping soul keeps the conditions for waking sensation and desire. A plant's soul may fall asleep as ours does but cannot sleep always. He calls a thing's inner self-appearance (Selbsterscheinung) its soul, and the outer appearance it stirs in us its body. Consciousness has a threshold (Schwelle des Bewußtseins), and sleep can sink below it, so that waking needs more stimulation.

q.t: Sensation and desire that sleep are simply not sensation and desire; and if we can still call our own soul a "soul" while we sleep, because it still carries within it the conditions for re-awakening sensation and desire, then something could never be called a soul where such an awakening was never to come.

We then define this "internal" self-appearance of the thing as its soul, contrasting it with the "external" self-appearance it stimulates in us—the latter being what we use to characterize its physical body.

Now, however, experience shows that consciousness can also sink below its threshold. That is to say, sleep and unconsciousness can deepen more and more, such that re-awakening becomes increasingly difficult; it requires more and more positive stimulation (in the sense of the former activity of consciousness) just to reach the threshold of consciousness again.

N.C. Paul, A Treatise on the Yoga Philos.a: Paul defines deep sleep (sushupti) as a temporary cessation of thought, sensation and mental emotion, and says the soul is then freed from earthly bonds. He gives about 22 heartbeats and 6 breaths per minute in deep sleep. He defines Yoga as the art of suspending circulation and respiration, and lists Samádhi as the eighth stage of Rája Yoga.

q.t: A deep and perfect sleep ( sushupti ) has been aptly defined as a temporary cessation of all the functions of animal life—namely, of thought, sensation, mental emotion, and all their combinations and modifications. In sushupti, the soul is freed from earthly bonds, and man is free from all sins.

Grey, Polynesian Mythology (with White,.a: In the Tai-nui narratives collected by White, dreams act as omens: a priest of a war party dreams of his side laid open, and Horo-whenua's dreams guide who is sent for Paoa. Ponga's attendant tells him to keep his spirit alive and to smother sorrow with a determined will. In Grey's account the sorcerer Hakawau enters an enchanted sleep to learn the outcome of his journey.

q.t: Horo-whenua slept, and dreamt that his hand was being pulled by a man, and was not pulled away by his combatant. He awoke and told the dream to his companions, but said, "I will sleep again, and when I awake let one man go to fetch Paoa."
Let your spirit live in you; food is food—eat it. Talk and laugh, and let the sorrow you feel be smothered by the power of your determined will; let it be kept hidden from the knowledge of others.

and in his slumber he saw that his genius spirit-guardian would triumph in the encounter, for it was so lofty and mighty, that in his dream its head reached the heavens, whilst its feet remained upon earth.

Kalevipoeg|||Slavic & Finnic.a: The epic describes sleep in which the soul's activity stays free while the dream offers its images as truth to the soul's clouded eye. It says that at the beginning of slumber, dream sensations resist outside impressions, and that waking is easier from deepest sleep than from early sleep. Kalevipoeg dreams of the maiden of the shadow-realm while real water wets him.

q.t: That, everyone can explain to themselves And confirm as true, Who has experienced it themselves: That at the beginning of slumber, The sensations of the dream Resist external impression.
But the slumber did not capture The activity of the soul, Left it to rule unhindered;

Kardec, Le livre des esprits|||Modern Eu.a: Kardec's spirits answer that the Spirit is never inactive in sleep. Its bonds to the body loosen, it enters more direct relation with other Spirits, and dreams show its freedom. In sleep it has memory of the past and sometimes foresight. The text distinguishes a vital soul for material life, an intellectual soul for intelligence, and a spirit soul for individuality after death. A spirit answers that thought is an attribute, and where thought is, the soul is.

k.g: the semi-material envelope of the soul
a faculty of perceiving things beyond the reach of the senses
a spirit currently inhabiting a human body

q.t: "No, the Spirit is never inactive. During sleep, the bonds that unite it to the body are loosened, and as the body does not need it, it traverses space and enters into more direct relation with other Spirits."

We could therefore say, and this would perhaps be best: the vital soul for the principle of material life; the intellectual soul for the principle of intelligence; and the spirit soul for the principle of our individuality after death.
« When thought is in a certain place, the soul is there too, since it is the soul that thinks. Thought is an attribute. »

Ludlow, The Hasheesh Eater|||Modern Euro.a: Ludlow describes a mind under hasheesh that remains conscious and perceives outer things without hallucination, yet sees each spoken word as a visible symbol. Every sensation takes a distinct inner type, appearing as form and as music. He proposes that the soul first accepts an impression as a thing of the sense, then intuits that it will be perceived again, which would explain a feeling of having lived the moment before. He describes a rising stair of Sense, Understanding and Intuition.

q.t: I found that his case was exactly analogous to those of B. and myself; for, like us, he recognized every possible sensation in distinct inner types. Our words made a visible, symbolic procession before his eyes, and every perception, regardless of the sense through which it entered, became tangible to him as form and audible as music.

At the moment of the soul's reception of a new impression, she first accepts it as a thing entirely of the sense; she tells us how large it is, and of what quality. To this definition of its boundaries and likeness succeeds, at times of high activity, an intuition of the fact that the sensation shall be perceived again in the future unveiling that is to throw open all the past.

Up this gradual stairway of Sense, Understanding, and Intuition, we mount to that height from which we are able to behold, with some degree of calmness, the infinite fields of intuitive Beauty and Truth, when the screen of the bodily is removed, and the scope of vision belonging to our highest faculty is realized to be immeasurably beyond all that our most rapturous visions ever conceived it.

Baudelaire, Les paradis artificiels|||Mo.a: Baudelaire separates natural dreaming, which draws on the sleeper's own character, life and memory, from a second kind he calls hieroglyphic, which is absurd and unconnected to the sleeper. Hashish intoxication stays within natural dreaming. He says hashish hallucination is progressive, almost voluntary, and ripened by imagination, with a pretext in some real sound or form. The intoxicated person lends the tree passions and melancholy, then feels identical with it.

q.t: That is natural dreaming; it is the man himself. But the other species of dream! The absurd, unforeseen dream, without relation or connection to the character, life, and passions of the sleeper!
In the second case, the hallucination is progressive, almost voluntary, and it only becomes complete and ripens through the action of the imagination. Finally, it has a pretext.
You first lend the tree your passions, your desire, or your melancholy. Its moans and its oscillations become your own, and soon you are the tree.

Cooke, The Seven Sisters of Sleep|||Mode.a: Cooke quotes a physician on opium: the senses report faithfully, the imagination exaggerates, multiplies and colors what they deliver, the reason yields to visions, and memory is generally asleep. On sleep, Cooke writes that the brain's expenditure of power in waking is balanced by repose, and that without sleep the overtaxed brain lapses into melancholy and madness. For hashish, the text says memory incorporates delusions with what it recalls, and the eye and ear delude the reason.

q.t: The senses convey no false impressions to the brain; all that is seen, heard, or felt, is faithfully delineated, but the imagination clothes each object in its own fanciful garb. It exaggerates, it multiplies, it colors, it gives fantastic shapes; there is a new condition arising out of ordinary perception, and the reason, abandoning itself to the imagination, does not resist the delight of indulging in visions.

During the hours of wakefulness, the active brain exerts its powers without cessation or rest, and during sleep, the expenditure of power is balanced again by repose. The physical energies are exhausted by labor, as are those of the mind by wakefulness; and if sleep does not come to reinvigorate the mental powers, the overtaxed brain gives way and lapses into melancholy and madness.

Memory not only recurs with ease to the past but incorporates delusions with it; for with whatever accuracy the facts may be remembered, they are painted with glowing colors and made sources of pleasure. The senses become instruments of deception; the eye and the ear are not only alive to every impression, but they delude the reason and disturb the brain with the fantasies to which they become subject.

Fechner, Elemente der Psychophysik|||Mod.a: Fechner distinguishes semi-conscious sensations from fully conscious ones. Semi-conscious sensations cannot be remembered, and fully conscious ones can. The threshold of full consciousness lies where the possibility of memory awakens, because distinguishing sensations requires holding them together in memory. For sleep, he describes the dreamer as a poet lost in an inner world to whom appearance becomes truth. When the main psychophysical wave sinks below the threshold, one inner point may rise toward a new awakening, which he links to somnambulism.

q.t: There is a characteristic difference between these two degrees of consciousness. One cannot remember semi-conscious sensations, whereas one can remember fully conscious ones.
The dreamer is a poet who lets the reins of his imagination go completely, and is entirely immersed and lost in an inner world, so that the appearance becomes truth to him.

Helmholtz, Die Lehre von den Tonempfindu.a: Helmholtz distinguishes two grades of becoming conscious of a sensation. In the lower grade, a sensation shapes the conceptions formed of external things and processes. He argues that the mind perceives the physical effect of pitch ratios on the auditory nerves, and that people often judge by experience without having the grounds clearly present to mind. He also says melodic motion expresses states of mental sensitiveness, as the words out of tune and Stimmung suggest.

q.t: We then become aware that two different kinds or grades must be distinguished in our becoming conscious of a sensation. The lower grade of this consciousness, is that where the influence of the sensation in question makes itself felt only in the conceptions we form of external things and processes, and assists in determining them.

According to the latter, the human mind perceives commensurable ratios of pitch numbers as such; according to our method, it perceives only the physical effect of these ratios, namely the continuous or intermittent sensation of the auditory nerves.
