Our thoughts may move fast or slowly, may wander about restlessly and aimlessly in anxious excitement, or may keep a determinate aim distinctly and energetically in view; they may lounge about without care or effort in pleasant fancies, or, driven back by some sad memories, may return slowly and heavily from the spot with short weak steps.

Brinton, Myths of the New World / Religi.a: Brinton cites language as evidence that Native American peoples tied the soul to breath and to the shadow. The Choctaw named an outside shadow, shilombish, and an inside shadow, shilup, and the New England tribes called the soul chemung. He reports beliefs in several souls. One soul gives bodily life and stays with the corpse, while a finer soul can leave the body in sleep or trance. The Sioux and Dakota are said to hold three or four souls with separate destinies.

q.t: The Choctaw believed that every man has an "outside shadow," shilombish, and an "inside shadow," shilup, both of which survive after his death. The New England tribes called the soul chemung, meaning the shadow.
The other soul is made of a more refined, ethereal texture. During life, it can leave the body during sleep or a trance to wander the world.

Callaway, The Religious System of the Am.a: Callaway records that, in Zulu thought, dreams, subjective apparitions and similar psychical phenomena are bound up with the Amatongo, the ancestral spirits, who make revelations by dreams. A dreamer who is stabbed in sleep by an apparent friend, or chased by a beast, takes the Itongo to have shown a danger and stays on guard. A Zulu informant also reports dreams of death followed by recovery. People say summer dreams are true and winter brings confused, unintelligible ones.

q.t: DREAMS, subjective apparitions, and similar psychical phenomena are in the native mind so intimately wrapped up with the Amatongo ancestral spirits, that this is the proper place for considering their views on such matters, without which their views on the Amatongo would be incomplete.

People say, summer dreams are true; but they do not say they are always true; but they say that summer dreams do not usually miss the mark. But they say the winter is bad, and produces confused imaginations, that is, very many unintelligible dreams.

New Thought and mind-cure (Evans, Wood,.a: These writers describe the mind as two faculties, the Will and the Understanding, also called love and intellect, which together contain the whole interior life. Mind is arranged in degrees, and consciousness is the observation that inner degrees take of the plane outside them. A Subjective Mind acts automatically on the body and accepts suggested conditions. Suggestion is named as the link between mind and body and the explanation offered for mental healing.

q.t: Man is endowed with two primary faculties, or powers of reception, called the Will and the Understanding, or the love and the intellect. These together constitute what we call the mind.
What we call consciousness is but the observation the inward degrees of mind take of what transpires in the plane external to them.

Suggestion is the connecting link between the mind and the body, and an understanding of its laws and principles enables one to see the driving cause of the strange phenomena of Faith Cures, under whatever name they may pass, and under whatever guise they may present themselves.

Von Hartmann, Philosophie des Unbewusste.a: Von Hartmann says attention has degrees because it consists of nerve vibrations, while consciousness is an immaterial reaction that either occurs or does not. Self-consciousness is consciousness of a specific content, the self, so its degree rises and falls, and it can nearly vanish during absorption in art or science. He holds that unity of consciousness between two moments requires the memory of the earlier moment to be present or possible, and cites Jessen's case of a girl who lost memory after seizures.

q.t: Consciousness, however, can have no degrees because it is an immaterial reaction that either occurs or does not; but when it does occur, it always happens in the same way.

Consciousness, by contrast, leaves its content entirely indefinite; it only requires a content in general if it is to manifest in reality. According to its concept, however, it is mere form, and its concept cannot take on gradual differences simply because the content—to which it is completely indifferent—happens to vary.

We can only recognize a unity of consciousness between a past and present moment where the memory of that past moment is present in the present, or where at least the possibility of this memory remains unhindered and open.

Tylor, Primitive Culture|||Modern Europe.a: Tylor reports that in tribal psychology a dream is the sleeper's soul traveling, or a visit from other souls. The North American Indians allowed that the rational soul may go out while the sensitive soul stays in the body. Trance and fainting are described as the soul's absence, and spirits are said to be met directly in dreams and visions, including nightmare demons and the incubi and succubi.

q.t: The North American Indians allowed themselves the alternative of supposing a dream to be a visit from the soul of the person or object dreamt of, or a sight seen by the rational soul, gone out for an excursion while the sensitive soul remains in the body.

Another account from among the same people explains the condition of men lying in a lethargy or trance: their souls have traveled forth to the banks of the River of Death, but have been driven back and return to re-animate their bodies.
As with souls, so it is with other spirits: a person's most distinct and direct interaction with them happens when they become actually present to the senses in dreams and visions.

Brentano, Psychologie vom empirischen St.a: Brentano lists several uses of the word consciousness: memory of one's acts, immediate knowledge of current psychic acts, return from sleep or fainting, and every representing. He chooses to use it as synonymous with psychic phenomenon or psychic act. He says psychic phenomena are those for which perception in the proper sense is possible, and cognition, joy and desire truly exist while color, tone and warmth exist only phenomenally and intentionally.

k.g: the ontological status of an object existing within a mental act

q.t: Sometimes it is used to designate every type of immediate knowledge of one's own psychic acts, in particular also a perception that accompanies current psychic acts.

We said that psychic phenomena are those for which alone a perception in the proper sense is possible. We can just as well say they are those phenomena to which, besides intentional existence, a real existence also pertains. Cognition, joy, desire truly exist; color, tone, warmth only phenomenally and intentionally.

Blavatsky, Isis Unveiled|||Theosophical.a: Blavatsky names the astral principle, or mind, jav-atma, the sentient soul. She calls it the ego, the intellectual life-principle and conscious entity of man, bound to the physical brain and hampered by it. The clarity of its visions depends on its relation to its higher Principle. Citing the Sohar, she describes souls as dual, with soul feminine and spirit masculine, and says man is a trinity while in the body.

q.t: The astral principle, or mind, called by the Hindu Yogin [a practitioner of yoga] jav-atma, is the sentient soul. It is inseparable from our physical brain, which it holds in subjection, and is in its turn equally hampered by it. This is the ego, the intellectual life-principle of man, his conscious entity.
Moreover, the Sohar teaches that the soul cannot reach the abode of bliss, unless she has received the "holy kiss," or the reunion of the soul with the substance from which she emanated—spirit.

Shortland, Maori Religion and Mythology|.a: Shortland records that the Maori take dreams and sudden movements of the body in sleep, called takiri, as omens or warnings from the Atua. The moe-papa dreams are unlucky death warnings, resembling what is termed night-mare. He also gives an account of the spirit leaving the body and traveling north to the Reinga, where eating the food offered prevents return to life, and he opens with an innate belief in the immortality of the soul.

q.t: The Maori has also a firm belief in omens derived from dreams, and from any sudden movements of the body or limbs during sleep, all which signs are believed to be warnings from the Atua.
When the spirit leaves the body it goes on its way northward, till it arrives at two hills. The first of these hills is a place on which to lament with wailings and cuttings.

THE religious feeling may be traced to the natural veneration of the child for the parent, joined to an innate belief in the immortality of the soul. What we know of the primitive religion of Aryans and Polynesians points to this source.

Sinnett, Esoteric Buddhism (with The Occ.a: The Mahatma Letters discuss what remains of memory, self-consciousness and perception after death, and assign these to the higher principles (Manas and Buddhi) and to the shell. They describe Deva Chan as a state in which the Ego dreams amid its earthly affections. Sinnett's Esoteric Buddhism describes a spiritual perceptiveness, a clairvoyant faculty, through which adepts impart knowledge to a pupil without words.

q.t: As I said in your note, it is no better than a reflected or borrowed light. "Memory" is one thing, and "perceptive faculties" quite another. A madman may remember very clearly some portion of his past life; yet he is unable to perceive anything in its true light, for the higher portion of his Manas and his Buddhi (the higher spiritual principles) are paralyzed in him, having left him.
Since the conscious perception of one's personality on earth is but an evanescent dream, that sense will be equally that of a dream in the Deva-Chan—only a hundred-fold intensified.

The whole scheme of evolution, which the foregoing chapters have portrayed, infiltrates into the regular chela's mind by reason of the fact that he is made to see the process taking place by clairvoyant vision.

Du Prel, Die Philosophie der Mystik|||Mo.a: Du Prel argues that dream-life shows the concept of the soul extends beyond consciousness, and that physiologists wrongly treat the two as identical. He names memory as the thread that holds personal self-consciousness together, and says a missing bridge of memory between deep sleep and waking hides the orderly dream. As sleep deepens, the confusion of the dream is reduced, which he traces in sleepwalking and somnambulism.

q.t: It is precisely this preliminary question that is answered in the negative by the dream, which shows that the concept of the soul extends beyond that of consciousness, much like the gravitational pull of a celestial body extends beyond its sphere of light.

Without this, the identity of the person within their self-consciousness would be abolished; sensations would be experienced only as "atomistically" isolated events, and there would be no overview of a series of such events. If no "bridge of memory" existed from one sensation to the next, self-consciousness would have to begin anew with every new sensation and would be displaced again by every following one.

When light sleep deepens, the confusion of the dream must be reduced. The cerebral nervous system—senses and brain—becomes increasingly insensitive, and thus those disturbing components that flowed to us from the external world via the senses, or remained as residues of the waking consciousness, vanish more and more from the dream.

Reference studies of Islam (Goldziher, H.a: The Kitābu 't-Ta'rīfāt, as quoted, lists three kinds of spirit. The human spirit (ar-Rūḥu 'l-Insānī) is the human mind, distinguishes man from animals, and is sometimes united to the body and sometimes separated from it, as in sleep or death. The Akhlāq-i-Jalālī assigns the reasonable mind a perceiving power and an impelling power, each with two divisions, and a later passage calls Intelligence a light in the heart.

k.t: mâ ḥu̠fiẓa marra, wamâ kutiba ḳarra
k.g: What is preserved in memory is fleeting, what is written down is lasting

q.t: (1) Ar-Rūhu 'l-Insānī (الروح الانسانی), the "human spirit," by which we understand the human mind. This distinguishes man from animals and is given to him by God’s decree from heaven. We know nothing of its true essence.
The reasonable mind has two powers: (1) the power of perceiving, and (2) the power of impelling; and each of these powers has two divisions.
When the heart of man has been revivified and illumined by the Primal Spirit, he has arrived at Intelligence; for Intelligence is a light in the heart, distinguishing between truth and vanity.

Bernheim, De la suggestion et de ses app.a: Bernheim holds that sleep, artificial or spontaneous, leaves the intellectual faculties intact and is a different cerebral state from waking, one he says psychologists have yet to study. Somnambulists show full consciousness of their being, answer questions, and know they are sleeping. Memory of the sleeping state returns on waking if the subject is told he will remember. Bernheim describes ideas as conscious in sleep and latent in waking.

q.t: Sleep, whether it be artificial or spontaneous, is not, I repeat, the abolition of intellectual faculties; it is a different cerebral state than that of being awake—a state difficult to define, the study of which remains to be done by psychologists.

Our ideas are conscious while we sleep; they have become latent when we are awake; we do not remember that we thought all night about not missing the hour, and we believe that the waking was spontaneous or unconscious.
Moreover, during their sleep, they demonstrate a perfect consciousness of their being; they answer the questions addressed to them; they know that they are sleeping.

Gurney, Myers & Podmore, Phantasms of th.a: Gurney, Myers and Podmore treat perception as a form of activity and describe the telepathic percipient as using a capacity outside voluntary control and outside the normal stream of consciousness. They suppose normal consciousness is a slice of the whole being. In the Newnham experiments they see an unconscious intelligence, a second self, and call the hypnotic trance an eclipse of normal consciousness repeatable at will.

k.g: a vision caused by mental communication

q.t: This power, plainly, is not of what we term a voluntary kind; it is not guided by B’s normal or primary stream of consciousness. But (as I have tried elsewhere to show) there is reason to suppose that our normal consciousness represents no more than a slice of our whole being.

These experiments are further interesting as suggesting, in the character of many of the replies, an unconscious intelligence—a second self quite other than Mrs. Newnham’s conscious self. “Unconscious intelligence” is no doubt a somewhat ambiguous phrase, and it is necessary to know in every case exactly what is meant by it.
The hypnotic trance is an eclipse of normal consciousness that can be repeated at will.

Binet & Féré, Le magnétisme animal|||Mod.a: Binet and Féré describe hypnotic memory as impaired only in recall, since a new sleep restores the memory the subject seemed to lose. They say the somnambulist keeps perfect memory, active intelligence, and a stimulated imagination, and is not an unconscious automaton. They hold that suggestion works by making one idea master the mind, since every idea is a mental image recalling a previous sensation.

q.t: This impairment is, however, superficial rather than deep; it only affects one portion of the memory—the ability to recall. The ability to retain information remains almost intact, since entering a new sleep state gives the subject back the complete memory they appeared to have lost in their waking state.

On the contrary, their memory is perfect, their intelligence is active, and their imagination is highly stimulated. Instances have been given of subjects who could, during somnambulism, perform intellectual feats that they were incapable of in their waking state.

Every kind of suggestion works by making one single idea take control of the subject’s mind. The suggestion of sleep falls into this category; hypnosis is achieved by focusing the mind on the idea of sleep.

Avenarius, Kritik der reinen Erfahrung||.a: Avenarius writes of the soul as striving to perform each required task with the smallest amount of force, so that habitual reactions and apperceptions are preferred. The soul distributes consciousness by intensity, thinking more ideas at lower consciousness-intensity within a limited production of consciousness. He says experience is wider than perception, since a single perception gives its object only under the perceiver's limits and may need supplementing and correcting.

k.g: mental processes of assimilating new experiences into existing ideas

k.t: principle of the least measure of force
k.g: the notion that human effort/thought naturally seeks the most economical path

q.t: However, the reason for the inclination to judge things, both new and old, in the way one is accustomed to judging, and thus the cause of frequent habitual reactions, lies in our soul's striving to execute a required performance with the smallest amount of force. Habitual reactions are the easiest, hence the soul's preference for them.

Since the production of consciousness is not unlimited, but restricted to a certain measure, the soul has only one means to increase the number of ideas themselves indefinitely, namely, to assign an ever lower intensity to the ideas: it thinks more ideas with the same measure of consciousness if it thinks them with lower consciousness-intensity.

Yet the concept of experience is broader than that of perception. The latter always offers only a single perceived object; its statement, conceived as a judgment, gives the object only as it presents itself to the perceiver under the limitations of the capacity for perception and of the respective external and internal standpoint.

Blavatsky, The Secret Doctrine (the seve.a: Blavatsky says consciousness implies limitation and needs an object and a knower, while Absolute Consciousness holds cognizer, thing cognized and cognition as one. She counts seven senses and seven states of consciousness in man. The mind on the sensuous plane serves the senses, and the spiritual mind, the upper aspect of impersonal Manas, takes no cognizance of them. She adds that dreaming and deep sleep must still hold consciousness.

k.g: the mysterious power of thought which produces objective results

q.t: Consciousness implies limitations and qualifications; it requires something to be conscious of, and someone to be conscious of it. But Absolute Consciousness contains the cognizer, the thing cognized, and the cognition—all three in itself, and all three one.
This, of course, regards only the mind on the sensuous plane. The spiritual mind (the upper portion or aspect of the impersonal Manas) takes no cognizance of the senses in the physical man.

The ordinary man has no experience of any state of consciousness other than that to which the physical senses link him. Men dream; they sleep the profound sleep which is too deep for dreams to impress the physical brain; and in these states, there must still be consciousness.

Blavatsky, The Key to Theosophy (with Th.a: Blavatsky's catechism distinguishes the Genesis "living Soul" or Nephesh, the vital animal soul, from the thinking Soul or mind and from the immortal Spirit. It says dream-life uses a different set of senses on another plane, with years of events passing through the mind in one instant. It states there are seven states of consciousness, and that memory is a fallible register while thoughts are imperishable.

q.t: The “Soul” mentioned in chapter 2 of Genesis (verse 7) is, as stated there, the “living Soul” or Nephesh (the vital, animal soul) with which God (we say “nature” and unchangeable law) endows man just like every animal. It is not at all the thinking Soul or mind; least of all is it the immortal Spirit.

We have a different set of senses in dream-life, do we not? We feel, talk, hear, see, taste and function in general on a different plane; the change of our state of consciousness is evidenced by the fact that a series of acts and events spanning years, as we think, pass ideally through our mind in one instant.

Furthermore, remember that memory is one thing and mind or thought is another; one is a recording machine, a register which very easily gets out of order; the other (thoughts) are eternal and imperishable.

Janet, L'automatisme psychologique|||Mod.a: Janet says the idea of the self (le moi) does not attach equally to all sensations, and we often attribute a sensation to the outside world. He describes the idea of the self as a judgment on the unity of gathered psychological phenomena, distinct from an association of ideas. He relates memory to sensitivity, so that memories acquired in one state of sensitivity are recalled only when that sensitivity is present.

k.g: a nervous condition characterized by muscular rigidity and lack of response to external stimuli

q.t: Most, on the contrary, awaken the idea of the self so little that we do not hesitate to attribute them to the outside world; instead of saying that it is we who experience the sensation of the color green, we say that it is the tree that possesses it.

When a certain number of psychological phenomena are gathered together, a very important new fact usually occurs in the mind: their unity, noticed and understood, gives rise to a particular judgment that we call the idea of the self [original: "le moi"].
For the image to be produced, and consequently for memory to take place, it is therefore absolutely necessary that the faculty of feeling that sensation still exists, at least in part.

A. B. Ellis, The Tshi-, Ewe- and Yoruba-.a: Ellis describes the kra as a guardian spirit that enters a man at birth and quits at death, and says the man himself, in shadowy form, goes on to another world. At death the kra becomes a sisa, which can be born again as a kra in a new body. Ellis links the kra to dreams as its nocturnal adventures, notes that its absence lets a sisa enter, and gives the Gã kla and the three Yoruba inmates as variants.

q.t: This word kra, though generally interpreted as “soul,” does not at all correspond to the European idea of a soul; for it is the man himself, in a shadowy or ghostly form, that continues his existence after death in another world, and not the kra. The latter is rather a guardian spirit, who lives in a man, and whose connection with him terminates at his death.

Because the quitting of a man by his tenanting kra is harmful to the man—since it affords an opportunity for a sisa [a ghost or wandering spirit] to enter, and he also feels the effects of the kra's nocturnal adventures—a quiet night's rest is highly valued.

In the first volume of this series, we found that the Tshi-speaking peoples believe that every man has a spirit dwelling in him termed a kra, which enters him at birth and quits him at death. This spirit is entirely distinct from the soul, which, at the death of the body, proceeds to the Land of the Dead and there continues the life formerly led by the man in the world.

Frazer, The Golden Bough (the soul as ma.a: Frazer says the savage conceives life as a concrete material thing that can be kept in a box or jar and can be bruised or smashed. It may be stored in a safe place, and the man stays immortal while it is unharmed. He also reports plural souls: the Caribs place souls in the head, heart and pulse points, the Hidatsa count four, and the Batta count three or seven, one of them always outside the body.

q.t: Unable to conceive of life abstractly as a “permanent possibility of sensation” or a “continuous adjustment of internal arrangements to external relations,” the savage thinks of it as a concrete material thing of a definite bulk, capable of being seen and handled, kept in a box or jar, and liable to be bruised, fractured, or smashed in pieces.

The divisibility of life, or, to put it otherwise, the plurality of souls, is an idea suggested by many familiar facts and has commended itself to philosophers like Plato as well as to savages. It is only when the notion of a soul, from being a quasi-scientific hypothesis, becomes a theological dogma that its unity and indivisibility are insisted upon as essential.

But, further, each Batta believes that he has seven or, on a more moderate computation, three souls. One of these souls is always outside the body, but nevertheless, whenever it dies—however far away it may be at the time—that same moment the man dies also.

William James, The Principles of Psychol.a: James treats pure sensation as an abstraction never realized in adult life. Sensation sets off brain processes shaped by past experience, and the first idea produced is that of the thing, whose consciousness is called perception. Imagination he defines as the faculty of reproducing copies of sensations once felt, reproductive when literal and productive when elements are recombined, and he notes that the blind can dream of sights after losing sight.

q.t: The first of these ideas is that of the thing to which the sensible quality belongs. The consciousness of specific material things present to the senses is nowadays called perception.

Fantasy, or Imagination, are the names given to the faculty of reproducing copies of originals once felt. The imagination is called ‘reproductive’ when the copies are literal; it is ‘productive’ when elements from different originals are recombined to create new wholes.

Codrington, The Melanesians|||Oceanian.a: Codrington reports that Melanesians use their word for soul of something belonging to each person's nature that gives life to the body and is the seat of thought and intelligence. In the Banks Islands the talegi animates the living person, and a ghost can damage or remove it. He notes that the Mota word atai never means shadow, and that in Maewo a professional dreamer sleeps to find the ghost holding a sick man's soul.

q.t: It may suffice to state that, whatever word the Melanesian people use for soul, they mean something essentially belonging to each person's nature which brings life to the body. It is the seat of thought and intelligence, exercising a power that is not of the physical body and is invisible in its action.

Life depends on the presence of the talegi in the body, and health depends upon its healthy condition. A ghost [original: "ghost"; here referring to the spirit of a deceased person.] can damage the talegi, either on its own or moved by magic charms, and then the man falls sick and his body is weak.

The dreamer sleeps and, in his dream, goes to the place where the sick man had been working. There, he is likely to meet someone resembling a small old man who is actually a ghost, and he learns the ghost's name.

Hudson, The Law of Psychic Phenomena|||M.a: Hudson holds that the subjective mind stays awake and active while the body sleeps. It accepts peripheral impressions as suggestions and draws logical conclusions from them, which he gives as the source of absurd dreams. He says its memory is perfect, that the objective mind only recollects, and that memory of hypnotic sleep varies inversely with its depth.

k.g: the communication of thoughts between minds without using physical senses
the process by which the subjective mind accepts and acts upon an idea

q.t: In fact, there are many similarities between the phenomena of normal sleep and those of hypnotism. For instance, it is well known that the memory of what occurred during hypnotic sleep is exactly inversely proportional to the depth of the sleep.

That the medium relates incidents of the sitter’s life which he had forgotten until reminded of them is not at all strange or unaccountable, when we remember that the memory of the subconscious mind is perfect.

In the meantime, it is appropriate to mention here that subjective memory appears to be the only type of memory that truly deserves that name; it is the only memory that is absolute. By comparison, the memory of the objective mind is more accurately described as "recollection."

Leadbeater, The Astral Plane / Clairvoya.a: Leadbeater describes the human being as having astral and mental bodies that serve as vehicles for the soul or ego. He says consciousness can be focused in these vehicles by training, and that most cultured people use their astral faculties little. In The Astral Plane he adds that during sleep the astral vehicle withdraws from the physical body, and the memory of its experiences is often confused.

q.t: The memory of these, which are often hopelessly confused and frequently transformed into a grotesque caricature of what really happened, will cause the man to think next morning what a remarkable dream he has had.

The more cultured and developed among us are beginning to govern desire by reason—that is to say, the center of consciousness is gradually transferring itself from the higher astral to the lower mental. Slowly, as the man progresses, it moves up further still, and the man begins to be dominated by principle rather than by interest and desire.

But in order to do either of these things, he must first learn how they are done; that is to say, he must learn to focus his consciousness in his astral body or in his mental body, just as it is now focused in the physical brain.

Prentiss & Morgan, Anhalonium lewinii (M.a: Prentiss and Morgan report subjects who took mescal buttons and saw colors, figures, landscapes and dances, with closed eyes. One subject kept a clear and active mind, could write notes, and could direct the visions by thinking on chosen subjects. Another saw few visions and described mental exhilaration, a sense of well-being, and thoughts too fast to write down; sleep was impossible for some hours after.

q.t: My mind was perfectly clear and active; the power to concentrate my thoughts upon any desired subject was only slightly lessened; seated at my desk, I could write of my sensations and experiences; stretched out upon the bed, with closed eyes, an ever-changing panorama of infinite beauty and grandeur, of infinite variety of color and form, hurried before me.

The production of visions is the most interesting of the physiological effects of Anhalonium Lewinii, as shown by these experiments. The visions ranged from ill-defined flashes of color to most beautiful figures, forms, landscapes, and dances; in fact, there seemed to be absolutely no limit to the variety of visions which the drug could produce.

He was perfectly happy and experienced a sense of superiority and well-being. He wrote continuously an account of his sensations, but experienced difficulty in writing down his thoughts, so fast did they follow one another.
The Indian messiah religion is the inspiration of a dream. Its ritual is the dance, the ecstasy, and the trance. Its priests are hypnotics and cataleptics.

Like Muhammad and Joan of Arc, and like the Shaker prophet of Puget Sound, Smohalla is subject to cataleptic trances, and it is while in this unconscious condition that he is believed to receive his revelations.

In her trance vision, she fell asleep and seemed (while still in the vision) to be awakened by the noise of a storm. When she looked, she saw the Storm Spirit approaching her, who said to her, "I come, the grandmother from on high."

Vivekananda, Raja Yoga|||Indian.a: Vivekananda describes the mind as working on three planes: one beneath consciousness, one accompanied by the feeling of egoism, and one above consciousness. He holds that instinct, reason and super-consciousness belong to one and the same mind. He treats Chitta as mind-stuff whose waves are called Vṛtti, names memory Smṛti, and calls the mind an instrument in the hands of the soul.

q.t: When the mind goes beyond this line of self-consciousness, it is called Samādhi, or super-consciousness. It is above consciousness.
When the peculiar kind of ripple called sleep throws the Chitta into a ripple of memory, it is called a dream. A dream is another form of the ripple which is called memory in the waking state.
Naturally, we see that the mind is not intelligent by itself; yet it appears to be intelligent. Why? Because the intelligent soul is behind it.

Paul Deussen, Philosophy of the Upanisha.a: Deussen sets out Shankara's account of the soul with ten indriya, five of perception and five of action, governed by the manas. The manas serves as understanding and as conscious will. In dreaming the manas stays active and the soul sees pictures built from waking impressions; in deep sleep the soul enters Brahman.

q.t: These are the indriya, the senses, which the soul puts forth as tentacles during life and at death draws back into itself. Upon these depend the two sides of conscious life, perception and action.

There are four states of the migratory soul: waking, dreaming, a state of deep sleep, and death. In the waking state, the soul, which in union with the manas dwells in the heart, rules the whole body, perceiving and acting through the medium of the manas and the indriya.
This self cannot be demonstrated because it is the presupposition of every demonstration; but also it cannot be disproved because even the denial implies an affirmation of it.
When a man or woman dies and the body is buried, there remains the spirit part called the Ulthana. This is practically the equivalent of the dead person's ghost.
If a woman conceives a child after being near this gap, it is believed that one of these spirit individuals has entered her body.

This usually means one of two things: either he had a dream in which he saw the ceremony performed—which is as real to him as an event in waking life—or he is more creative and inventive than his peers.

k.g: hosts; the wandering spectral host of the unforgiven dead

Husserl, Logische Untersuchungen (with I.a: Husserl lists perceptions, fantasy- and image-representations, conceptual thinking, doubts, joys, pains, hopes, fears, wishes and volitions as experiences or contents of consciousness. He separates inner perception, meaning perception of one's own experiences, from adequate (evident) perception, in which the object is corporeally present in the perceiving itself. He also states that a perception can never be the imagination of what is perceived, and an imagination can never be the perception of what is imagined.

k.g: acts that present an object to consciousness, such as perception or judgment
the content or object-sense of an act
the state of self-givenness or certainty

q.t: In this sense, perceptions, fantasy- and image-representations, acts of conceptual thinking, conjectures and doubts, joys and pains, hopes and fears, wishes and volitions, etc., as they take place in our consciousness, are experiences or contents of consciousness.

Every perception is characterized by the intention to grasp its object as self-present, as it is, existing, and intended. The perception corresponds to this intention; it is adequate when the object is truly "there" as what it is, corporeally present, therefore present in the perceiving itself and one with it.
A perception can never be the imagination of what is perceived, and an imagination can never be the perception of what is imagined.

k.g: a chronic, deteriorating psychotic disorder often characterized by rapid cognitive decline

Podmore, Modern Spiritualism: A History.a: Podmore reports Myers's comparison of workday consciousness to the visible spectrum and to a newspaper, with deeper activities surfacing in sleep or trance. He describes sleep, hypnosis and related states as a dissociation of consciousness, in which part of activity proceeds without the control of the central personality. The German somnambules taught that man is body, soul and spirit, with the soul clothed after death by an ethereal Nervengeist.

k.g: a person in a trance or sleepwalking state

q.t: To adopt his own simile, our workday consciousness may be compared to the visible spectrum: it is but a fraction, and a seemingly accidental fraction, of a larger whole.

The common characteristic of all these states is a division or "dissociation" of consciousness. While in ordinary waking life all our activities are consciously and deliberately subordinated to a common purpose, in these conditions of psychic instability, a part—or sometimes the whole—of our activity proceeds without the control, and occasionally without the knowledge, of the central personality.
The central point of these teachings is that man consists of body, soul, and spirit, the two latter surviving death and forming the spiritual man.

As our mental fields succeed one another, each has its center of interest, around which the objects of which we are less and less attentively conscious fade to a margin so faint that its limits cannot be assigned. Some fields are narrow and some are wide.
Our senses, namely, have assured us of certain states of fact; but mystical experiences are as direct perceptions of fact for those who have them as any sensations ever were for us.

Insane conditions have this advantage, that they isolate special factors of the mental life, and enable us to inspect them unmasked by their more usual surroundings. They play the part in mental anatomy which the scalpel and the microscope play in the anatomy of the body.

Myers, Human Personality and Its Surviva.a: Myers defines sleep psychologically as the suspension of waking consciousness and proposes viewing it as a secondary personality, in which the suspension of the supraliminal life may be the liberation of the subliminal. He lists powers that sleep sometimes enhances, such as muscular control in somnambulism and visualization in hypnagogic illusions. He defines any act or condition as conscious if it is potentially memorable, and describes dreams as dramatic, with a conversation partner who represents another part of the dreamer.

q.t: From a psychological perspective, sleep is the suspension of waking consciousness. But this is only a negative definition. We must seek its positive characteristics, viewing it as a secondary personality.

This being so, I cannot see how we can phrase our definition more simply than by saying that any act or condition must be regarded as conscious if it is potentially memorable—if it can be recollected, under any circumstances, by the subject concerned.

Waking life involves focusing attention on a single thread of thought within a tangled mess of ideas. In patients with hysteria, we see some cases where such focus is impossible, and other cases where the focus is involuntary or follows a path that is not desirable to pursue.

Steiner, Wie erlangt man Erkenntnisse de.a: Steiner says the ego reveals its nature in the self-conscious soul, through an inner activity he calls self-recollection. He names the sentient soul, joined to the astral body, and the intellectual soul, where the ego works with what it has gained from perception. Ordinary life passes between waking, sleeping and dreaming, and the soul loses consciousness in sleep. A third soul-state is what gives cognizance of higher worlds.

q.t: The real nature of the ego is first revealed in the self-conscious soul. Through feeling and reason, the soul loses itself in other things, but as the self-conscious soul, it lays hold of its own essence.

The ego rises to a higher stage of its being when it centers its activity on what it has gained for itself out of its knowledge of objective things. It is by means of this activity that the ego detaches itself more and more from the objects of perception, in order to work within that which is its own possession.

Cognizance of higher worlds is obtained by man when, in addition to sleeping and waking, he attains to yet a third soul-state. While awake, the soul is given up, as it were, to the impressions of the senses and to such concepts as are excited by sense-impressions.

Macdonald, The Religious Attitude and Li.a: Macdonald's passages describe the rational soul as perceiving in two ways: through the five external senses and through the internal powers of the brain, both working by means of the animal spirit. In sleep the animal spirit withdraws from the external senses to the internal sense, and the soul returns to the forms stored in memory. The imagination clothes ideas received by the soul in images from memory, and the text says the soul's own form is perception and rational thought, complete only through joining the body.

q.t: We have already stated that perception by the rational soul is of two kinds: perception through external means—namely, the five senses—and perception through internal means—namely, the powers of the brain.

Thus, it brings them back to the body through its apparatus of internal senses. Then the imagination takes these ideas and clothes them in images from the stores of memory that are suited to represent them.

The form of the soul, by which its existence is complete, is perception itself and rational thought. It exists, in the first instance, in potentiality—equipped to perceive and receive forms, both universal and particular.

It is realized that man is mind first and body afterward; that the diligent study of psychology is almost more necessary than that of physiology to secure a mens sana in corpore sano [a healthy mind in a healthy body].

The greater (God) responds to the cry for help of the lesser (the soul), because the lesser and the greater (the human soul and the divine soul) are all equally compacted of the same Essence, the One Spirit. The Universal Spirit discloses Itself to be the individual jīva [The individual soul or living being.] as soon as the latter turns to it, because the two are one and the same.
He gives up all sense of separateness together with his worn-out body, and realizes that "I am the Changeless Universal Consciousness, in which all change appears as a dream."

In our present state of consciousness we may enter a dream state, in that dream state by dreaming we enter a second dream state, and theoretically, though not by common experience, there may be no limit to super-imposed dream states, each one in itself a state of consciousness distinct from the waking consciousness.

In the waking state this censor is always on the alert to keep out of consciousness all subconscious processes or deposits, but in sleep the censor is less alert, and allows some subconscious content to escape over into the ordinary consciousness. The result is a dream distorted out of all recognition of its origin.

How many of us can recall without some mental stimulus certain acts performed ten years ago? A good deal of our present life is no longer vivid, much of it is forgotten, and in old age many of the memories of youth and of mature life will be subconscious.

The latter form of thinking, provided it is not constantly corrected by adapted thinking, must necessarily produce a predominantly subjectively distorted view of the world. We designate this state of mind as infantile. It lies in our individual past and in the past of humanity.

The conclusion—that the era which created myths thought in a childlike, i.e., fantastic manner, just as the dream still does today to the highest degree (associatively or analogically)—follows almost of its own accord.
Dream thinking moves in a backward manner toward the raw material of memory. "The structure of the dream thoughts is dissolved during the process of regression into its raw material."

Junod, The Life of a South African Tribe.a: Junod reports that the Thonga name the soul moya (spirit), hika (breath) among the Ronga, and ntjhuti or shitjhuti (shadow). Breath is the vital principle, and relatives wait for its departure at death. The shadow separates from the body at death and continues as a god, the shikwembu, and Junod records that Thonga ideas on the subject are not dogmatic. The Thonga generally dislike dreams, and magicians claim to bring back a stolen spirit to a sick person.

q.t: They call it moya (the spirit), and in the Ronga clans, hika (the breath). The plural form mahika, in the expression ku ba ni mahika, means "to be out of breath." This is the vital principle of man, and when someone is dying, his relatives sit near him "waiting for the departure of breath" [original: "langusela ku suka ka hika"].
Finally, the definitive separation of the soul [original: "unsheathing of personality"] takes place at death. The body decays, but the shadow departs and continues its life as a god, or shikwembu.

Ouspensky, Tertium Organum|||Theosophica.a: Ouspensky distinguishes consciousness from thought, feeling and sensation, and calls it a background on which these appear, more or less bright, with definable forms or phases. He defines sensation as an elementary change in the state of the mind, and says sensations leave traces in memory that group by similarity. He writes that animals are conscious through sensations and emotions, with intellect only embryonic, while in man the growth of consciousness is the growth of intellect together with the higher emotions.

q.t: Thus, consciousness (whether it is this or something else) is a background upon which thoughts, feelings, and sensations reveal themselves. This background can be more or less bright.

The sensations we feel leave a certain trace in our memory. The accumulating memories of sensations begin to blend in consciousness into groups; according to their similarity, they tend to associate, to sum up, or to be contrasted.
The animal is conscious through its sensations and emotions. The intellect is present in the animal only in an embryonic state, as an emotion of curiosity, a pleasure of knowing.

Nukariya, The Religion of the Samurai (r.a: Nukariya writes that Zen teaches there is no soul, and that body and mind are each a temporary form of life. He describes the body as the mind observed outwardly through the senses and the mind as the body experienced inwardly through introspection. He names Enlightened Consciousness as the center of spiritual life, the mind of minds, and describes the Real Self as a mutable, ever-changing life existing as the union of body and mind.

q.t: Thus, the body is the mind observed outwardly in its relation to the senses; the mind is the body experienced inwardly in its relation to introspection.
Enlightened Consciousness is, according to Zen, the center of spiritual life. It is the mind of minds, and the consciousness of consciousness. It is the Universal Spirit awakened in the human mind.
The Self is a living entity, not immutable like a soul, but a mutable and ever-changing life, which is body when observed by the senses, and which is mind when experienced by introspection.

Of the entire dream-work, Freud says (Traumdeutung, p. 338) comprehensively that it is "not merely more careless, more incorrect, more easily forgotten, or more fragmentary than waking thought; it is something qualitatively quite different and therefore not in the least comparable with it. It does not, in fact, think, calculate, or judge, but limits itself to remodeling.
II. The functional category is characterized by the fact that the condition, structure, or capacity for work of the individual consciousness (or the psychic apparatus) is itself portrayed.
The dreamer thus approaches his own childhood, just as he approaches the childhood of the human race, by reaching back for a more primitive perceptual mode of thought.

Densmore, Teton Sioux Music|||Native Ame.a: Densmore records that the Sioux sought dreams and treated their obligations as binding, as a vow was. Dreams were announced to the tribe, and a dream from a supernatural source could lead the dreamer into the treatment of the sick. Medicine-men are said to receive their power through dreams at night. Fasting visions of the same animal formed the basis of dream societies.

q.t: Dreams were sought by the Sioux, but it was recognized that a dream would correspond to the character of the man. Thus, it was said that "a young man would not be great in mind, so his dream would not be like that of a chief; it would be ordinary in kind, yet he would still have to do whatever the dream directed him to do."
The owl moves at night when men are asleep. The medicine-man gets his power through dreams at night and believes that his dream is clear, like the owl’s vision.

Societies based on dreams (known as "dream societies") were composed of men who, in their fasting visions, had seen the same animal. The common experience of the vision bound the men together, and societies were thus formed.

Jaspers, Psychologie der Weltanschauunge.a: Jaspers describes self-reflected attitudes, in which consciousness turns back on the soul and makes the I, self, or personality an object. He says the self is never fully seen, and that we mistake schemata of the self for the real self. He also reports earlier accounts of the faculties, including Spinoza's three types of knowledge, Kant's sensibility, intellect, and reason, and Kierkegaard's account of self-becoming.

q.t: It is a primal phenomenon [original: "Urphänomen"] of our soul that after the direction of consciousness toward the world of extra-conscious objects, a reversal of direction toward the soul itself occurs, as it were. Following consciousness, there is self-consciousness.

In the first type (opinion or representation), individual things are presented through the senses in a confused, mutilated, and unordered way, or we remember such individual things upon hearing or reading words. In the second type (reason), common notions and adequate ideas of the properties of things are formed.
Self-consciousness is, as the word says, consciousness. It is formed in reflection. "The more consciousness, the more self" [3)].

Anthropology of jinn, possession and sai.a: The Moroccan accounts treat dreams as a source of knowledge about the future. Interpretations follow the laws of association by similarity or contrast, and a prayer rite called istihâra, or sleeping at a saint's shrine, is used to seek answers in sleep. Šîṭan sends false dreams, especially to those who omit the evening prayer, and causes nocturnal pollution by making the sleeper believe the dream woman is real.

q.t: This practice is called the stihâra or, in the literary language, istihâra. The same name is given to the practice of sleeping at the shrine of a saint or in a sacred cave to receive during sleep answers to a pressing question.

It is reasonable to suppose that the interpretation of a dream is sometimes based on experience, a sequence of facts being taken for a causal connection or a foreshadowing. Yet there can be no doubt that in the vast majority of cases the dicta of oneiromancy dream divination are a priori in nature, being applications of the laws of association either by similarity or contrast.
Satan makes himself unpleasant to men in many ways. He inflames them with anger and inspires them with fear. He deceives them with false dreams.

k.g: the soul; the inner personality of a man
the totality of all psychic processes, conscious and unconscious
Jung’s term for the part of the mind containing memories and impulses common to all humankind, from which universal symbols and myths arise

q.t: Thinking is that psychological function which, in accordance with its own laws, brings given presentations into conceptual connection. It is an apperceptive [the process of understanding something perceived in terms of previous experience] activity and, as such, must be differentiated into active and passive thought-activity.
Primarily, therefore, sensation is sense-perception: perception transmitted via the sense organs and "bodily senses" (kinesthetic, vasomotor sensation, etc.).
We define the soul, on the one hand, as the relationship to the unconscious, but on the other hand also as a personification of unconscious contents.

Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (angakkoq n.a: In these tales the wizard calls on helping spirits and travels to the underworld while his body stays where it is. In the Kúnigseq story the helping spirit warns him not to eat the berries offered there, or he will never return. Another wizard calls down a magic sleep on a household, and the people fall asleep one by one.

k.g: a trance state where the shaman's soul leaves the body to travel to the spirit realm

q.t: And now the wizard began calling down a magic sleep upon those in the hut, and one by one they sank to sleep and began to snore.
Ushtâna, which refers to animal life, sustains the body. This animal life is maintained by the five senses. A moderate use of all five senses is good for maintaining life.

If it is the soul of a wicked person, it remains within the boundaries [original: "precincts"] of this world for three nights, remembering all the wickedness of its past life and feeling lost about where to go.

The first three nights must be, so to speak, nights of "vigils"—meaning that when the candidate sleeps, he must remain in a watchful or wakeful state of mind so as not to let his sleep be disturbed by worldly thoughts.

Surendranath Dasgupta, History of Indian.a: Dasgupta describes the Sāṃkhya-Yoga view that the intellect (buddhi, or citta) constantly changes and is made of sattva. Its mental images become conscious through a dual reflection between intellect and soul (puruṣa), which must be assumed to explain the light of consciousness. Sleep is defined as a mental state whose substratum is a feeling of emptiness, recalled on waking. Memory retains perceptions as saṃskāras, and appears in dreams as well as waking states.

q.t: We must assume the existence of the soul ( puruṣa ) to explain the light of consciousness, as well as to explain human experience and moral effort.

When a cognition is produced, it is produced only as an objective cognition—for example, "This is a pot." However, after this, it is again related to the self by the mind as "I know this pot." This is achieved by the mind coming into contact once more to reperceive the knowledge that had already been generated in the soul.

Sleep is that mental state which has for its objective substratum the feeling of emptiness. It is called a state or notion of mind, for it is recalled upon awakening; when we feel that we have slept well, our minds are clear; when we have slept badly, our minds are listless, wandering, and unsteady.

Freud, Eine Teufelsneurose im siebzehnte.a: Freud treats the painter's pact with the Devil as a neurosis and reads its details through unconscious mental activity (unbewußte Geistestätigkeit). He says the unconscious handles numbers as dreams do, keeping the number while changing its denominator by Verdichtung and Verschiebung. He describes the neurosis as a buildup of libido (Libidostauung) that finds an outlet through the repressed unconscious by regression to old fixations, and he names a longing for the father (Vatersehnsucht) as its source.

q.t: We know from dreams how "unconscious mental activity" unbewußte Geistestätigkeit [the hidden processes of the mind that function outside of our conscious awareness] handles numbers. If we encounter a five in a dream, for example, it can always be traced back to a significant five in waking life;
A buildup of libido [original: "Libidostauung"] that cannot be satisfied in reality finds an outlet through the repressed unconscious with the help of regression to old fixations.

Rattray, Ashanti|||African.a: Rattray describes the person in terms of spiritual elements such as the sunsum, linked here to a child's personality and strength, and the ntoro, a spirit inherited from the father. The pages also mention the saman, the ghost of a dead person, and the sasa, a vengeful spirit. Most of the pages shown concern chiefs, law and family custom.

q.t: Sometimes a child who does not have a strong sunsum spirit or personality will die after such ridicule.

Very briefly, the ntoro is the male totemic spirit [a spirit associated with a specific animal or natural element inherited through the male line] which every child, male or female, inherits from its father.

George Grimm, The Doctrine of the Buddha.a: Grimm presents the Buddha's argument that none of the senses, forms, contacts, sensations, thirst, thinking or consciousness is the I, because each is seen to originate and perish. A further passage lists corporeal form, sensation, perception, the activities of the mind and consciousness as transitory, painful and not the Ego. He also states that six kinds of consciousness, from eye-consciousness to mental consciousness, each arise in dependence on a sense organ and its object.

q.t: We perceive the originating and perishing of thirst. But if originating and perishing are perceived, the result would be: ‘My I originates and perishes.’ Therefore it is inadmissible to assert thirst to be the I.

He does not consider sensation... perception... the activities of the mind... consciousness as the Ego, nor the Ego as consisting in them, nor themselves as comprised in the Ego, nor the Ego as comprised in them.
Through the eye—which is just the activity of the eye directed towards seeing—and forms consciousness arises: 'visual consciousness' accordingly is the term applied.

Th. Stcherbatsky, The Conception of Budd.a: Stcherbatsky's passages state that consciousness cannot apprehend itself, using the images of a sword that cannot cut its own edge and a fingertip that cannot touch itself. If the support of mind were other than mind there would be two minds, and if it were mind itself, mind could not observe mind. A Nyāya-Vaiśesika account describes the soul as an all-pervading substance in which consciousness is only an occasional quality, absent in Nirvāna.

q.t: Consciousness cannot apprehend its own self. The trenchancy of a sword cannot cut its own trenchancy. The tip of a finger cannot touch that very tip.

By the power of absorption the internal organ is kept back from all contact with the soul and the senses. No consciousness is then produced, all life is annihilated but the substance of the soul reverts in Nirvāna to its original and natural condition ( svarūpāvasthā the state of abiding in one's own nature ).
The mind does not observe the mind. Just as a blade of a sword cannot cut itself, and the tip of a finger cannot touch the same tip of the finger, in the same way, the mind cannot see the mind.

Klüver, Mescal: The 'Divine' Plant and I.a: Klüver reports on the mescal state through subjects' records, with attention to visual perception, synesthesia, dreams and changes in thinking. He describes lost spontaneity, loss of the ability to organize and abstract, and a narrowing of consciousness. He also notes euphoria and a "thought intoxication" that may prove productive, and proposes mescal as a tool for studying perception.

q.t: Thus, for Beringer, the three main constituents of the mescal psychosis are: 1, abnormal sensory phenomena; 2, a fundamental change in conscious states and attitudes; 3, abnormal emotional states.
The ability to organize and to abstract material is lost; the determining tendencies suffer. To concentrate on something for a long while becomes impossible.
Thus, consciousness is narrowed down to the experience of sensory and imaginal details.

Cassirer, Philosophie der symbolischen F.a: Cassirer, discussing Kant, says perception cannot be a merely sensory consciousness, since the transcendental unity of apperception conditions every possible perception, and imagination has its own spontaneity. Discussing Leibniz, he describes the ego as reaching toward the future, so consciousness exists by reaching beyond the given present. Discussing Bergson, he separates motor memory, a form of habit, from spiritual memory, in which the I looks back into time and finds itself.

k.g: the tendency or drive toward perception
perception through the lens of expression

q.t: And it now becomes evident that, just as there is a spontaneity of pure understanding, of logical-scientific thinking and constructing, there is also a spontaneity of pure imagination. It, too, is by no means merely reproductive, but originally productive.

There is a purely motor memory, which consists in nothing other than a sequence of practiced movements and which is thus merely a form of habit. But from this type of movement-memory, of mechanism and automatism, the true spiritual memory is strictly and fundamentally separated.
Both are inseparably connected: for consciousness exists only because it does not persist within itself, but constantly reaches out beyond itself, beyond the given present, to the non-given.
